ELA.overview: English 10 runs about 60 minutes a day: read (often aloud together), annotate, discuss, and write — with a major written product every unit. Read each text before your student does; ask the text-dependent questions below and always require the student to point to the line that proves the answer. Grade writing with the rubrics in each week's key, conference about one or two goals at a time, and save the Week 1 baseline for comparison at semester and year end.

weeks.prep: Print or bookmark 'The Most Dangerous Game' (CommonLit), set up a reading journal (composition book or doc), sticky notes. Read the story yourself first (about 30 minutes). Parent preview: the story involves a hunter who hunts people; violence is mostly implied.
misconceptions: Students write summaries that include opinions ('This exciting story...'). Model an objective summary: who, what, where, how it ends — no judgments.
Confusing foreshadowing with any description. Foreshadowing is a detail that hints at a later event (e.g., the island's sinister name).
weeks.assessment_key: Objective summary (model content): Big-game hunter Sanger Rainsford falls off a yacht near Ship-Trap Island and swims ashore. He finds the chateau of General Zaroff, a Russian aristocrat who, bored with hunting animals, hunts shipwrecked men. Rainsford refuses to join him and is forced to become the prey for three days. He uses traps (a Malay man-catcher, a Burmese tiger pit, a Ugandan knife trap) that injure Zaroff, kill a hound and kill Zaroff's servant Ivan, then leaps into the sea. That night he surprises Zaroff in his bedroom; they fight, and Rainsford sleeps in Zaroff's bed, implying Zaroff is dead. Score with: Rubric (4-point): 4 = accurate, complete, objective (no opinion or 'I'), in the student's own words, key events in order; 3 = one minor inaccuracy or stray opinion; 2 = missing major events or retells too much detail; 1 = inaccurate or mostly opinion. Plot diagram: full credit for a quotation at each stage — exposition (yacht/Whitney conversation), rising action (Zaroff's offer; the hunt), climax (bedroom confrontation), falling action/resolution ('He had never slept in a better bed, Rainsford decided.').

days.guide: Walk through the reading survey together and help set up the journal (sections for vocabulary, quotes, responses). The student writes a one-page reader autobiography; save it unmarked as the baseline writing sample for comparison in Weeks 18 and 35.

questions.q: What should a reader autobiography include?
questions.a: Memorable books and when they were read, reading habits, strengths and struggles as a reader and writer, and a goal for this year.

days.guide: Read the opening conversation aloud together, pausing to model one annotation ('Ship-Trap — a name that warns of a trap'). The student reads to the midpoint (Zaroff's explanation of his hunting) and marks every foreshadowing clue.

questions.q: What does Whitney say about Ship-Trap Island, and why is it foreshadowing?
questions.a: He says sailors have a curious dread of the place and it has an evil name; it hints that something dangerous awaits on the island.

questions.q: Early on Rainsford says the world is made up of 'two classes—the hunters and the huntees.' How does this line foreshadow the plot?
questions.a: Rainsford, a hunter, is soon forced to become the hunted, testing his own belief.

days.guide: Review the plot diagram stages. The student finishes the story and places one quoted sentence at each stage; check that the climax is the final bedroom confrontation rather than the leap into the sea.

questions.q: Which traps does Rainsford build, and what does each do?
questions.a: A Malay man-catcher (injures Zaroff's shoulder), a Burmese tiger pit (kills one of the hounds), and a Ugandan knife trap (kills Ivan).

questions.q: What does the final line, 'He had never slept in a better bed,' tell the reader?
questions.a: That Rainsford won the fight and Zaroff is dead — the outcome is implied, not stated.

days.guide: Teach the three phrase types with one example each (prepositional: 'on the island'; participial: 'Gripping the rail, he...'; appositive: 'Zaroff, a Cossack aristocrat, ...'). The student labels ten sentences, then writes five sentences starting with participial phrases.

questions.q: Label the phrase: 'Bracing himself, Rainsford waited.'
questions.a: 'Bracing himself' is a participial phrase modifying Rainsford.

questions.q: Label the phrase in 'Ivan, a giant of a man, carried a revolver.'
questions.a: 'a giant of a man' is an appositive phrase renaming Ivan.

days.guide: The student writes the 150-word objective summary, then discusses whether Rainsford is changed, citing two lines. Score the summary with the assessment key. Close by asking the question(s) below; the student answers aloud and points to the exact line in the text (or their own draft) that supports the answer.

questions.q: Is Rainsford changed by the end? Give one piece of evidence.
questions.a: Model answer: Yes — at the start he says 'Who cares how a jaguar feels?' but while hunted he realizes he 'knew now how an animal at bay feels.' Yet he ends by killing Zaroff and sleeping in his bed, so readers can argue he has also become a hunter of men.

weeks.prep: Print 'The Cask of Amontillado' (Project Gutenberg) and get highlighters. Read it once yourself. Parent preview: the narrator walls up a man alive; no graphic gore.
misconceptions: Confusing verbal irony (saying the opposite of what one means) with dramatic irony (the audience knows something a character doesn't). Many moments in the story are both — have the student label who knows what.
Dropping quotes into a paragraph without introducing them ('plop quotes'). Teach the lead-in: speaker + context + quote.
weeks.assessment_key: Irony quiz (answers): 1) Fortunato's name means 'fortunate' — situational irony, since he is doomed. 2) 'I shall not die of a cough.' / 'True—true' — dramatic/verbal irony; Montresor knows he will die another way. 3) 'I drink to your long life' — verbal irony. 4) Montresor shows a trowel when Fortunato asks if he is a mason — verbal/dramatic irony (a stonemason's tool). 5) Point of view → first person, Montresor, a possibly unreliable narrator. Paragraph rubric: 4 = clear claim on reliability; two accurate quotes, each introduced (e.g., his unexplained 'thousand injuries'; 'My heart grew sick—on account of the dampness of the catacombs'); analysis explains how the quote proves the claim; 3 = good claim, thin analysis; 2 = evidence summarized not quoted; 1 = no claim.

days.guide: Read the story aloud together (about 25 minutes); the student takes Montresor's lines. Pause after each of Montresor's lines to Fortunato and ask, 'Does he mean that?' The student highlights verbal irony.

questions.q: What does Montresor say is his motive at the start, and what is missing?
questions.a: He says Fortunato caused him 'a thousand injuries' and then an insult, but he never says what the insult was, so readers can't judge his claim.

questions.q: What does 'I must not only punish, but punish with impunity' mean?
questions.a: He wants revenge without being caught or punished himself.

days.guide: Model one row of the chart ('I drink to your long life' / a toast / he plans to kill him). The student completes six rows, labeling each verbal or dramatic.

questions.q: Explain the irony when Montresor produces a trowel to prove he is a mason.
questions.a: Fortunato means the secret society of Freemasons; Montresor means a literal bricklayer — he is about to wall Fortunato in (verbal and dramatic irony).

questions.q: Why is the Montresor family motto 'Nemo me impune lacessit' ironic?
questions.a: It means 'No one attacks me with impunity' — it announces revenge, but Fortunato doesn't understand the warning.

days.guide: Introduce each root with its meaning (ven- come, mort- death, cred- believe, jur- swear/law) and the story words impunity (without punishment), immolation (sacrifice), retribution (payback). The student builds a 12-word web and uses three words in sentences.

questions.q: Give two words from the root cred- and their meanings.
questions.a: Credible (believable), incredulous (unwilling to believe), credit (belief/trust).

questions.q: What does 'retribution' mean, and how does it fit the story?
questions.a: Punishment given in return for a wrong; Montresor seeks retribution for the insult.

days.guide: Teach TIQA with a model paragraph. The student writes a paragraph answering whether Montresor is reliable, using two introduced quotes and analysis that is longer than the quotes. Close by asking the question(s) below; the student answers aloud and points to the exact line in the text (or their own draft) that supports the answer.

questions.q: Give one piece of evidence that Montresor may be unreliable.
questions.a: His heart 'grew sick—on account of the dampness of the catacombs' — he blames the damp for what may be guilt; or he never explains the insult; or he tells the story fifty years later.

days.guide: Give the five-item irony and point-of-view quiz from the assessment key (about 15 minutes) and go over it together. Then return the TIQA paragraph with one comment on each quote; the student rewrites each quote with a lead-in that names the speaker and situation (e.g., As Montresor leads Fortunato deeper, he insists, '...').

questions.q: How long ago did the murder take place, according to the ending?
questions.a: Half a century — 'For the half of a century no mortal has disturbed them.'

weeks.prep: Print 'An Occurrence at Owl Creek Bridge' (Bierce) and 'The Necklace' (Maupassant) from Gutenberg. Find the 1961 short film by Robert Enrico (often shown as a Twilight Zone episode; check library streaming). Parent preview: Owl Creek depicts an execution by hanging; the film shows the hanging at the end.
misconceptions: Missing that Part III of Owl Creek is imagined. Point to the clues: unnaturally sharp senses, strange stars, the endless road, the pain in his neck.
Reading 'The Necklace' as simply 'don't lie.' Push to the deeper theme of class aspiration and appearances.
weeks.assessment_key: Comparison response rubric: 4 = explains specific planted clues in both stories (Owl Creek: time slowing, ticking watch, hyper-sharp senses, unfamiliar stars, swollen neck; The Necklace: Madame Forestier's easy offer, her not opening the case on return, Mathilde's focus on appearances) and how structure (Bierce's nonlinear sections; Maupassant's chronological ten years) makes the twist earned; 3 = clues identified with partial analysis; 2 = summary of endings; 1 = off-topic. Discussion checklist: prepared 3 open questions; cited text at least twice; responded to others; invited another speaker.

days.guide: Explain the three-part structure before reading. The student marks where time slows (the ticking watch), jumps back (Part II flashback), and the long escape, and sketches a real-time vs. imagined-time timeline.

questions.q: How did Peyton Farquhar end up on the bridge?
questions.a: A Federal scout disguised as a Confederate soldier told him about the bridge, and he was caught trying to burn it.

questions.q: What actually happens to Farquhar at the end?
questions.a: He is hanged; his body swings beneath the bridge. The escape was imagined in the moment before death.

days.guide: Watch the film (about 25 minutes). The student lists three director choices different from Bierce. Close by asking the question(s) below; the student answers aloud and points to the exact line in the text (or their own draft) that supports the answer.

questions.q: Name one major difference between the 1961 film and the story.
questions.a: The film leaves out Part II's backstory about the scout (and uses almost no dialogue, adding a song during the escape).

days.guide: Briefly explain class in 19th-century France (clerks vs. wealthy society). The student reads 'The Necklace' and annotates details about status that drive Mathilde. Close by asking the question(s) below; the student answers aloud and points to the exact line in the text (or their own draft) that supports the answer.

questions.q: Why does Mathilde borrow the necklace?
questions.a: She feels ashamed to go to the ball without jewels and wants to look rich among wealthy guests.

questions.q: What is the twist at the end?
questions.a: Madame Forestier reveals the necklace was paste (fake), worth at most 500 francs, while the Loisels spent ten years paying off 36,000 francs for a real diamond replacement.

days.guide: First have the student list three clues for each twist in a two-column chart. Then they write the 250-word comparison with a topic sentence that names both authors' techniques, one quote per story, and a closing sentence on which twist is better prepared. Check that the response analyzes structure, not just plot.

questions.q: What clue in 'The Necklace' hints the necklace might not be valuable?
questions.a: Madame Forestier lends it easily, and when it is returned she doesn't even open the case.

days.guide: The student writes three open questions the night before (questions with more than one defensible answer) and marks evidence for each. During the 15-minute discussion they lead, cite the text at least twice and invite others in; you tick the checklist in the assessment key and debrief for two minutes afterward.

questions.q: What does each twist reveal about its main character?
questions.a: Farquhar's romantic dreams of heroism and home; Mathilde's vanity and how appearances cost her years of hardship.

weeks.prep: Writing notebook; have the Unit 1 stories handy as mentor texts. Prepare the Unit 1 test (assessment key). Show the student MLA format on Purdue OWL.
misconceptions: Starting the story with a long description or waking up. In medias res means starting in the middle of action.
Punctuating dialogue incorrectly. Show: "I'm here," she said. — comma inside the quotation marks, new paragraph for each new speaker.
weeks.assessment_key: Narrative rubric (W.9-10.3): 4 = engaging in medias res opening, clear point of view, effective structural device (flashback/twist), sensory detail and pacing that build suspense, correctly punctuated dialogue, satisfying resolution; 3 = most elements with minor lapses; 2 = flat pacing or confusing sequence; 1 = incomplete. Unit 1 test (sample answers): foreshadowing — hints of future events; verbal irony — saying the opposite of what is meant; dramatic irony — audience knows more than a character; situational irony — outcome opposite of what's expected; unreliable narrator — narrator whose account can't be fully trusted (e.g., Montresor); in medias res — beginning in the middle of action; flashback — interrupting to show an earlier event (Owl Creek Part II). Cold read: score short answers 2 points each for a correct claim plus quoted evidence.

days.guide: Brainstorm suspense situations together. The student fills a plot mountain, chooses first or third person, and picks one structural trick. Close by asking the question(s) below; the student answers aloud and points to the exact line in the text (or their own draft) that supports the answer.

questions.q: Which mentor story used in medias res or flashback, and how?
questions.a: 'An Occurrence at Owl Creek Bridge' opens in the middle of the hanging, then flashes back in Part II to explain how Farquhar got there.

days.guide: Read Connell's opening for its sensory details. The student drafts the opening scene in medias res with three sensory details and one foreshadowing clue; underline each. Close by asking the question(s) below; the student answers aloud and points to the exact line in the text (or their own draft) that supports the answer.

questions.q: What makes an opening 'in medias res'?
questions.a: It drops the reader into action already happening, with background filled in later.

days.guide: Show how Connell's sentences shorten during the chase. The student finishes the draft and writes a climax with short, punchy sentences. Close by asking the question(s) below; the student answers aloud and points to the exact line in the text (or their own draft) that supports the answer.

questions.q: Why do short sentences speed up pacing?
questions.a: They are read quickly, mimicking rapid action and rising heartbeat.

days.guide: Read the checklist together: dialogue punctuation, varied sentence openers, show-don't-tell. The student revises with a colored pen, then reads the whole story aloud to you while you note any spot where you got confused or lost interest; they fix those spots before typing.

questions.q: Correct the punctuation: "Run she shouted".
questions.a: "Run!" she shouted.

days.guide: The student formats the final story in MLA style (header, title, double spacing, 12-pt font) and submits it. Then give the Unit 1 test (about 40 minutes): terms section plus a short cold-read passage with written answers that must quote the text.

questions.q: What is the difference between dramatic and situational irony?
questions.a: Dramatic irony: the audience knows something a character doesn't. Situational irony: what happens is the opposite of what's expected.

weeks.prep: Get a translation of Antigone (the Fitts and Fitzgerald translation uses Prologue/Parodos/Scene/Ode/Exodos labels). Find a short video on Greek theater (e.g., TED-Ed or Crash Course Theater). Parent preview: the play includes suicides offstage.
misconceptions: Thinking the Chorus is a narrator. It is a group of Theban elders who comment, react and represent community values.
Mixing up family members. Keep the family tree visible all unit.
weeks.assessment_key: Reading quiz (answers): 1) What has Creon decreed? → Eteocles is buried with honor; Polyneices must lie unburied, and anyone who buries him will be put to death. 2) Why do the brothers die? → They killed each other fighting over Thebes (Polyneices attacked with an Argive army). 3) Why does Ismene refuse to help? → She fears death and says they are women who cannot defy the state. 4) Creon's main idea in his first speech → loyalty to the state comes before loyalty to friends or family. 5) What does the Sentry report? → Someone has sprinkled dust on Polyneices' body. Values chart: full credit for three cited lines each showing Antigone values divine law/family duty/honor and Ismene values safety/obedience/caution.

days.guide: Watch a 5–10 minute video on Greek theater together (TED-Ed or Crash Course Theater). The student takes Cornell notes — questions on the left, notes on the right, summary at the bottom — covering masks, chorus, the Dionysia festival and Aristotle's elements of tragedy; quiz each other on the terms at the end.

questions.q: Define hamartia and catharsis.
questions.a: Hamartia is the tragic hero's error or flaw; catharsis is the release of pity and fear the audience feels.

questions.q: What role did the chorus play in Greek tragedy?
questions.a: A group that sang and danced between scenes, commenting on action and voicing community views.

days.guide: Read a one-page summary of the Oedipus myth together (Oedipus unknowingly kills his father and marries his mother, Jocasta). The student builds a family tree that includes Creon as Jocasta's brother and the four children, then explains aloud how the curse on the family leads into Antigone.

questions.q: How are Antigone and Creon related?
questions.a: Creon is Antigone's uncle — brother of her mother, Jocasta.

questions.q: Who are Antigone's siblings?
questions.a: Ismene, Polyneices and Eteocles.

days.guide: Read the Prologue aloud, parent as Ismene. The student charts differences in values with three lines each. Close by asking the question(s) below; the student answers aloud and points to the exact line in the text (or their own draft) that supports the answer.

questions.q: What does Antigone ask Ismene to do, and how does Ismene respond?
questions.a: To help bury Polyneices; Ismene refuses, saying they are women and cannot defy the king's law.

days.guide: Read the Parodos and Scene 1. The student paraphrases Creon's speech. Close by asking the question(s) below; the student answers aloud and points to the exact line in the text (or their own draft) that supports the answer.

questions.q: Paraphrase Creon's view of loyalty in Scene 1.
questions.a: A ruler and citizen must put the state first; anyone who values a friend above the country is worthless, and enemies of the state (like Polyneices) get no honor.

questions.q: What is the Parodos about?
questions.a: The Chorus celebrates Thebes' victory over the attacking Argive army.

days.guide: Give the reading-check quiz (assessment key). The student writes a journal entry on divine vs. civic law. Close by asking the question(s) below; the student answers aloud and points to the exact line in the text (or their own draft) that supports the answer.

questions.q: Which law does Antigone follow, and which does Creon defend?
questions.a: Antigone follows divine law (the gods' law requiring burial of the dead); Creon defends civic law (his decree for the state).

weeks.prep: Antigone text, character chart from Week 5. Plan to read Scene 2 aloud with the student.
misconceptions: Seeing Creon as purely evil. He has a real argument about order after civil war; his flaw is pride and refusal to listen.
Treating Haemon as only a love interest. His argument is political: the city sympathizes with Antigone.
weeks.assessment_key: Quiz on Scenes 2–3 (answers): 1) How is Antigone caught? → The Sentry's guards catch her returning to the body after it was uncovered. 2) Antigone's defense → Creon's decree is not the gods' law; the unwritten laws of the gods are higher. 3) What does Ismene try to do? → Claim a share of the guilt; Antigone refuses. 4) What is Creon's sentence? → Antigone will be sealed alive in a stone vault/tomb. 5) Haemon's key arguments → the city mourns Antigone; a wise man listens; a ruler who thinks only he is right is empty; trees that bend in a flood survive. 6) Haemon's parting threat → her death will cause another death. Annotation check: full credit for at least 8 labeled rhetorical moves across Scenes 2–3.

days.guide: Read Scene 2 aloud. The student annotates rhetorical moves (appeal to the gods, accusation, insult, appeal to loyalty). Close by asking the question(s) below; the student answers aloud and points to the exact line in the text (or their own draft) that supports the answer.

questions.q: What argument does Antigone make for defying Creon?
questions.a: She says the decree was not made by the gods, and the gods' unwritten, unchanging laws matter more than a mortal king's edict.

questions.q: How does Creon respond to Antigone's defiance?
questions.a: He treats it as a challenge to his authority and pride, saying he won't be ruled by a woman, and condemns her.

days.guide: Explain stichomythia: rapid alternating single lines. Perform the exchange; then the student explains its effect. Close by asking the question(s) below; the student answers aloud and points to the exact line in the text (or their own draft) that supports the answer.

questions.q: How does stichomythia heighten conflict?
questions.a: Quick one-line exchanges feel like a duel — each speaker snaps back, showing neither will yield.

days.guide: Read Ode 2. The student identifies the extended metaphor of the curse as a storm/sea and writes a short paragraph on its effect. Close by asking the question(s) below; the student answers aloud and points to the exact line in the text (or their own draft) that supports the answer.

questions.q: What does the storm imagery in Ode 2 suggest about the curse on Oedipus's house?
questions.a: The curse is like waves of a storm rolling over the family generation after generation — overwhelming and unstoppable.

days.guide: Read Scene 3 aloud. The student lists Haemon's three strongest points. Close by asking the question(s) below; the student answers aloud and points to the exact line in the text (or their own draft) that supports the answer.

questions.q: Which image does Haemon use to argue his father should yield?
questions.a: Trees that bend in a flooding stream survive while stiff ones are torn up (and a sailor who never slackens sail capsizes).

questions.q: How does the conversation between Creon and Haemon end?
questions.a: In anger; Haemon leaves, warning that Antigone's death will cause another, and that Creon will never see him again.

days.guide: Give the Scenes 2–3 quiz from the assessment key and check the annotations. Then the student writes a half-page journal entry taking a side — is Creon a tyrant or a ruler doing his duty? — supported by at least one quoted line.

questions.q: Give one line of evidence that Creon is a tyrant.
questions.a: He tells Haemon the city belongs to the ruler / he refuses to listen to anyone, insisting the state is his to command.

weeks.prep: Antigone text; locate a filmed production (e.g., a National Theatre recording, library DVDs, or YouTube). Parent preview: Exodos describes Antigone's, Haemon's and Eurydice's suicides (narrated, not staged).
misconceptions: Thinking Creon's reversal comes too late by chance. It's because he delays — show the cause-effect chain.
Writing a theme as one word ('pride'). A theme is a complete statement about life.
weeks.assessment_key: Seminar rubric: 4 = makes a clear claim (Antigone or Creon), cites at least four lines accurately, responds to others' evidence, asks a follow-up question; 3 = claim with 2–3 citations; 2 = opinions without text; 1 = minimal. Strong evidence for Creon as tragic hero: he falls from high status through hubris, experiences a reversal and recognition ('I alone am guilty') and survives to suffer. For Antigone: noble, principled, her stubbornness contributes to her fate. Theme statements (model): 'Pride that refuses to listen destroys those it means to protect.' 'Following conscience may require sacrifice.' Score 3 = three complete thematic sentences with justification for the chosen one.

days.guide: Read Scene 4 (Antigone's farewell) and Scene 5 (Teiresias). The student marks the moment Creon begins to reverse. Close by asking the question(s) below; the student answers aloud and points to the exact line in the text (or their own draft) that supports the answer.

questions.q: What does Teiresias warn Creon about?
questions.a: The gods reject Thebes' sacrifices because of the unburied body; Creon will pay with a death in his own family.

questions.q: When does Creon change his mind?
questions.a: After Teiresias leaves and the Choragos urges him to free Antigone and bury Polyneices; he agrees to go himself.

days.guide: Finish the Exodos. The student builds a cause-effect chain from the decree to the deaths. Close by asking the question(s) below; the student answers aloud and points to the exact line in the text (or their own draft) that supports the answer.

questions.q: What happens in the Exodos?
questions.a: Antigone has hanged herself in the tomb; Haemon attacks Creon, then kills himself; Queen Eurydice kills herself on hearing the news; Creon is left broken.

questions.q: What lesson does the Choragos state at the end?
questions.a: Wisdom is the key to happiness; the gods punish the proud, and proud men learn wisdom too late, in old age.

days.guide: Watch one scene (Scene 2 or the Exodos works well) from a filmed production. The student writes three notes on how the actor plays Creon (voice, movement, facial expression) and compares each to how they imagined him while reading; discuss which interpretation the text supports better.

questions.q: How might an actor show Creon's pride physically?
questions.a: Stiff posture, raised voice, refusing eye contact, turning his back on others.

days.guide: Hold the seminar using the rubric. The student must cite at least four lines. Close by asking the question(s) below; the student answers aloud and points to the exact line in the text (or their own draft) that supports the answer.

questions.q: Give an argument that Creon is the tragic hero.
questions.a: He is a high-status figure whose hubris causes a reversal; he recognizes his error too late and suffers the loss of his son and wife — evoking pity and fear.

days.guide: Model the difference between a topic ('pride') and a theme (a complete statement about life). The student drafts three theme statements, chooses the strongest, and writes a short paragraph justifying it with two lines from the play.

questions.q: Turn 'pride' into a complete theme statement for Antigone.
questions.a: For example: 'Leaders who let pride stop them from listening bring ruin on themselves and others.'

weeks.prep: Excerpt of Thoreau's 'Civil Disobedience' (Gutenberg), Antigone text. Prepare the Unit 2 test (assessment key).
misconceptions: Ignoring the counterclaim. A strong argument acknowledges the best opposing reason and rebuts it.
Non-parallel lists ('to read, writing, and to think'). Match grammatical forms.
weeks.assessment_key: Argument essay rubric (W.9-10.1): 4 = precise claim; two reasons each supported by quotes from Antigone and Thoreau; fair counterclaim (e.g., Creon must keep order after civil war) with a rebuttal; logical transitions; formal style; MLA citations; 3 = all parts with thinner analysis; 2 = missing counterclaim or evidence; 1 = no clear claim. Unit 2 test (sample answers): tragic hero, hamartia, hubris, catharsis, chorus, ode, stichomythia, reversal; vocabulary from the play; short answer: 'How does Sophocles use the Chorus?' → to comment on action, voice community values and advise Creon (Choragos).

days.guide: Read the excerpt together. The student lists parallels to Antigone. Close by asking the question(s) below; the student answers aloud and points to the exact line in the text (or their own draft) that supports the answer.

questions.q: What does Thoreau say about unjust laws?
questions.a: He asks whether we should obey them, and argues people should not lend themselves to injustice; 'Under a government which imprisons any unjustly, the true place for a just man is also a prison.'

questions.q: How is Antigone like Thoreau?
questions.a: Both break a law they believe is unjust, act openly, and accept the penalty.

days.guide: Model an outline. The student outlines claim, two reasons, counterclaim and rebuttal. Close by asking the question(s) below; the student answers aloud and points to the exact line in the text (or their own draft) that supports the answer.

questions.q: What is a counterclaim for 'Antigone is right'?
questions.a: Creon must enforce laws to keep order in a city just torn by civil war; one person defying the law threatens stability.

days.guide: Review the outline together, then the student drafts the 700–900 word essay in one sitting if possible. Require at least two quotes from Antigone and one from Thoreau, each with a lead-in and analysis; you check only that the claim and counterclaim are both present.

questions.q: How should a quote from a translated play be cited in MLA?
questions.a: With line numbers if the translation provides them (e.g., (Sophocles, lines 450–455)), or scene/page as given.

days.guide: Teach parallel structure. The student revises three sentences in the draft. Close by asking the question(s) below; the student answers aloud and points to the exact line in the text (or their own draft) that supports the answer.

questions.q: Revise: 'Antigone is brave, loyal, and she has stubbornness.'
questions.a: 'Antigone is brave, loyal, and stubborn.'

days.guide: The student submits the final essay; score it with the rubric in the assessment key. Then give the Unit 2 test on tragic conventions and vocabulary (about 40 minutes) and review answers together.

questions.q: Define hubris.
questions.a: Excessive pride or self-confidence that leads to a downfall.

weeks.prep: Folger Julius Caesar (free online at folger.edu with audio), short reading on Caesar and the Roman Republic.
misconceptions: Thinking the play is mainly about Caesar. He dies in Act 3; the focus is Brutus and the conspiracy.
Reading line by line rather than sentence by sentence. Teach reading to the punctuation, not to the line end.
weeks.assessment_key: Act 1 quiz (answers): 1) Why do Flavius and Marullus scold the commoners? → For celebrating Caesar's triumph over Pompey's sons when they once cheered Pompey. 2) What does the Soothsayer say? → 'Beware the ides of March.' 3) What does Casca report? → Antony offered Caesar a crown three times; he refused each time, then fell in an epileptic fit. 4) Cassius's 'fault... is not in our stars' means → people, not fate, are responsible for being underlings. 5) How does Cassius plan to sway Brutus? → by throwing forged letters from 'citizens' into his window. 6) Two omens in 1.3 → a slave's hand burning without harm, a lion near the Capitol, an owl hooting at noon, men on fire walking the streets. Scansion: full credit for correct stress marks on five lines (da-DUM ×5).

days.guide: Read a short history of Caesar (crossing the Rubicon, dictator for life). The student notes why senators feared him. Close by asking the question(s) below; the student answers aloud and points to the exact line in the text (or their own draft) that supports the answer.

questions.q: Why did many senators fear Julius Caesar?
questions.a: He had gained enormous power — named dictator for life — and they feared he would become king and end the Republic.

days.guide: Teach iambic pentameter (five da-DUM feet). The student scans five lines and notices commoners speak prose. Close by asking the question(s) below; the student answers aloud and points to the exact line in the text (or their own draft) that supports the answer.

questions.q: Scan: 'The fault, dear Brutus, is not in our stars.'
questions.a: the FAULT / dear BRU / tus IS / not IN / our STARS — five iambs (some readers stress 'not' instead of 'is').

questions.q: Who speaks in prose in 1.1, and why?
questions.a: The commoners (cobbler, carpenter) — prose often marks lower-status characters or casual speech.

days.guide: Listen to 1.1–1.2 with Folger audio. The student charts Cassius's manipulation of Brutus. Close by asking the question(s) below; the student answers aloud and points to the exact line in the text (or their own draft) that supports the answer.

questions.q: Explain 'The fault, dear Brutus, is not in our stars, / But in ourselves, that we are underlings.'
questions.a: Cassius says their low position is their own fault, not fate — implying they can act to change it.

days.guide: Read 1.3. The student lists omens and their effect on mood. Close by asking the question(s) below; the student answers aloud and points to the exact line in the text (or their own draft) that supports the answer.

questions.q: How do the omens affect the mood?
questions.a: They create fear and unease, suggesting the natural order is disturbed and something terrible is coming.

days.guide: Give the Act 1 quiz and assign the journal on Cassius. Close by asking the question(s) below; the student answers aloud and points to the exact line in the text (or their own draft) that supports the answer.

questions.q: What does Caesar say about Cassius's 'lean and hungry look'?
questions.a: Such men think too much and are dangerous; Caesar distrusts him.

weeks.prep: Folger Julius Caesar. Parent preview: the assassination scene is violent but stylized.
misconceptions: Accepting Brutus's reasoning at face value. Point out he admits Caesar hasn't done wrong yet — he kills for what Caesar might become.
Thinking Brutus is simply a villain. He believes he acts for Rome; that's what makes him tragic.
weeks.assessment_key: Quiz on Acts 2–3.1 (answers): 1) Brutus's reasoning in 'It must be by his death' → Caesar might be corrupted by the crown, so kill him like a serpent's egg before it hatches. 2) Why does Brutus refuse to kill Antony? → He wants them to be 'sacrificers, but not butchers.' 3) Calpurnia's dream → Caesar's statue spouting blood as Romans bathed their hands in it. 4) How does Decius change Caesar's mind? → He reinterprets the dream as Rome drawing revival from Caesar, and says the Senate will offer a crown. 5) Caesar's last words → 'Et tu, Brute?—Then fall, Caesar.' 6) Why does Cassius object to Antony speaking? → Antony may stir the people against them. Timeline: full credit for correct order — forged letters, conspirators meet at Brutus's house, Calpurnia's dream, Artemidorus's warning, assassination, Antony's arrival.

days.guide: Read 2.1. The student paraphrases the soliloquy line by line and identifies the flaw in reasoning. Close by asking the question(s) below; the student answers aloud and points to the exact line in the text (or their own draft) that supports the answer.

questions.q: What is the flaw in Brutus's reasoning?
questions.a: He admits Caesar has not abused power yet; he kills him for what he might do — speculation, not evidence.

questions.q: What does the 'serpent's egg' metaphor mean?
questions.a: Caesar is like a snake's egg: harmless now, but dangerous once hatched, so it should be killed in the shell.

days.guide: Read 2.2–2.4. The student compares Portia and Calpurnia. Close by asking the question(s) below; the student answers aloud and points to the exact line in the text (or their own draft) that supports the answer.

questions.q: How does Portia prove she can be trusted with Brutus's secret?
questions.a: She shows a voluntary wound she gave herself in the thigh.

questions.q: What famous line does Caesar say about cowards?
questions.a: 'Cowards die many times before their deaths; / The valiant never taste of death but once.'

days.guide: Read 3.1 aloud. The student tracks stage directions and discusses why Brutus lets Antony speak. Close by asking the question(s) below; the student answers aloud and points to the exact line in the text (or their own draft) that supports the answer.

questions.q: Why does Brutus allow Antony to speak at the funeral?
questions.a: He believes it will look honorable and that he can speak first and set terms; he underestimates Antony.

days.guide: Assign sides (switch halfway if time allows). Each side prepares three cited lines and a one-minute opening, then debate for 10–15 minutes with rebuttals; the student keeps debate notes for the assessment and ends by stating which side had stronger evidence.

questions.q: Cite a line the conspirators could use to justify the killing.
questions.a: Brutus: 'Not that I loved Caesar less, but that I loved Rome more' (3.2), or his serpent's egg reasoning.

days.guide: Give the Acts 2–3.1 quiz from the assessment key. The student then builds a timeline of the conspiracy from the forged letters to Antony's arrival after the assassination, checking order against the play.

questions.q: What does Antony vow in his soliloquy over Caesar's body?
questions.a: Revenge and civil war — 'Cry havoc and let slip the dogs of war.'

weeks.prep: Folger 3.2 and a video of Antony's speech (e.g., Marlon Brando, 1953 film). Find three modern ads or speeches.
misconceptions: Thinking repetition is just emphasis. In Antony's speech 'honourable man' becomes sarcasm — meaning reverses.
Confusing ethos (credibility) with emotion. Pathos is emotion; ethos is trust in the speaker.
weeks.assessment_key: Performance rubric: 4 = memorized 12–20 lines accurately, deliberate pauses, emphasis that shows irony in 'honourable man,' clear volume and eye contact; 3 = minor slips; 2 = read rather than performed; 1 = incomplete. Timed response rubric: 4 = claims that Brutus relies on logos in short abstract prose and assumes the crowd agrees, while Antony uses pathos (Caesar's body, wounds, mantle, will), irony, refutation (refused crown three times; wept for the poor; brought ransoms to Rome) and calculated pauses; uses at least three quotes; 3 = good comparison, fewer quotes; 2 = summary; 1 = off-topic.

days.guide: Define ethos, pathos, logos. The student identifies each in three modern ads or speeches. Close by asking the question(s) below; the student answers aloud and points to the exact line in the text (or their own draft) that supports the answer.

questions.q: An ad says 'Nine out of ten dentists recommend...' Which appeal?
questions.a: Primarily ethos (expert authority), with a logos-style statistic.

days.guide: Read Brutus's speech. The student marks logos and parallel structure. Close by asking the question(s) below; the student answers aloud and points to the exact line in the text (or their own draft) that supports the answer.

questions.q: Find parallel structure in Brutus's speech.
questions.a: 'As Caesar loved me, I weep for him; as he was fortunate, I rejoice at it; as he was valiant, I honour him; but as he was ambitious, I slew him.'

questions.q: Why does Brutus speak in prose?
questions.a: To sound plain and reasonable to the common people.

days.guide: Read Antony's speech. The student tracks each 'honourable man' and how the meaning shifts. Close by asking the question(s) below; the student answers aloud and points to the exact line in the text (or their own draft) that supports the answer.

questions.q: How does Antony refute the claim that Caesar was ambitious?
questions.a: He reminds them Caesar brought captives' ransoms to Rome's treasury, wept when the poor cried, and refused the crown three times.

questions.q: What does Antony use to stir pathos?
questions.a: Caesar's body and bloody mantle, pointing to each dagger hole, and finally the will leaving money (75 drachmas) and gardens to every citizen.

days.guide: The student chooses 12–20 lines, marks the script with slashes for pauses and underlines for emphasis, and practices aloud daily. Watch a film version of the speech for ideas, then the student performs; score with the performance rubric, especially the ironic emphasis on 'honourable man.'

questions.q: Why pause after 'My heart is in the coffin there with Caesar'?
questions.a: To appear overcome by grief, letting the crowd react and turn sympathetic.

days.guide: Set a 40-minute timer. The student spends 5 minutes planning (claim plus three pieces of evidence), 30 writing and 5 proofreading; grade with the timed response rubric and point out one strength and one goal.

questions.q: In one sentence, why does Antony's speech succeed where Brutus's fails?
questions.a: Antony moves the crowd emotionally with concrete evidence and irony, while Brutus relies on abstract reasoning and his own reputation.

weeks.prep: Folger Julius Caesar; film clips (1953 Mankiewicz version with Marlon Brando, and a 2012 version such as the RSC production). Prepare the unit test.
misconceptions: Assuming Caesar is the tragic hero because of the title. Use Aristotle's criteria — Brutus has the flaw, reversal and recognition.
Forgetting the ghost's significance — Caesar's spirit lives on in the revenge.
weeks.assessment_key: Unit test (sample answers): Passage IDs — 'The fault, dear Brutus...' (Cassius to Brutus, 1.2); 'Et tu, Brute?' (Caesar, 3.1); 'This was the noblest Roman of them all' (Antony about Brutus, 5.5); 'Cowards die many times...' (Caesar to Calpurnia, 2.2). Rhetoric: identify pathos in Antony's showing of the mantle; parallelism in Brutus's speech. Essay rubric (4-point): clear thesis on the tragic hero, at least three quotes, Aristotelian terms used correctly.

days.guide: Read 4.3. The student analyzes how the friendship unravels. Close by asking the question(s) below; the student answers aloud and points to the exact line in the text (or their own draft) that supports the answer.

questions.q: What do Brutus and Cassius argue about in 4.3?
questions.a: Brutus accuses Cassius of taking bribes ('itching palm') and refusing him gold; Cassius feels insulted. They reconcile after Brutus reveals Portia has died.

questions.q: What appears to Brutus at the end of 4.3?
questions.a: Caesar's ghost, saying it will see him at Philippi.

days.guide: Read Act 5. The student records each death and Antony's tribute. Close by asking the question(s) below; the student answers aloud and points to the exact line in the text (or their own draft) that supports the answer.

questions.q: How do Cassius and Brutus die?
questions.a: Cassius, believing Titinius was captured, has Pindarus kill him; Brutus runs onto his own sword held by Strato.

questions.q: What does Antony say about Brutus?
questions.a: 'This was the noblest Roman of them all' — the only conspirator who acted for the common good, not envy.

days.guide: Compare the funeral scene in two films. The student writes which is more persuasive. Close by asking the question(s) below; the student answers aloud and points to the exact line in the text (or their own draft) that supports the answer.

questions.q: What should the comparison focus on?
questions.a: Specific director and actor choices (setting, crowd reactions, pacing, delivery) and how they shape the speech's effect.

days.guide: Review Aristotle's criteria: noble stature, tragic flaw (hamartia), reversal, recognition, and audience pity and fear. The student fills the chart for Caesar and for Brutus with a quote in each box, then writes a two-sentence verdict.

questions.q: Make a case that Brutus is the tragic hero.
questions.a: He is noble and respected; his hamartia is idealism and misjudgment (trusting Antony, believing others act for Rome); he suffers reversal at Philippi and dies by his own hand, evoking pity.

days.guide: Give the Julius Caesar unit test from the assessment key (about 60 minutes): passage identification, rhetoric analysis and a short essay. Grade together and have the student correct any misidentified passages.

questions.q: Who says 'Caesar, now be still; I killed not thee with half so good a will'?
questions.a: Brutus, as he dies.

weeks.prep: Speech planning sheet, phone for video. Help the student identify a local issue and two credible sources (local news, city/county websites).
misconceptions: Confusing a topic with a position. 'Parks' is a topic; 'Our city should fund a new skate park' is a position.
Overloading devices. Each device should serve a point.
weeks.assessment_key: Speech rubric: Content (4) — clear position, two credible facts with sources, a quotation, logical organization; Rhetoric (4) — anaphora, antithesis, rhetorical question and tricolon used effectively; Delivery (4) — eye contact, pace, volume, 3–4 minutes, answers questions thoughtfully. 10–12 = proficient.

days.guide: Brainstorm three local issues (parks, transit, library hours, school start times) and pick the one the student cares about most. The student writes a one-sentence position and finds two credible facts and one quotation, recording source, author and date for each.

questions.q: How can you tell if a source is credible?
questions.a: Check the author's expertise, the publisher, the date, evidence cited and whether other reliable sources agree.

days.guide: Teach anaphora, antithesis, rhetorical question and tricolon with examples. The student drafts the speech, labeling each device. Close by asking the question(s) below; the student answers aloud and points to the exact line in the text (or their own draft) that supports the answer.

questions.q: Give an example of antithesis from Julius Caesar.
questions.a: 'Not that I loved Caesar less, but that I loved Rome more.'

questions.q: What is a tricolon?
questions.a: A series of three parallel words or phrases, e.g., 'I came, I saw, I conquered.'

days.guide: The student revises for audience and time, marking pauses (/) and emphasis (underline). Close by asking the question(s) below; the student answers aloud and points to the exact line in the text (or their own draft) that supports the answer.

questions.q: How long is a 3–4 minute speech, roughly?
questions.a: About 400–550 words at a typical speaking pace.

days.guide: Record two run-throughs on a phone. The student watches each and self-scores eye contact, pace and volume on a 1–4 scale, then picks one thing to fix before the second take.

questions.q: What is one strategy to slow down a rushed speech?
questions.a: Mark planned pauses after key lines and breathe at each one.

days.guide: Gather the family as an audience. The student delivers the speech and then takes two questions; score with the speech rubric and give one specific compliment and one goal. Close by asking the question(s) below; the student answers aloud and points to the exact line in the text (or their own draft) that supports the answer.

questions.q: How should a speaker handle a question they can't answer?
questions.a: Acknowledge it honestly, give what they do know, and offer to follow up.

weeks.prep: Things Fall Apart (library), map of Nigeria. Parent preview: the novel includes domestic violence, the killing of a boy (Ikemefuna), and later a suicide.
misconceptions: Reading Okonkwo as the voice of Igbo culture. Achebe shows many Igbo characters (Obierika, Nwoye, Ezeudu) who question or temper his rigidity.
Seeing Igbo society as 'primitive.' Achebe shows its law, religion, art, commerce and debate.
weeks.assessment_key: Reading quiz (answers): 1) How did Okonkwo become famous? → He threw Amalinze the Cat in a wrestling match. 2) What is Okonkwo's greatest fear? → Failure and weakness — becoming like his father, Unoka. 3) What was Unoka like? → Lazy, in debt, loved music and his flute; he died without titles. 4) Why does Ikemefuna come to Umuofia? → As compensation from Mbaino after a man from Mbaino killed an Umuofia woman (wife of Ogbuefi Udo). 5) Who kills Ikemefuna? → Okonkwo, because he was afraid of being thought weak. 6) Who warned him not to take part? → Ogbuefi Ezeudu. Character chart: full credit for traits with page-cited examples for Okonkwo, Nwoye, Ekwefi. Proverb log: 8 proverbs each with page and explanation.

days.guide: Read a short background article on the Igbo and British colonization of Nigeria (late 1800s to 1960 independence). The student locates Igboland in southeastern Nigeria on a map and lists three things they expect the novel to show about Igbo life before colonization.

questions.q: When did Achebe publish the novel, and what was he responding to?
questions.a: 1958; he wanted to tell African history from an African point of view, responding to colonial-era novels that portrayed Africans negatively.

days.guide: The student reads chapters 1–4 (about 45 minutes) and keeps a two-column log: Okonkwo's fears and actions on the left, how each connects to Unoka on the right. Discuss the log, asking for page numbers.

questions.q: Why does Okonkwo work so hard and rule his household harshly?
questions.a: He fears failure and weakness and is ashamed of his father, Unoka, who was idle and died in debt.

days.guide: Explain how proverbs work in oral cultures and model one. The student collects eight proverbs with page numbers and writes what each means and what Igbo value it reveals; discuss the two most interesting.

questions.q: What does 'Proverbs are the palm-oil with which words are eaten' mean?
questions.a: Proverbs make speech smooth and meaningful; skillful talk in Igbo culture uses them.

questions.q: What does 'If a child washes his hands he could eat with kings' reveal?
questions.a: Igbo society values achievement — a person can rise by their own effort.

days.guide: The student reads chapters 5–8. Because Ikemefuna's death is upsetting, discuss it together first; then the student writes a journal entry on why Okonkwo strikes the blow and how it affects Nwoye and Okonkwo himself.

questions.q: Why does Okonkwo strike the blow that kills Ikemefuna?
questions.a: He is afraid of being thought weak.

questions.q: How does Nwoye react?
questions.a: Something gives way inside him; he grows distant from his father (this later contributes to his conversion).

days.guide: Give the reading quiz from the assessment key. Then check the character chart for Okonkwo, Nwoye and Ekwefi: each trait needs an example with a page number. Close by asking the question(s) below; the student answers aloud and points to the exact line in the text (or their own draft) that supports the answer.

questions.q: Who is Ezinma?
questions.a: Okonkwo and Ekwefi's daughter, the only one of Ekwefi's children to survive; Okonkwo's favorite.

weeks.prep: Things Fall Apart; glossary at the back of most editions.
misconceptions: Thinking Okonkwo's exile is punishment for murder. It's for an accidental killing — a 'female' crime — so he gets seven years.
Assuming Igbo justice is arbitrary. The egwugwu trial shows a structured process.
weeks.assessment_key: Analysis paragraph rubric: 4 = names the flaw (fear of weakness leading to rashness, anger and violence), three accurate cited examples (beating Ojiugo during the Week of Peace; killing Ikemefuna; shooting at Ekwefi; later killing the messenger), analysis linking each to the flaw; 3 = two strong examples; 2 = summary; 1 = no claim. Vocabulary check (answers): chi — personal god/spirit; obi — head of household's hut; egwugwu — masked ancestral spirits who judge; ogbanje — a child who dies and returns to be reborn; iyi-uwa — stone linking an ogbanje to the spirit world; ilo — village playground/meeting ground; ndichie — elders; efulefu — worthless man; agbala — woman, or a man with no titles; osu — outcast dedicated to a god.

days.guide: Read chapters 9–10. The student notes how justice works. Close by asking the question(s) below; the student answers aloud and points to the exact line in the text (or their own draft) that supports the answer.

questions.q: What happens in the egwugwu trial?
questions.a: The masked egwugwu hear a dispute between Uzowulu and his wife's family; they rule that Uzowulu must go to his in-laws with a pot of wine and beg his wife to return.

questions.q: What is found in chapter 9?
questions.a: Ezinma's iyi-uwa, which the medicine man digs up, believed to end her ogbanje cycle.

days.guide: Read chapters 11–13. The student explains how the exile happens. Close by asking the question(s) below; the student answers aloud and points to the exact line in the text (or their own draft) that supports the answer.

questions.q: Why is Okonkwo exiled?
questions.a: At Ezeudu's funeral his gun explodes and kills Ezeudu's sixteen-year-old son; it is an accidental ('female') killing, so he must flee to his motherland for seven years.

questions.q: Who carries Ezinma to the cave in chapter 11?
questions.a: Chielo, the priestess of Agbala; Ekwefi follows.

days.guide: Show how to use context clues before the glossary. The student defines ten Igbo words (e.g., chi, obi, egwugwu, ogbanje) and writes five sentences about the novel using them correctly; quiz orally.

questions.q: What is a chi?
questions.a: A person's personal god or spirit, connected to their destiny.

days.guide: Model a topic sentence that names Okonkwo's flaw. The student writes a paragraph with three cited examples, each followed by analysis of how it shows the flaw; check that analysis is at least as long as the quotes.

questions.q: Give one example of Okonkwo's rashness before the exile.
questions.a: He beats his wife Ojiugo during the sacred Week of Peace, or shoots at Ekwefi with his gun.

days.guide: Lead a 15-minute family discussion: which traditions does Achebe present as strengths and which as weaknesses? Ask the student to support each claim with a specific scene, and push for nuance — Achebe shows both.

questions.q: Give one strength and one weakness Achebe shows.
questions.a: Strengths: democratic councils, justice, art, proverbs, community. Weaknesses: throwing away twins, the osu outcasts, harshness toward the vulnerable.

weeks.prep: Things Fall Apart, Yeats's 'The Second Coming' (Poetry Foundation).
misconceptions: Seeing Mr. Brown and Reverend Smith as the same. Brown is accommodating; Smith is rigid and provokes conflict.
Thinking the ending is neutral. The Commissioner's single 'reasonable paragraph' shows colonizers erasing African history.
weeks.assessment_key: Quiz (answers): 1) Where does Okonkwo spend his exile? → Mbanta, his mother's village. 2) Why does Nwoye join the Christians? → The hymns and the new religion answer his questions about twins thrown away and Ikemefuna's killing. 3) Who are the osu? → Outcasts who are drawn to the church. 4) What happens to Abame? → It is wiped out after villagers kill a white man. 5) How does Mr. Brown differ from Reverend Smith? → Brown is respectful, learns about Igbo religion, builds a school and hospital; Smith is strict and confrontational. 6) What does Enoch do? → Unmasks an egwugwu. 7) How does Okonkwo die? → He kills a court messenger, then hangs himself. Final-paragraph analysis rubric: 4 = explains that the Commissioner reduces Okonkwo's life to 'a reasonable paragraph' in 'The Pacification of the Primitive Tribes of the Lower Niger' and links it to Achebe's purpose of writing Africa's own history; 3 = correct idea, little evidence; 2 = summary; 1 = off-topic.

days.guide: Read 'The Second Coming.' The student explains how Achebe uses its line as his title. Close by asking the question(s) below; the student answers aloud and points to the exact line in the text (or their own draft) that supports the answer.

questions.q: What line from Yeats gives Achebe his title?
questions.a: 'Things fall apart; the centre cannot hold.'

questions.q: How does the title fit the novel?
questions.a: Igbo society and Okonkwo's life break apart under colonial and missionary pressure.

days.guide: Read chapters 14–19. The student tracks Nwoye's conversion. Close by asking the question(s) below; the student answers aloud and points to the exact line in the text (or their own draft) that supports the answer.

questions.q: What advice does Uchendu give Okonkwo in exile?
questions.a: That 'Mother is supreme' — a man finds refuge in his motherland in sorrow, so Okonkwo should not despair.

questions.q: Why does Christianity attract outcasts?
questions.a: It welcomes osu, mothers of twins and others rejected by traditional society.

days.guide: Read chapters 20–25. The student annotates Mr. Brown vs. Reverend Smith. Close by asking the question(s) below; the student answers aloud and points to the exact line in the text (or their own draft) that supports the answer.

questions.q: How does Mr. Brown win converts?
questions.a: By respecting the clan, discussing religion with Akunna, and building a school and hospital.

days.guide: Read the last paragraph aloud slowly. The student underlines word choices that reveal the Commissioner's attitude ('primitive,' 'pacification,' 'a reasonable paragraph') and writes a paragraph on what Achebe is saying about who writes history.

questions.q: What is the title of the Commissioner's book, and why is it ironic?
questions.a: 'The Pacification of the Primitive Tribes of the Lower Niger' — Achebe's whole novel shows a complex society, and 'pacification' disguises conquest.

days.guide: Give the Parts 2–3 quiz from the assessment key. Then the student completes a cause-effect chart of colonial change (missionaries → converts → divided clan → government courts → Okonkwo's final act).

questions.q: Why don't the clansmen fight after Okonkwo kills the messenger?
questions.a: They let the other messengers escape and ask 'Why did he do it?' — the clan is too divided; Okonkwo realizes they will not go to war.

weeks.prep: Things Fall Apart, Purdue OWL MLA guide, highlighters.
misconceptions: Writing a thesis that is a fact ('Okonkwo dies at the end'). A thesis is an arguable claim.
Comma splices. Use a semicolon, a period, or a conjunction.
weeks.assessment_key: Draft checkpoint conference (checklist): arguable thesis answering the prompt; three body paragraphs each with a topic sentence; at least eight quotations, each introduced and analyzed; MLA in-text citations (Achebe page); semicolons/colons used correctly at least three times. Mark each Met/Not yet and set two revision goals. Sample strong thesis: 'Achebe parallels Okonkwo's rigid fear of weakness with Umuofia's inability to adapt, so that one man's fall mirrors the collapse of a society divided by colonialism.'

days.guide: Review three prompt choices. The student picks one and writes a working thesis that makes an arguable claim and previews three reasons; test it by asking, 'Could someone disagree?' Close by asking the question(s) below; the student answers aloud and points to the exact line in the text (or their own draft) that supports the answer.

questions.q: Revise this weak thesis: 'Okonkwo is a character in Things Fall Apart.'
questions.a: For example: 'Okonkwo's fear of weakness drives the violent decisions that lead to his downfall.'

days.guide: The student gathers eight quotations with page numbers and sorts them into three body-paragraph columns, writing a one-line note on what each proves. Check that each paragraph has at least two strong quotes.

questions.q: Why plan evidence before drafting?
questions.a: To make sure each paragraph has enough proof and the argument is balanced.

days.guide: The student drafts the 1,000-word essay from the evidence map, using MLA in-text citations (Achebe 61). Encourage drafting straight through without editing; you check that each paragraph opens with a topic sentence linked to the thesis.

questions.q: Format an MLA in-text citation for page 61.
questions.a: (Achebe 61).

days.guide: Teach semicolons, colons and conjunctive adverbs. The student adds three correct uses to the draft. Close by asking the question(s) below; the student answers aloud and points to the exact line in the text (or their own draft) that supports the answer.

questions.q: Fix: 'Okonkwo was strong, however he was afraid.'
questions.a: 'Okonkwo was strong; however, he was afraid.'

questions.q: When do you use a colon?
questions.a: After an independent clause to introduce a list, explanation or quote.

days.guide: The student scores their own draft with the rubric, then reads it aloud to catch run-ons and missing words. Hold the draft checkpoint conference in the assessment key and agree on two revision goals.

questions.q: Why read your essay aloud?
questions.a: You hear missing words, awkward phrasing and run-ons that the eye skips.

weeks.prep: Semester notes; prepare the semester exam: a cold-read passage (e.g., a short story excerpt from CommonLit), terms list, grammar items, and an argument prompt.
misconceptions: Over-reliance on summary in timed writing. Remind: claim, evidence, analysis.
Studying terms only as definitions. Practice identifying them in passages.
weeks.assessment_key: Semester exam answer key (terms): foreshadowing, irony (verbal/dramatic/situational), unreliable narrator, tragic hero, hamartia, hubris, catharsis, chorus, stichomythia, soliloquy, iambic pentameter, ethos/pathos/logos, anaphora, antithesis, tricolon, proverb, allusion. Grammar: correct comma splices with semicolons; identify participial/appositive phrases; parallel structure. Timed argument essay rubric (4-point): claim, two pieces of evidence, counterclaim, organization, conventions. Final TFA essay rubric (4-point): thesis, evidence (8 quotations), analysis, organization, MLA format and Works Cited, conventions.

days.guide: The student submits the polished Things Fall Apart essay with a Works Cited page. Score it with the rubric and return comments for the portfolio later in the year. Close by asking the question(s) below; the student answers aloud and points to the exact line in the text (or their own draft) that supports the answer.

questions.q: Format a Works Cited entry for Things Fall Apart (Anchor, 1994).
questions.a: Achebe, Chinua. Things Fall Apart. Anchor Books, 1994.

days.guide: The student makes flashcards for the literary and rhetorical terms from Units 1–4 (term on front; definition and an example from a text on back). Quiz each other, setting aside missed cards for a second round.

questions.q: What is the difference between a soliloquy and an aside?
questions.a: A soliloquy is a long speech alone on stage revealing thoughts; an aside is a brief remark to the audience others on stage don't hear.

days.guide: Give a practice cold-read passage (CommonLit or a released test). The student reads questions first, annotates, then answers; go over the reasoning for each multiple-choice answer, not just the letter.

questions.q: What's a good strategy for a cold-read passage?
questions.a: Read the questions first, annotate the passage for key details, then return to the text for evidence.

days.guide: Give the semester exam (about 2 hours, can be split): cold-read analysis, terms, grammar and a timed argument essay. Grade with the assessment key. Close by asking the question(s) below; the student answers aloud and points to the exact line in the text (or their own draft) that supports the answer.

questions.q: Define allusion and give an example from this semester.
questions.a: A reference to another work or event; Achebe's title alludes to Yeats's 'The Second Coming.'

days.guide: Hand back the Week 1 reader autobiography beside the final essay. The student writes a one-page reflection naming specific growth with examples (thesis, evidence, sentence variety) and one goal for second semester.

questions.q: Name two specific signs of growth to look for.
questions.a: Stronger thesis statements and better integrated, analyzed quotations (also sentence variety and fewer errors).

weeks.prep: Print the five poems (Poetry Foundation). Find two WWI recruitment posters (Library of Congress). Parent preview: Owen and Sassoon describe gas death and a soldier's suicide.
misconceptions: Assuming all war poems share the same view. Brooke's is idealistic (1914); Owen and Sassoon wrote from the trenches with bitter realism.
Confusing poet and speaker. Refer to 'the speaker.'
weeks.assessment_key: Comparative response rubric: 4 = thesis compares two poets' views; analyzes specific images and tone words (e.g., Brooke's 'some corner of a foreign field / That is for ever England' — peaceful and patriotic — vs. Owen's 'guttering, choking, drowning' and 'the old Lie' — horrified and bitter); explains how imagery creates tone; 3 = accurate but less precise; 2 = summary; 1 = off-topic.

days.guide: Read about trench warfare and recruitment. The student analyzes two posters for appeals. Close by asking the question(s) below; the student answers aloud and points to the exact line in the text (or their own draft) that supports the answer.

questions.q: What appeal does a poster saying 'Your country needs YOU' use?
questions.a: Pathos — patriotism and guilt — plus ethos of national authority.

days.guide: Read 'The Soldier' and 'Dulce et Decorum Est.' The student charts tone words and images. Close by asking the question(s) below; the student answers aloud and points to the exact line in the text (or their own draft) that supports the answer.

questions.q: What is the tone of Brooke's 'The Soldier'?
questions.a: Patriotic, peaceful, idealistic — dying for England makes a foreign field 'for ever England.'

questions.q: What is 'the old Lie' in Owen's poem?
questions.a: 'Dulce et decorum est pro patria mori' — it is sweet and fitting to die for one's country.

days.guide: Read the gas attack stanza aloud twice. The student lists sensory images by sense (sight, sound, touch) and writes a paragraph on how the imagery puts the reader in the scene and prepares for 'the old Lie.'

questions.q: What image does Owen use for the gassed soldier?
questions.a: He sees the man drowning 'as under a green sea' — 'guttering, choking, drowning.'

questions.q: What is the effect of 'Gas! GAS! Quick, boys!'?
questions.a: The sudden exclamations and dashes create panic and urgency, pulling the reader into the moment.

days.guide: Read Sassoon and McCrae. The student identifies each speaker's attitude. Close by asking the question(s) below; the student answers aloud and points to the exact line in the text (or their own draft) that supports the answer.

questions.q: Who speaks in 'In Flanders Fields,' and what do they ask?
questions.a: The dead soldiers ('We are the Dead'); they ask the living to take up the torch and continue the fight.

questions.q: What is Sassoon's attitude toward the 'smug-faced crowds'?
questions.a: Bitter scorn — they cheer soldiers but never know 'the hell where youth and laughter go.'

days.guide: The student plans with a T-chart of images and tone words for two poets, then writes a 400-word comparison with a thesis about each poet's view of war. Grade with the rubric.

questions.q: Name a contrast between Brooke's and Owen's imagery.
questions.a: Brooke uses gentle English nature images; Owen uses graphic, physical images of suffering.

weeks.prep: Night by Elie Wiesel (Marion Wiesel translation), USHMM Holocaust Encyclopedia (ushmm.org). Parent preview: Night describes atrocities, including children burned and hangings; read it yourself first and plan to discuss feelings. Allow breaks.
misconceptions: Thinking the Jews of Sighet 'should have known.' Discuss denial, propaganda, and how unimaginable the truth seemed.
Reading Night as a novel. It is a memoir — Wiesel's own experience.
weeks.assessment_key: Reading quiz (answers): 1) Who is Moishe the Beadle? → A poor, humble man who teaches Eliezer Kabbalah. 2) What happens to him? → Deported as a foreign Jew, he escapes a mass shooting in Poland and returns to warn Sighet; no one believes him. 3) What does Madame Schächter scream on the train? → 'Fire! I see a fire!' 4) What do they see at Birkenau? → Flames from a chimney/crematorium. 5) What advice is Eliezer given at selection? → Say he is eighteen (his father says forty). 6) What happens to his mother and sister Tzipora? → They are separated and killed. Faith chart: full credit for at least four quotes tracking change, including 'Never shall I forget those flames that consumed my faith forever.'

days.guide: Use the USHMM Holocaust Encyclopedia to build a timeline 1933–1945 with about ten events (Hitler becomes chancellor 1933, Nuremberg Laws 1935, Kristallnacht 1938, WWII begins 1939, Wannsee Conference 1942, Hungary deportations 1944, liberation 1945). Discuss where Sighet fits.

questions.q: When was Sighet's Jewish community deported?
questions.a: Spring 1944 (May), after Germany occupied Hungary in March 1944.

days.guide: Read section 1. The student analyzes why people ignore Moishe. Close by asking the question(s) below; the student answers aloud and points to the exact line in the text (or their own draft) that supports the answer.

questions.q: Why don't the Jews of Sighet believe Moishe?
questions.a: His story seems impossible; they think he's mad, want to believe the war will end soon, and hope for safety.

days.guide: Read section 2. Discuss the fire symbolism. Close by asking the question(s) below; the student answers aloud and points to the exact line in the text (or their own draft) that supports the answer.

questions.q: How do people treat Madame Schächter, and what does her vision foreshadow?
questions.a: They tie, gag and beat her to keep her quiet; her vision of fire foreshadows the crematoria at Birkenau.

days.guide: Read section 3. The student tracks Eliezer's faith with quotes. Close by asking the question(s) below; the student answers aloud and points to the exact line in the text (or their own draft) that supports the answer.

questions.q: How does Eliezer react when others recite the Kaddish?
questions.a: He feels anger at God — 'Why should I bless His name?'

days.guide: Give the reading quiz. Then read the 'Never shall I forget' passage aloud; the student writes a journal response on what Wiesel says he will never forget and how the repetition affects the reader. Allow time to talk about feelings.

questions.q: What literary device structures the 'Never shall I forget' passage?
questions.a: Anaphora — repetition of 'Never shall I forget' at the start of lines.

weeks.prep: Night. Parent preview: sections 4–9 include hangings, beatings, a son killing his father for bread, and the father's death. Read Wiesel's 1986 Nobel speech (nobelprize.org).
misconceptions: Assuming Eliezer failed his father. Discuss guilt and the impossible conditions.
Thinking 'silence' means just not speaking. Wiesel means the indifference of bystanders and nations.
weeks.assessment_key: Seminar rubric (4-point): claim about silence; at least three cited passages (e.g., the world's silence, the hanging of the pipel, the Nobel line 'Silence encourages the tormentor, never the tormented'); responds to others; asks questions. Exit response model: 'Wiesel argues that silence helps tormentors because victims are abandoned when bystanders say nothing; in Night, the world's inaction allowed deportations to continue.'

days.guide: Read sections 4–5. The student records dehumanization and resistance. Close by asking the question(s) below; the student answers aloud and points to the exact line in the text (or their own draft) that supports the answer.

questions.q: Describe the hanging of the young pipel.
questions.a: The boy dies slowly; a man asks 'Where is God now?' and Eliezer hears a voice answer that God is hanging on the gallows.

days.guide: Read sections 6–7. Chart Eliezer's responsibility toward his father. Close by asking the question(s) below; the student answers aloud and points to the exact line in the text (or their own draft) that supports the answer.

questions.q: What happens with Rabbi Eliahu's son?
questions.a: He runs ahead and abandons his father during the march; Eliezer prays never to do the same.

questions.q: What does Juliek do in the barracks at Gleiwitz?
questions.a: Plays Beethoven on his violin; he is found dead the next morning.

days.guide: Finish the book. Analyze the mirror image. Close by asking the question(s) below; the student answers aloud and points to the exact line in the text (or their own draft) that supports the answer.

questions.q: What does Eliezer see in the mirror at the end?
questions.a: 'A corpse' gazing back — the look never left him.

days.guide: Read the key section of Wiesel's 1986 Nobel Peace Prize acceptance speech aloud. The student underlines his call to take sides and writes a paragraph connecting it to two moments of silence or indifference in Night.

questions.q: Quote Wiesel's Nobel statement about neutrality.
questions.a: 'We must always take sides. Neutrality helps the oppressor, never the victim. Silence encourages the tormentor, never the tormented.'

days.guide: Hold a 20-minute Socratic seminar: 'Why does Wiesel say silence helps the tormentor?' The student brings three cited passages and asks at least one follow-up question; end with a written exit response.

questions.q: When was Buchenwald liberated?

weeks.prep: Night, the WWI poems, and two USHMM Holocaust Encyclopedia articles (e.g., 'Auschwitz' and 'Deportations'). Show the student the Purdue OWL pages on MLA in-text citation and attributive tags. Prepare the Unit 5 test.
misconceptions: Using first person ('I think') in informative writing. Model rewriting in third person with an objective tone.
Dropping a fact into a paragraph without naming its source. Every borrowed idea needs an attributive tag or a citation.
weeks.assessment_key: Informative essay rubric (W.9-10.2): 4 = clear thesis explaining how witness literature preserves memory; organized body paragraphs; accurate evidence from Night, at least one WWI poem and two USHMM articles; an attributive tag for every source; objective tone; MLA Works Cited; 3 = minor gaps in evidence or citation; 2 = thin evidence or opinionated tone; 1 = incomplete. Unit 5 test (sample answers): 1) Memoir vs. novel → a memoir is the author's true account of their own experience. 2) Imagery in 'Dulce' → the gassed soldier 'drowning' under a 'green sea.' 3) Speaker of 'In Flanders Fields' → the dead soldiers. 4) Significance of Madame Schächter's vision → foreshadows the crematoria fires. 5) Wiesel's view of silence → it helps the tormentor, never the tormented. 6) Tone of Brooke's 'The Soldier' → idealistic, patriotic.

days.guide: Discuss what 'witness literature' means and brainstorm what Night and the WWI poems preserve that textbooks may not (individual voices, sensory detail, emotion). The student writes a working thesis and a three-part plan.

questions.q: What is witness literature?
questions.a: Writing by people who lived through or saw historical atrocities, created to preserve memory and testify for those who cannot.

questions.q: Draft a sample thesis for this essay.
questions.a: For example: 'Through personal testimony and vivid imagery, Night and the poems of Wilfred Owen preserve the human reality of mass suffering so that later generations cannot forget or deny it.'

days.guide: Model the difference between paraphrase (your words, same length), summary (shorter) and quote (exact words) using one USHMM paragraph. The student takes labeled notes from two articles with full MLA source information.

questions.q: What is the difference between a paraphrase and a summary?
questions.a: A paraphrase restates a specific passage in your own words at about the same length; a summary condenses the main ideas into a shorter form.

days.guide: Show three attributive tags ('According to the USHMM...', 'Wiesel recalls...', 'Owen depicts...'). The student drafts the 900-word essay, highlighting each tag to check that every source is introduced. Close by asking the question(s) below; the student answers aloud and points to the exact line in the text (or their own draft) that supports the answer.

questions.q: Rewrite with an attributive tag: 'Over 1 million people were murdered at Auschwitz.'
questions.a: 'According to the U.S. Holocaust Memorial Museum, approximately 1.1 million people were murdered at Auschwitz.'

days.guide: Read a paragraph aloud and circle every 'I,' 'you,' slang word or vague word ('stuff,' 'really'). The student revises for academic vocabulary and objective tone throughout. Close by asking the question(s) below; the student answers aloud and points to the exact line in the text (or their own draft) that supports the answer.

questions.q: Revise for objective tone: 'I think Night is really sad and you can't stop reading it.'
questions.a: 'Night conveys profound grief in a narrative that compels the reader forward.'

days.guide: The student submits the final essay, then takes the Unit 5 test from the assessment key. Grade the test together and discuss any missed text details. Close by asking the question(s) below; the student answers aloud and points to the exact line in the text (or their own draft) that supports the answer.

questions.q: Why is Night classified as a memoir rather than a novel?
questions.a: It is Elie Wiesel's own account of his experiences in the Holocaust, written in the first person about real events.

weeks.prep: The trailer or a 3-minute clip of 'They Shall Not Grow Old' (Peter Jackson, 2018; preview first — it shows real wartime footage including dead soldiers), 'Dulce et Decorum Est,' and the Library of Congress digital collections. Slide software.
misconceptions: Thinking documentary film is objective and poetry is subjective. Both involve choices: what to show, cut, colorize, or emphasize.
Using images without crediting them. Every image needs a caption with title, creator/date if known, and source.
weeks.assessment_key: Multimedia presentation rubric (SL.9-10.5): 4 = five slides that pair specific poem lines with relevant archival images; captions cite each source; 4-minute talk explains how each image and line reinforce or complicate each other; clear voice and eye contact; 3 = solid pairing, explanation less specific; 2 = images loosely related or uncited; 1 = incomplete.
