days.guide: Teach five terms with quick sketches: long shot, close-up, pan, cut, montage (and note colorization in Jackson's film). Watch the clip twice; the second time the student logs each shot type they see.

questions.q: What effect does a close-up of a soldier's face create?
questions.a: It builds emotional connection and focuses attention on individual experience.

questions.q: What is a montage?
questions.a: A sequence of short shots edited together to compress time or build an idea or mood.

days.guide: Have the student list details of the trenches in the clip and in Owen's poem in two columns. Then discuss what each medium emphasizes and why. Close by asking the question(s) below; the student answers aloud and points to the exact line in the text (or their own draft) that supports the answer.

questions.q: What can Owen's poem do that the film clip cannot?
questions.a: Use figurative language (the 'green sea,' 'like old beggars under sacks') and give a speaker's inner thoughts and bitter judgment ('the old Lie').

questions.q: What can the film do that the poem cannot?
questions.a: Show real faces, movement and setting directly, often with sound, making the history visually concrete.

days.guide: The student picks one WWI poem and chooses five key lines. For each, they sketch a slide plan: the line, an archival image idea from the Library of Congress, and why they belong together.

questions.q: What makes a strong poem–image pairing?
questions.a: An image that directly echoes or deliberately contrasts a specific line, so the pairing creates new meaning.

days.guide: The student builds the five slides, searching loc.gov for images (keywords like 'trench,' 'gas mask,' 'recruitment poster'). Each slide needs the poem line, the image and a caption citing the source.

questions.q: What information belongs in an image caption citation?
questions.a: Title or description, creator and date if known, the collection (e.g., Library of Congress), and the URL.

days.guide: The student presents for about 4 minutes, explaining how image and text work together. Score with the rubric and give one glow and one grow. Close by asking the question(s) below; the student answers aloud and points to the exact line in the text (or their own draft) that supports the answer.

questions.q: Name one delivery skill to focus on during the presentation.
questions.a: Making eye contact rather than reading slides, or pausing after each image so the audience can look.

weeks.prep: Texts and audio of FDR's 'Four Freedoms' (1941), Churchill's 'We Shall Fight on the Beaches' (June 4, 1940), Gandhi's 'Quit India' (August 8, 1942), and Mandela's Rivonia statement 'I Am Prepared to Die' (April 20, 1964). Brief historical context for each.
misconceptions: Treating every speech as the same kind of persuasion. Purpose and audience differ: Congress, Parliament, a political party, a courtroom.
Assuming Mandela simply rejected nonviolence. He explains that peaceful protest was met with bans and violence, and the ANC chose sabotage designed to avoid loss of life.
weeks.assessment_key: Rhetorical analysis chart (expected content): FDR — purpose: prepare Americans to support allies against Axis aggression; audience: Congress and the nation; appeals: logos (security), pathos (universal freedoms); key: freedom of speech, of worship, from want, from fear. Churchill — purpose: steel Britain after Dunkirk; audience: Parliament/nation; anaphora 'we shall fight...'; defiant, resolute tone; 'we shall never surrender.' Gandhi — purpose: demand immediate British withdrawal from India; audience: All-India Congress Committee; nonviolence framed as courage; 'Do or Die.' Mandela — purpose: explain his actions at trial; audience: court and world; ethos and logos (history of peaceful protest, Sharpeville, banning of the ANC); closing pathos: 'an ideal for which I am prepared to die.' Score 4 = all cells accurate with a quote per speech.

days.guide: Give one paragraph of context (January 1941, before the U.S. entered WWII). Listen to the key section; the student identifies the four freedoms and the reasons FDR gives. Close by asking the question(s) below; the student answers aloud and points to the exact line in the text (or their own draft) that supports the answer.

questions.q: What are the Four Freedoms?
questions.a: Freedom of speech and expression, freedom of every person to worship God in their own way, freedom from want, and freedom from fear.

questions.q: Why did FDR give this speech in January 1941?
questions.a: To build support for aiding nations fighting the Axis (leading to Lend-Lease) while the U.S. was not yet at war.

days.guide: Explain Dunkirk (May–June 1940 evacuation). Listen to the ending; the student marks every repetition and describes the tone. Close by asking the question(s) below; the student answers aloud and points to the exact line in the text (or their own draft) that supports the answer.

questions.q: Identify the anaphora in Churchill's speech.
questions.a: 'We shall fight on the beaches, we shall fight on the landing grounds, we shall fight in the fields and in the streets, we shall fight in the hills; we shall never surrender.'

questions.q: What is the tone, and how does the repetition create it?
questions.a: Defiant and resolute; the steady repetition sounds unshakable, like a drumbeat of determination.

days.guide: Explain the 1942 context (India under British rule during WWII). The student reads the excerpt and notes how Gandhi presents nonviolence as strength, not weakness. Close by asking the question(s) below; the student answers aloud and points to the exact line in the text (or their own draft) that supports the answer.

questions.q: What was the 'Quit India' demand, and what mantra did Gandhi give?
questions.a: Immediate end of British rule in India; 'Do or Die.'

questions.q: How does Gandhi frame nonviolence as strength?
questions.a: He presents it as requiring courage and discipline — resisting without hatred or weapons takes more strength than violence.

days.guide: Explain apartheid and the Rivonia Trial. The student reads the excerpt and lists Mandela's reasons for turning to armed resistance. Close by asking the question(s) below; the student answers aloud and points to the exact line in the text (or their own draft) that supports the answer.

questions.q: What justification does Mandela give for armed resistance?
questions.a: Decades of peaceful protest were met with bans and violence (e.g., the 1960 Sharpeville massacre and the banning of the ANC), leaving no legal path; they chose sabotage designed to avoid loss of life.

questions.q: What is Mandela's famous closing statement?
questions.a: He cherished the ideal of a democratic and free society — 'if needs be, it is an ideal for which I am prepared to die.'

days.guide: The student completes the comparison chart (purpose, audience, appeals, key quote) for all four speeches. Review using the assessment key. Close by asking the question(s) below; the student answers aloud and points to the exact line in the text (or their own draft) that supports the answer.

questions.q: Which two speakers most rely on pathos, and how?
questions.a: Churchill (defiance and national pride) and Mandela (his willingness to die for freedom); FDR and Gandhi also use pathos, but each chart cell should name the specific technique.

weeks.prep: 'Letter from Birmingham Jail' (April 16, 1963; available from the King Institute at Stanford), the Universal Declaration of Human Rights (un.org), sample op-eds for fallacy practice.
misconceptions: Thinking King rejects all laws. He argues for obeying just laws and openly breaking unjust ones while accepting the penalty.
Labeling any argument they disagree with as a fallacy. A fallacy is an error in reasoning, not an opinion they dislike.
weeks.assessment_key: Timed rhetorical analysis rubric: 4 = identifies King's purpose and audience (the eight white clergymen who called his actions 'unwise and untimely,' and a wider national audience); analyzes at least two devices in the chosen paragraph (e.g., the long periodic sentence beginning 'when you have seen vicious mobs lynch your mothers and fathers...' building pathos; allusions to Socrates or Aquinas for ethos; logical definition of just/unjust laws); explains effect on the audience; 3 = devices named with partial analysis; 2 = summary; 1 = off-topic.

days.guide: Explain the context: King was jailed in Birmingham; eight white clergymen published a statement calling the protests unwise and untimely. The student reads the first half and outlines each criticism with King's response.

questions.q: How does King answer the charge that he is an 'outsider'?
questions.a: He says he was invited, and that 'Injustice anywhere is a threat to justice everywhere' — we are caught in 'an inescapable network of mutuality.'

questions.q: How does King respond to 'wait'?
questions.a: He says 'wait' has almost always meant 'never,' and 'justice too long delayed is justice denied.'

days.guide: The student finishes the Letter and writes King's definitions of just and unjust laws in their own words. Then they write a short paragraph connecting King's reasoning to Antigone's defense to Creon.

questions.q: How does King define just and unjust laws?
questions.a: A just law squares with the moral law or law of God and uplifts human personality; an unjust law is out of harmony with moral law, degrades human personality, or is imposed on a minority that had no voice in making it.

questions.q: How does King's position connect to Antigone?
questions.a: Both break a human law they consider unjust because a higher law demands it, and both accept the penalty openly.

days.guide: Read the UDHR preamble together, then the student skims all 30 articles. They choose three that King's letter supports and pair each with a line from the Letter. Close by asking the question(s) below; the student answers aloud and points to the exact line in the text (or their own draft) that supports the answer.

questions.q: Name an article King's letter supports.
questions.a: Article 1 (all humans born free and equal in dignity and rights), Article 2 (no discrimination by race), Article 7 (equal protection of the law), Article 20 (peaceful assembly), or Article 21 (taking part in government/voting).

days.guide: Teach eight fallacies with examples: ad hominem, straw man, false dilemma, slippery slope, bandwagon, hasty generalization, appeal to authority, red herring. The student finds fallacies in sample op-eds. Close by asking the question(s) below; the student answers aloud and points to the exact line in the text (or their own draft) that supports the answer.

questions.q: 'Either we ban phones in school or students will never learn anything.' Name the fallacy.
questions.a: False dilemma (either-or).

questions.q: 'My opponent can't be trusted on taxes—he's been divorced twice.' Name the fallacy.
questions.a: Ad hominem — attacking the person instead of the argument.

days.guide: The student writes a 40-minute rhetorical analysis of one paragraph from the Letter. Score with the rubric. Close by asking the question(s) below; the student answers aloud and points to the exact line in the text (or their own draft) that supports the answer.

questions.q: What is the purpose of King's very long sentence listing the experiences of Black Americans?
questions.a: To make the reader feel the weight of accumulated injustice and show why 'wait' is impossible — the sentence's length itself enacts the endless waiting.

weeks.prep: Public library card and database access (e.g., Gale, EBSCO), Purdue OWL MLA pages, note-taking template. Help the student narrow a topic (e.g., the Civil Rights Act, the Rwandan genocide, apartheid's end, the Universal Declaration).
misconceptions: Choosing a topic too broad ('human rights'). Narrow it to a question that can be answered in 5–7 pages.
Trusting a source because it looks professional. Apply the CRAAP test every time.
weeks.assessment_key: Annotated bibliography check: each entry has a correct MLA citation (Author. 'Title.' Container, Publisher, Date, URL/DOI) and a 3–5 sentence annotation summarizing the source, evaluating credibility (CRAAP: Currency, Relevance, Authority, Accuracy, Purpose), and stating how it will be used. 4 = four entries all complete and correctly formatted; 3 = minor formatting errors; 2 = annotations lack evaluation; 1 = fewer than four sources.

days.guide: Model narrowing: topic → subtopic → question. The student drafts a focused research question. Close by asking the question(s) below; the student answers aloud and points to the exact line in the text (or their own draft) that supports the answer.

questions.q: Make this question more focused: 'What about human rights in Africa?'
questions.a: For example: 'How did international sanctions contribute to the end of apartheid in South Africa?'

days.guide: Show how to search a database with keywords and filters. The student finds six sources and evaluates each with CRAAP. Close by asking the question(s) below; the student answers aloud and points to the exact line in the text (or their own draft) that supports the answer.

questions.q: What does each letter of CRAAP stand for?
questions.a: Currency, Relevance, Authority, Accuracy, Purpose.

days.guide: Model one annotated entry. The student writes four. Close by asking the question(s) below; the student answers aloud and points to the exact line in the text (or their own draft) that supports the answer.

questions.q: What three things should an annotation do?
questions.a: Summarize the source, evaluate its credibility, and explain how it will be used in the paper.

days.guide: Show a note-card or digital template with source, page and type (P/S/Q). The student takes organized notes from at least four sources, labeling paraphrase, summary and direct quote. Close by asking the question(s) below; the student answers aloud and points to the exact line in the text (or their own draft) that supports the answer.

questions.q: Why label notes P, S or Q?
questions.a: To avoid accidental plagiarism — you'll know which words are the author's and need quotation marks.

days.guide: The student writes a thesis and detailed outline, assigning sources to each section. Check the annotated bibliography with the rubric. Close by asking the question(s) below; the student answers aloud and points to the exact line in the text (or their own draft) that supports the answer.

questions.q: What should a research thesis do?
questions.a: Answer the research question with an arguable or explanatory claim that previews the main points.

weeks.prep: Outline, notes, word processor, Purdue OWL MLA formatting guide. Plan a 5-minute presentation time with an audience.
misconceptions: Paragraphs that are strings of quotes. Each body paragraph needs the student's analysis tying sources to the thesis.
Works Cited errors: missing hanging indent, not alphabetized, or containing sources not cited in the paper.
weeks.assessment_key: Research paper rubric: Thesis and focus (4); Evidence — at least two sources per body paragraph, accurately cited (4); Analysis and synthesis (4); Organization and transitions (4); MLA format and Works Cited (4); Conventions (4). 20–24 = proficient. Presentation rubric: clear summary of findings, visual aid, 5 minutes, answers questions accurately (4-point).

days.guide: Model a body paragraph that synthesizes two sources (topic sentence, source A, source B, analysis connecting them). The student drafts body paragraphs. Close by asking the question(s) below; the student answers aloud and points to the exact line in the text (or their own draft) that supports the answer.

questions.q: What does 'synthesis' mean in a research paper?
questions.a: Combining information from multiple sources to make a point neither source makes alone.

days.guide: Show hook types (striking fact, anecdote, question). The student drafts an introduction and a conclusion that answers 'So what?' Close by asking the question(s) below; the student answers aloud and points to the exact line in the text (or their own draft) that supports the answer.

questions.q: What should a conclusion do besides restate the thesis?
questions.a: Explain the significance — why the findings matter today or what they suggest.

days.guide: The student revises for logic and support, then checks every in-text citation against a Works Cited entry. Build the Works Cited page together using Purdue OWL. Close by asking the question(s) below; the student answers aloud and points to the exact line in the text (or their own draft) that supports the answer.

questions.q: How is a Works Cited page formatted?
questions.a: Titled 'Works Cited,' alphabetized by author's last name, double-spaced, with hanging indents.

days.guide: The student does a final grammar edit (reading aloud backwards by sentence helps catch errors) and checks MLA format. Submit the paper and score with the research rubric. Close by asking the question(s) below; the student answers aloud and points to the exact line in the text (or their own draft) that supports the answer.

questions.q: What goes in the MLA header?
questions.a: Student name, teacher name, course, date — on separate lines at the top left.

days.guide: The student presents findings for 5 minutes with Q&A. Score with both rubrics. Close by asking the question(s) below; the student answers aloud and points to the exact line in the text (or their own draft) that supports the answer.

questions.q: How should a presenter use notes?
questions.a: Use brief cue cards with key points, not a script to read word for word.

weeks.prep: Fahrenheit 451 (Ray Bradbury). Read Part 1 yourself first. Parent preview: Mildred's overdose and a woman who chooses to burn with her books.
misconceptions: Reading the novel as only about censorship by government. Beatty explains the public stopped reading first; the government just followed.
Missing that Clarisse is a catalyst — she makes Montag question his life.
weeks.assessment_key: Part 1 quiz (answers): 1) What is Montag's job? → A fireman who burns books. 2) What question from Clarisse unsettles him? → 'Are you happy?' 3) What happens to Mildred? → She overdoses on sleeping pills; technicians pump her stomach. 4) What are the 'parlor walls'? → Wall-sized TV screens with an interactive 'family.' 5) How does the old woman die? → She lights the match and burns with her books. 6) According to Beatty, how did book burning start? → Mass media sped up, books were condensed, minorities objected to content, and people chose entertainment over thought; the government simply encouraged it. Symbolism log: fire (destruction → later warmth), mirror (self-reflection), the Hearth and the Salamander (fireman's emblems), the hound (technology as threat).

days.guide: Define dystopia (a society that appears ideal but is oppressive) and list traits. Discuss why governments might censor. Close by asking the question(s) below; the student answers aloud and points to the exact line in the text (or their own draft) that supports the answer.

questions.q: Name three traits of a dystopia.
questions.a: Government control, loss of individuality, propaganda, surveillance, restricted information.

days.guide: Read through Montag's meeting with Clarisse. Analyze fire and mirror symbolism. Close by asking the question(s) below; the student answers aloud and points to the exact line in the text (or their own draft) that supports the answer.

questions.q: What does Clarisse ask Montag that unsettles him?
questions.a: 'Are you happy?'

questions.q: What does the mirror symbolize when Montag sees himself in Clarisse's eyes?
questions.a: Self-reflection — she makes him see himself honestly for the first time.

days.guide: Read through the Mechanical Hound scenes. Analyze technology's effect on Mildred. Close by asking the question(s) below; the student answers aloud and points to the exact line in the text (or their own draft) that supports the answer.

questions.q: How does technology affect Mildred?
questions.a: She's absorbed in the parlor walls and seashell radios, emotionally empty and disconnected from Montag.

days.guide: Read Beatty's speech. Discuss which claims sound plausible today. Close by asking the question(s) below; the student answers aloud and points to the exact line in the text (or their own draft) that supports the answer.

questions.q: According to Beatty, what caused book burning?
questions.a: Faster media, shorter attention spans, condensed books, and groups being offended.

days.guide: Give the Part 1 quiz from the assessment key. Then check the symbolism log: each symbol (fire, mirror, salamander, Hound) needs a quote and an interpretation. Close by asking the question(s) below; the student answers aloud and points to the exact line in the text (or their own draft) that supports the answer.

questions.q: What are the Hearth and the Salamander?
questions.a: The fireman's symbols — the salamander, believed to live in fire.

weeks.prep: Fahrenheit 451 Parts 2–3, Matthew Arnold's 'Dover Beach' (Poetry Foundation), one current article on technology, attention or censorship for the seminar.
misconceptions: Thinking Faber's 'three things' are just books. He says books are only one container for what society lacks.
Reading the ending as hopeless. The phoenix and the book people suggest renewal.
weeks.assessment_key: Seminar rubric (4-point): clear claim about whether the novel describes our world; at least three novel citations (e.g., the parlor walls, seashell radios, Beatty's speech, Faber's three things) and one from the current article; respectful responses; follow-up questions. Theme essay outline: 4 = arguable theme thesis (e.g., 'Bradbury suggests that a society that trades thought for entertainment destroys its own humanity'), three body points with assigned quotes, a counterpoint; 3 = complete with weaker evidence; 2 = topic but no thesis; 1 = incomplete.

days.guide: Read Part 2, 'The Sieve and the Sand.' The student lists Faber's three missing things and explains each in their own words. Close by asking the question(s) below; the student answers aloud and points to the exact line in the text (or their own draft) that supports the answer.

questions.q: What three things does Faber say society is missing?
questions.a: Quality (texture) of information; leisure to digest it; and the right to act on what we learn from the interaction of the first two.

questions.q: What does the title 'The Sieve and the Sand' refer to?
questions.a: Montag's childhood memory of trying to fill a sieve with sand — like trying to absorb the Bible quickly on the train; knowledge slips away.

days.guide: Read 'Dover Beach' aloud. Discuss its 'Sea of Faith' and its ending, then reread the scene where Montag reads it to Mildred's friends. Close by asking the question(s) below; the student answers aloud and points to the exact line in the text (or their own draft) that supports the answer.

questions.q: Why does 'Dover Beach' make Mrs. Phelps cry?
questions.a: The poem's sadness about a world without faith, joy or peace ('ignorant armies clash by night') breaks through her numbness and makes her feel the emptiness of her own life.

questions.q: What does the speaker of 'Dover Beach' ask of his love?
questions.a: 'Ah, love, let us be true / To one another!' — to hold onto each other in a confused, faithless world.

days.guide: Read Part 3, 'Burning Bright.' The student traces Montag's escape and analyzes Granger's phoenix story and the book people. Close by asking the question(s) below; the student answers aloud and points to the exact line in the text (or their own draft) that supports the answer.

questions.q: What does Granger say about the phoenix?
questions.a: Like the phoenix, humanity burns itself up and rises again — but humans can remember their mistakes and so might stop repeating them.

questions.q: Who are the book people?
questions.a: Exiles who each memorize a book to preserve it until society is ready to rebuild; Montag carries parts of Ecclesiastes and Revelation.

days.guide: Hold the seminar: 'Does Fahrenheit 451 describe our world?' Each participant uses novel evidence and the current article. Close by asking the question(s) below; the student answers aloud and points to the exact line in the text (or their own draft) that supports the answer.

questions.q: What novel detail most resembles modern technology?
questions.a: The seashell radios (earbuds) or the parlor walls (large screens, interactive media).

days.guide: Model a thesis that states a theme, not a topic. The student outlines the analysis with three body points and quotes assigned to each, plus one counterpoint. Close by asking the question(s) below; the student answers aloud and points to the exact line in the text (or their own draft) that supports the answer.

questions.q: Turn 'censorship' into a theme statement.
questions.a: For example: 'When people give up thinking for comfort, censorship becomes unnecessary because they censor themselves.'

weeks.prep: Orwell's 'Politics and the English Language' (1946) and excerpts of Animal Farm (chapters 6, 8 and 10, where the commandments change). A jargon-filled paragraph (corporate or bureaucratic memo) for revision.
misconceptions: Thinking Orwell objects to all long words. He objects to vague, inflated language that hides meaning.
Confusing euphemism with polite speech. Political euphemism disguises something unpleasant (e.g., 'collateral damage' for civilian deaths).
weeks.assessment_key: Response essay rubric: 4 = thesis connecting Orwell's argument (vague, euphemistic language lets people avoid thinking and makes 'lies sound truthful and murder respectable') to Fahrenheit 451 (Beatty's 'everyone made equal,' firemen as 'custodians of our peace of mind,' parlor-wall chatter); two quotes from each text; clear analysis; 3 = sound but less precise; 2 = summary; 1 = off-topic.

days.guide: Read the essay together. The student lists the six rules and paraphrases each. Close by asking the question(s) below; the student answers aloud and points to the exact line in the text (or their own draft) that supports the answer.

questions.q: What are Orwell's six rules?
questions.a: 1) Never use a metaphor, simile or figure of speech you are used to seeing in print. 2) Never use a long word where a short one will do. 3) If it is possible to cut a word out, always cut it out. 4) Never use the passive where you can use the active. 5) Never use a foreign phrase, scientific word or jargon if there's an everyday English equivalent. 6) Break any of these rules sooner than say anything outright barbarous.

days.guide: Model revising one sentence ('It is incumbent upon all personnel to facilitate the optimization of workflow' → 'Everyone should work efficiently'). The student revises the jargon paragraph using the rules.

questions.q: Revise using Orwell's rules: 'Mistakes were made in the implementation of the policy.'
questions.a: 'We made mistakes when we put the policy in place.' (active voice, plain words, names who acted).

days.guide: Read the excerpts where the commandments change. The student analyzes propaganda techniques (rewriting history, euphemism, fear, repetition). Close by asking the question(s) below; the student answers aloud and points to the exact line in the text (or their own draft) that supports the answer.

questions.q: How does the commandment 'All animals are equal' change by the end?
questions.a: It becomes 'All animals are equal, but some animals are more equal than others.'

questions.q: Who spreads the pigs' propaganda, and how?
questions.a: Squealer, who uses confusing statistics, threats ('Jones will come back'), and rewrites the commandments.

days.guide: Show examples of euphemism ('pre-owned' for used, 'collateral damage' for civilian deaths). The student finds three examples in ads or news and explains what each hides or softens. Close by asking the question(s) below; the student answers aloud and points to the exact line in the text (or their own draft) that supports the answer.

questions.q: What does the euphemism 'downsizing' hide?
questions.a: That workers are being fired or laid off.

days.guide: The student plans a thesis linking Orwell's essay to Fahrenheit 451 and writes a 500-word response. Grade with the rubric. Close by asking the question(s) below; the student answers aloud and points to the exact line in the text (or their own draft) that supports the answer.

questions.q: Give one connection between Orwell's essay and Beatty.
questions.a: Beatty uses smooth, reasonable-sounding language ('peace of mind,' making everyone 'equal') to disguise censorship — exactly the language Orwell warns about.

weeks.prep: Fahrenheit 451, notes; prepare the Unit 7 test with a cold-read dystopian excerpt (e.g., the opening of 'Harrison Bergeron' by Kurt Vonnegut, available on CommonLit).
misconceptions: Writing an original dystopia that only copies Bradbury. A transformation keeps the premise but changes the banned thing, the setting, or the point of view.
Peer feedback that is only praise. Require two specific 'grows' tied to the rubric.
weeks.assessment_key: Writing rubric — Theme analysis option: thesis, three quoted pieces of evidence, analysis, organization, conventions (4-point each). Story option: a dystopian world clearly established, a conflict that comments on society, narrative technique (dialogue, pacing, description), conventions. Unit 7 test (sample answers with 'Harrison Bergeron' excerpt): 1) Dystopian feature → enforced equality via handicaps. 2) Who enforces it → the Handicapper General, Diana Moon Glampers. 3) How it connects to Beatty's 'everyone made equal' → both societies flatten individuality to avoid discomfort. 4) Define allusion, symbol, dystopia.

days.guide: Explain both options. The student chooses and plans with a short outline. Close by asking the question(s) below; the student answers aloud and points to the exact line in the text (or their own draft) that supports the answer.

questions.q: What does it mean to 'transform' Bradbury's premise?
questions.a: Keep the core idea (a society destroying knowledge) but change something important — e.g., music or art is banned, or the story is told by a censor.

days.guide: The student drafts 900–1,200 words in one or two sittings. For the analysis option, check thesis and evidence; for the story option, check that the world and its rules are clear by page one.

questions.q: What should a dystopian story's opening establish?
questions.a: The world's rules and atmosphere, and a hint of what's wrong.

days.guide: Exchange with a parent or peer using the rubric: two glows and two grows. Close by asking the question(s) below; the student answers aloud and points to the exact line in the text (or their own draft) that supports the answer.

questions.q: What makes feedback useful?
questions.a: Being specific, tied to the rubric, and suggesting how to fix the issue.

days.guide: The student revises based on the two 'grows' first, then proofreads. Submit the final draft and score with the writing rubric. Close by asking the question(s) below; the student answers aloud and points to the exact line in the text (or their own draft) that supports the answer.

questions.q: How should you prioritize revisions?
questions.a: Fix big issues (thesis, structure, clarity) before small ones (word choice, commas).

days.guide: Give the Unit 7 test with a cold-read dystopian excerpt (e.g., opening of 'Harrison Bergeron'). Grade with the assessment key. Close by asking the question(s) below; the student answers aloud and points to the exact line in the text (or their own draft) that supports the answer.

questions.q: What makes 'Harrison Bergeron' dystopian?
questions.a: The government forces everyone to be equal by handicapping anyone above average.

weeks.prep: A Doll's House (Henrik Ibsen, Gutenberg; R. Farquharson Sharp or similar translation). Background on 19th-century Norwegian women's legal status.
misconceptions: Seeing Nora as silly. Her playful surface hides a serious secret and real sacrifice.
Thinking Torvald is a cartoon villain. He reflects society's expectations of a respectable husband.
weeks.assessment_key: Quiz on Acts 1–2 (answers): 1) What secret is Nora keeping? → She secretly borrowed money to pay for a trip to Italy that saved Torvald's life, and forged her father's signature. 2) Who lent the money? → Krogstad. 3) Why does Krogstad threaten Nora? → Torvald is firing him from the bank; he'll reveal the forgery unless she saves his job. 4) Torvald's pet names → little lark, squirrel, spendthrift, featherhead/featherbrain, skylark. 5) What does Nora do in the tarantella scene? → Dances wildly to distract Torvald from the letterbox containing Krogstad's letter. 6) Who is Dr. Rank, and what does he reveal? → Family friend; he's dying and in love with Nora. Character analysis: full credit for a paragraph on Nora's double life with two quotes.

days.guide: Read background on women's legal status in 1870s Norway. The student lists what Nora could not legally do. Close by asking the question(s) below; the student answers aloud and points to the exact line in the text (or their own draft) that supports the answer.

questions.q: What legal restriction makes Nora's loan a crime?
questions.a: Married women could not borrow money without their husband's consent; Nora forged her father's signature as guarantor.

days.guide: Read Act 1. The student charts Torvald's pet names and what they reveal. Close by asking the question(s) below; the student answers aloud and points to the exact line in the text (or their own draft) that supports the answer.

questions.q: What do Torvald's pet names reveal?
questions.a: He sees Nora as a child or pet, not an equal.

questions.q: What does the macaroon scene show?
questions.a: Nora secretly eats forbidden sweets and lies — small rebellions against Torvald's control.

days.guide: Read Act 2. Analyze the tarantella as a symbol. Close by asking the question(s) below; the student answers aloud and points to the exact line in the text (or their own draft) that supports the answer.

questions.q: What does the tarantella symbolize?
questions.a: Nora's desperation and inner turmoil — a frantic dance to delay discovery, like the legend of dancing to cure a tarantula bite.

days.guide: The student lists every secret the audience knows that Torvald doesn't (the loan, the forgery, the macaroons, Krogstad's letter). For each, they explain the tension it creates in a scene.

questions.q: Give one example of dramatic irony.
questions.a: Torvald says forgers poison their homes and children, not knowing Nora is a forger.

days.guide: Give the Acts 1–2 quiz from the assessment key. Then the student writes a short character analysis of Nora's double life with two quotes. Close by asking the question(s) below; the student answers aloud and points to the exact line in the text (or their own draft) that supports the answer.

questions.q: Who is Mrs. Linde?
questions.a: Nora's old friend, a widow who comes to town looking for work.

weeks.prep: A Doll's House Act 3; Tagore's 'Where the Mind is Without Fear'; Hughes's 'Let America Be America Again'; McKay's 'If We Must Die.'
misconceptions: Reading Nora's departure as simply leaving her children. Discuss her argument that she must become a person first.
Missing the irony of Hughes's title. The America he wants 'never has been yet.'
weeks.assessment_key: Comparative response rubric (4-point): thesis comparing how Nora and one poem's speaker claim identity; two quotes from each (Nora: 'I have been your doll-wife'; 'I believe that before all else I am a human being'; Hughes: 'America never was America to me'; McKay: 'Like men we'll face the murderous, cowardly pack'; Tagore: 'Where the mind is without fear and the head is held high'); analysis of form/tone; organization.

days.guide: Read Act 3. Analyze Nora's final speech line by line. Close by asking the question(s) below; the student answers aloud and points to the exact line in the text (or their own draft) that supports the answer.

questions.q: What does Nora mean by 'I have been your doll-wife, just as at home I was papa's doll-child'?
questions.a: She has been treated as a plaything all her life, never as an independent person.

days.guide: Debate whether Nora's leaving is justified. Discuss the 1879 reception and the alternate German ending. Close by asking the question(s) below; the student answers aloud and points to the exact line in the text (or their own draft) that supports the answer.

questions.q: How did audiences react in 1879?
questions.a: Many were shocked; a German production required an alternate ending where Nora stays for the children, which Ibsen called a 'barbaric outrage.'

days.guide: Read Tagore's poem. Connect its freedom vision to Unit 6 speeches. Close by asking the question(s) below; the student answers aloud and points to the exact line in the text (or their own draft) that supports the answer.

questions.q: What freedom does Tagore envision?
questions.a: A world where the mind is without fear, knowledge is free, and people aren't divided by 'narrow domestic walls.'

days.guide: Read Hughes and McKay. Analyze form and tone. Close by asking the question(s) below; the student answers aloud and points to the exact line in the text (or their own draft) that supports the answer.

questions.q: What form does McKay use?
questions.a: A Shakespearean sonnet.

days.guide: The student plans a thesis comparing Nora and one poem's speaker. They write the comparative response with two quotes from each text, then score it with the rubric together. Close by asking the question(s) below; the student answers aloud and points to the exact line in the text (or their own draft) that supports the answer.

questions.q: What does Nora say she is 'before all else'?
questions.a: 'A human being.'

weeks.prep: Poetry notebook; reread Tagore's poem. Prepare the Unit 8 test: drama and poetry terms with a cold-read poem (e.g., Claude McKay's 'America' or Langston Hughes's 'Harlem').
misconceptions: Writing a 'poem' that is just chopped prose. Discuss line breaks and imagery.
Monologue that summarizes plot. It should reveal the character's inner conflict.
weeks.assessment_key: Creative portfolio rubric (4-point each): imitation poem follows Tagore's 'Where...' structure with vivid images and a final turn; extended metaphor sustained throughout; monologue reveals a minor character's perspective in voice; performance with expression. Unit 8 test (sample answers with 'Harlem'): 1) 'What happens to a dream deferred?' → rhetorical question. 2) 'Does it dry up / like a raisin in the sun?' → simile. 3) Final line 'Or does it explode?' → italicized, isolated for emphasis, suggests violent frustration. Terms: soliloquy, monologue, dramatic irony, sonnet, extended metaphor, refrain.

days.guide: Reread Tagore's poem aloud and note the repeated 'Where...' clauses and final prayer. The student writes their own 10–15 line imitation using the same structure about their vision of freedom.

questions.q: What makes Tagore's structure distinctive?
questions.a: Repeated 'Where...' clauses that build to a final prayer: 'Into that heaven of freedom, my Father, let my country awake.'

days.guide: Brainstorm metaphors for identity (a river, a house, a tree). The student picks one and writes a poem extending it through at least eight lines, then reads it aloud. Close by asking the question(s) below; the student answers aloud and points to the exact line in the text (or their own draft) that supports the answer.

questions.q: What is an extended metaphor?
questions.a: A comparison sustained through several lines or a whole poem.

days.guide: Brainstorm minor characters from the year's texts (Ismene, Calpurnia, Nwoye, Mrs. Linde, Mildred). The student writes a 1-minute monologue in that character's voice revealing an inner conflict. Close by asking the question(s) below; the student answers aloud and points to the exact line in the text (or their own draft) that supports the answer.

questions.q: How is a monologue different from a soliloquy?
questions.a: A monologue is a long speech to others; a soliloquy is spoken alone, revealing private thoughts.

days.guide: The student rehearses the monologue or a poem three times, marking pauses and emphasis. They perform for family; give feedback on voice, expression and pacing. Close by asking the question(s) below; the student answers aloud and points to the exact line in the text (or their own draft) that supports the answer.

questions.q: What makes a performance effective?
questions.a: Clear voice, expression that matches emotion, and purposeful pauses.

days.guide: Give the Unit 8 test on drama and poetry terms with a cold-read poem (e.g., 'Harlem'). Grade with the assessment key. Close by asking the question(s) below; the student answers aloud and points to the exact line in the text (or their own draft) that supports the answer.

questions.q: What is a refrain?
questions.a: A repeated line or phrase in a poem.

weeks.prep: All graded work from the year, a digital portfolio folder (Google Drive or similar).
misconceptions: Revision that only fixes commas. Deep revision rethinks thesis, structure and evidence.
Reflective letters that only praise. Require specific evidence of growth.
weeks.assessment_key: Portfolio rubric (4-point each): three strong pieces (narrative, analysis, argument/research); evidence of substantial revision (tracked changes); reflective letter (600 words) that cites specific growth with examples; polished digital publication.

days.guide: The student reviews all graded work from the year and selects three best pieces (narrative, analysis, argument/research). They write a sentence explaining each choice. Close by asking the question(s) below; the student answers aloud and points to the exact line in the text (or their own draft) that supports the answer.

questions.q: Why include different types of writing?
questions.a: To show range — narrative, analytical and argumentative skills.

days.guide: The student deeply revises one essay based on earlier feedback, tracking changes. Focus on thesis, structure and analysis — not just commas. Close by asking the question(s) below; the student answers aloud and points to the exact line in the text (or their own draft) that supports the answer.

questions.q: What does deep revision look like?
questions.a: Strengthening the thesis, reorganizing, adding analysis, cutting weak evidence.

days.guide: The student revises a second piece for style: varied sentence openers, precise verbs, parallelism. Highlight three before/after sentences to discuss. Close by asking the question(s) below; the student answers aloud and points to the exact line in the text (or their own draft) that supports the answer.

questions.q: Name two style improvements.
questions.a: Varying sentence openings, using precise verbs.

days.guide: The student writes a 600-word reflective letter explaining growth as a reader and writer. Require at least two before/after examples from their own work. Close by asking the question(s) below; the student answers aloud and points to the exact line in the text (or their own draft) that supports the answer.

questions.q: What makes a reflective letter strong?
questions.a: Specific examples of growth — before/after excerpts.

days.guide: The student assembles the portfolio as a digital document or website with the three pieces and the letter. Score it with the portfolio rubric. Close by asking the question(s) below; the student answers aloud and points to the exact line in the text (or their own draft) that supports the answer.

questions.q: Why publish?
questions.a: To share work with an audience and preserve it.

weeks.prep: Review notes; a CAASPP-style practice performance task (search 'CAASPP ELA practice test grade 11' — the closest released high school test — at caaspp.org). Prepare the final exam.
misconceptions: Spending too long on one part of the exam. Teach time budgeting.
Reading only the first part of a prompt.
weeks.assessment_key: Final exam (sample answers): Literary cold read — identify theme, a device and its effect, with quoted evidence (2 points each). Informational cold read — central idea, author's purpose, rhetorical appeal. Grammar — fix comma splices, parallelism, semicolon use. Argument essay rubric (4-point): claim, evidence, counterclaim, organization, conventions. Portfolio presentation rubric: 6-minute talk, slides, specific growth examples, clear delivery (4-point).

days.guide: The student builds a one-page study guide: each major text with its themes, key quotes and terms. Quiz orally on the guide. Close by asking the question(s) below; the student answers aloud and points to the exact line in the text (or their own draft) that supports the answer.

questions.q: Name three texts studied this year and their main themes.
questions.a: Antigone (divine vs. human law); Things Fall Apart (tradition vs. change); Fahrenheit 451 (censorship and thought).

days.guide: Give a CAASPP-style practice performance task (read sources, answer questions, write an essay). Review the scoring and discuss time management. Close by asking the question(s) below; the student answers aloud and points to the exact line in the text (or their own draft) that supports the answer.

questions.q: What is a performance task?
questions.a: A multi-source research and writing task.

days.guide: Give the final exam (about 2 hours, can split): cold reads, grammar and a timed argument essay. Grade with the assessment key. Close by asking the question(s) below; the student answers aloud and points to the exact line in the text (or their own draft) that supports the answer.

questions.q: What is a strong argument essay structure?
questions.a: Introduction with claim, body paragraphs with evidence, counterclaim and rebuttal, conclusion.

days.guide: The student presents the portfolio in a 6-minute talk with slides. Score with the rubric and celebrate the year's growth. Close by asking the question(s) below; the student answers aloud and points to the exact line in the text (or their own draft) that supports the answer.

questions.q: What should the presentation emphasize?
questions.a: Growth over the year with specific examples.

days.guide: Help the student choose five books for summer (mix of genres, one classic, one contemporary). They set specific reading goals with dates. Close by asking the question(s) below; the student answers aloud and points to the exact line in the text (or their own draft) that supports the answer.

questions.q: What makes a good reading goal?
questions.a: Specific, measurable, and realistic.

HSS.overview: Modern World History meets about 60 minutes a day around primary sources: source each document (author, date, audience, purpose), read closely, then discuss and write. Expect a quiz or written product most Fridays and a DBQ each unit; use the rubrics in the keys. Several units (imperial atrocities, WWI, the Armenian Genocide, the Holocaust, Hiroshima) contain disturbing material — preview sources and leave time to talk.

weeks.prep: Set up a history notebook (sections for notes, sources, vocabulary). Print excerpts of Pericles' Funeral Oration (from Thucydides), Plato's Allegory of the Cave, and Aristotle's Politics (Book III classification). Find a modern news photograph for sourcing practice.
misconceptions: Thinking Athenian democracy included everyone. Only adult male citizens voted — women, enslaved people and foreigners (metics) were excluded.
Equating 'republic' and 'democracy.' Rome was a republic: citizens elected representatives; Athens practiced direct democracy.
weeks.assessment_key: Quiz (answers): 1) Direct democracy → citizens vote on laws themselves (Athens). 2) Who could participate in Athenian democracy? → Adult male citizens only. 3) In the Allegory of the Cave, the shadows represent → appearances/ignorance; leaving the cave represents → education/philosophy and seeing truth. 4) Aristotle's good forms and corrupt forms → monarchy/tyranny, aristocracy/oligarchy, polity/democracy (mob rule). 5) Roman checks → two consuls who could veto each other, a Senate, tribunes who could veto on behalf of plebeians. 6) Twelve Tables → Rome's first written laws (c. 450 BCE), posted publicly. Constructed response rubric (4-point): clear claim naming one idea (e.g., Roman republicanism/checks and balances, Greek citizen participation, written law); two specific connections to U.S. government (Senate, veto, elected representatives, written Constitution); explanation of influence.

days.guide: Teach the SOURCING routine with a modern photograph: Who made it? When? For what audience? Why? The student sets up the notebook and sources the photo, then predicts how the source's perspective might shape what it shows.

questions.q: What four questions make up 'sourcing' a document?
questions.a: Who created it (author), when, for what audience, and for what purpose.

questions.q: Why does sourcing matter?
questions.a: A source's author, date and purpose shape what it includes and leaves out, so historians weigh reliability and perspective.

days.guide: Source the Funeral Oration first: given by Pericles in 431 BCE to honor Athenian war dead, recorded by Thucydides. The student reads the excerpt and lists what Athenians valued about democracy, then notes who was excluded.

questions.q: According to Pericles, why is Athens called a democracy?
questions.a: Power is in the hands of the many, not a few; everyone is equal before the law, and advancement depends on merit, not class.

questions.q: What was the purpose and audience of the speech?
questions.a: To honor the war dead and inspire Athenians to keep fighting in the Peloponnesian War — so it praises Athens and may idealize it.

days.guide: Read the Allegory of the Cave aloud and sketch it. Then read Aristotle's classification and have the student fill a 3×2 chart of rule by one/few/many in good and corrupt forms.

questions.q: What does Plato's allegory suggest about who should rule?
questions.a: Those who have escaped ignorance and seen the truth — philosophers — should rule (philosopher-kings), not the uninformed majority.

questions.q: What is the corrupt form of rule by the few in Aristotle's scheme?
questions.a: Oligarchy (the good form is aristocracy).

days.guide: Read a short overview of the Roman Republic, the Twelve Tables and Cicero's idea of natural law. The student diagrams consuls, Senate, assemblies and tribunes with arrows showing who checks whom.

questions.q: How did the Roman Republic prevent one person from gaining too much power?
questions.a: Two consuls served one-year terms and could veto each other; the Senate advised and controlled funds; tribunes could veto actions harmful to plebeians.

questions.q: Why were the Twelve Tables important?
questions.a: They put laws in writing and posted them publicly, so laws applied to all and could not be changed at a judge's whim.

days.guide: Give the quiz from the assessment key (about 20 minutes). Then the student writes a constructed-response paragraph: which Greek or Roman idea most shapes U.S. government today? Check understanding with the question(s) below; on document days the student must name the source (author, date, purpose) in the answer.

questions.q: Name one Roman institution that resembles part of the U.S. government.
questions.a: The Senate (U.S. Senate), or the veto power (presidential veto), or elected representatives (republic).

weeks.prep: Print excerpts: Exodus 20 (Ten Commandments), a prophetic passage such as 2 Samuel 12 (Nathan confronts King David), Matthew 5–7 (Sermon on the Mount), Japan's 1947 Constitution (Articles 9, 14, 20, 21) and Germany's Basic Law Article 1. Note to parent: these religious texts are studied as historical sources of ideas, per CA standard 10.1.1.
misconceptions: Thinking ancient ideas transferred directly into the Constitution. Ideas passed through centuries of medieval and Enlightenment thought.
Assuming every constitution modeled on the U.S. is identical. Japan's Article 9 renouncing war has no U.S. equivalent.
weeks.assessment_key: Unit 1 essay rubric (4-point): Thesis — explains how at least two ancient traditions shaped the U.S. Constitution and spread globally; Evidence — specific ideas (Greek citizen participation, Roman republic and checks, rule of law in the Twelve Tables, the Hebrew idea that law binds even kings, Christian ideas of individual worth and conscience) and a global example (Japan 1947 Articles 14 and 21; Germany's Basic Law Article 1 'Human dignity shall be inviolable'); Analysis — explains the link rather than listing; Writing — organized, cited.

days.guide: Read Exodus 20 and the story of Nathan rebuking King David. Discuss how a covenant creates law that binds rulers as well as subjects; the student writes two sentences connecting this to 'rule of law.'

questions.q: What idea about rulers appears when the prophet Nathan condemns King David?
questions.a: Even a king is subject to a higher moral law and can be held accountable.

days.guide: Read selections from the Sermon on the Mount (the Beatitudes, the Golden Rule, 'love your enemies'). The student identifies ideas of individual worth and conscience and explains how they could support ideas of equality.

questions.q: What is the Golden Rule as stated in Matthew 7:12?
questions.a: Do to others what you would have them do to you.

questions.q: How could the idea that every person has worth to God influence political thought?
questions.a: It supports the belief that all individuals deserve dignity and equal treatment, which later fed ideas of natural rights.

days.guide: Draw a Venn diagram: Greco-Roman (reason, citizenship, natural law, civic duty) and Judeo-Christian (moral law from God, individual worth, conscience); the overlap includes law above rulers and duty to community. The student fills it with at least four items per section.

questions.q: Name one idea both traditions share.
questions.a: Law should be above any individual ruler (rule of law), or that there is a higher law (natural/divine) that human law should follow.

days.guide: Compare Japan's 1947 constitution (written under U.S. occupation) with the U.S. Bill of Rights in a two-column chart. The student finds at least three parallels and one difference. Check understanding with the question(s) below; on document days the student must name the source (author, date, purpose) in the answer.

questions.q: Which article of Japan's constitution parallels the First Amendment?
questions.a: Article 21 (freedom of assembly, association, speech, press) and Article 20 (freedom of religion).

questions.q: What is unique about Article 9?
questions.a: Japan renounces war as a sovereign right and the threat or use of force to settle international disputes.

days.guide: The student outlines, then writes a one-page essay on how ancient ideas shaped the U.S. Constitution and its global spread. Score with the rubric. Check understanding with the question(s) below; on document days the student must name the source (author, date, purpose) in the answer.

questions.q: What does Germany's Basic Law Article 1 say, and why after WWII?
questions.a: 'Human dignity shall be inviolable' — written in 1949 in reaction to Nazi crimes against human dignity.

weeks.prep: Excerpts of Magna Carta (1215; clauses 12, 39, 40) and the English Bill of Rights (1689) from the Avalon Project or British Library; Locke's Second Treatise (chapters on the state of nature and dissolution of government); Hobbes's Leviathan ch. 13; Montesquieu's Spirit of Laws (Book XI ch. 6); Rousseau's Social Contract (Book I).
misconceptions: Treating Hobbes and Locke as agreeing because both use a social contract. Hobbes wants an absolute sovereign; Locke wants limited government and a right to revolution.
Thinking Magna Carta created democracy. It protected barons' rights and limited the king, a first step toward rule of law.
weeks.assessment_key: Dialogue rubric (accuracy of ideas): 4 = each philosopher's view stated accurately in his own terms — Hobbes (life in the state of nature 'solitary, poor, nasty, brutish, and short'; people give power to an absolute sovereign for security), Locke (natural rights of life, liberty and property; government by consent; right to overthrow a government that violates rights), Montesquieu (separation of legislative, executive and judicial powers to prevent tyranny), Rousseau ('Man is born free, and everywhere he is in chains'; legitimacy comes from the general will of the people); philosophers respond to one another; 3 = mostly accurate; 2 = one or more views confused; 1 = superficial.

days.guide: Read a short overview of the Scientific Revolution and Enlightenment. The student builds a timeline: Copernicus (1543), Galileo, Newton's Principia (1687), Hobbes (1651), Locke (1689–90), Montesquieu (1748), Voltaire, Rousseau (1762), and explains how applying reason to nature led to applying reason to government.

questions.q: How did the Scientific Revolution lead to the Enlightenment?
questions.a: Thinkers saw that reason and observation could discover natural laws, so they applied reason to society and government, looking for natural rights and better institutions.

days.guide: Read key clauses together. The student lists rights protected by each document and who they protected. Check understanding with the question(s) below; on document days the student must name the source (author, date, purpose) in the answer.

questions.q: What does Magna Carta clause 39 guarantee?
questions.a: No free man may be imprisoned, stripped of rights or property, or punished except by the lawful judgment of his peers or by the law of the land.

questions.q: Name two limits the English Bill of Rights (1689) placed on the monarch.
questions.a: The king could not suspend laws, levy taxes, or keep a standing army in peacetime without Parliament's consent; elections must be free; no excessive bail or cruel and unusual punishment.

days.guide: Read Hobbes chapter 13 and Locke's state-of-nature passages. The student charts each thinker's view of human nature, purpose of government, and what happens if government fails. Check understanding with the question(s) below; on document days the student must name the source (author, date, purpose) in the answer.

questions.q: How does Hobbes describe life without government?
questions.a: 'Solitary, poor, nasty, brutish, and short' — a war of all against all.

questions.q: According to Locke, what may people do if government violates their natural rights?
questions.a: They may alter or overthrow it and form a new government.

days.guide: Read excerpts of Montesquieu and Rousseau. The student summarizes each main idea in one sentence and connects it to a U.S. institution. Check understanding with the question(s) below; on document days the student must name the source (author, date, purpose) in the answer.

questions.q: What is Montesquieu's main idea and its U.S. reflection?
questions.a: Separating legislative, executive and judicial powers prevents tyranny — reflected in the three branches and checks and balances.

questions.q: What does Rousseau mean by the 'general will'?
questions.a: Legitimate government follows the collective will of the people for the common good, not any individual's private interest.

days.guide: The student writes a one- to two-page dialogue among Hobbes, Locke, Montesquieu and Rousseau at a dinner party debating 'What makes government legitimate?' Score with the rubric for accuracy. Check understanding with the question(s) below; on document days the student must name the source (author, date, purpose) in the answer.

questions.q: Which philosopher would most strongly reject a right to revolution?
questions.a: Hobbes — he argued subjects should obey the sovereign to avoid chaos.

weeks.prep: Declaration of Independence (archives.gov), a summary of the Haitian Revolution and an excerpt of the 1801 Haitian (Saint-Domingue) Constitution, Bolívar's Jamaica Letter (1815) excerpt. Chart template for Day 5.
misconceptions: Thinking the American Revolution created full equality. Enslaved people, women and Native Americans were excluded.
Overlooking Haiti: it was the only successful revolution led by enslaved people and the first independent Black republic (1804).
weeks.assessment_key: Comparison chart (expected content): American (1775–1783) — leaders: colonial elites (Washington, Jefferson); causes: taxation without representation, Enlightenment rights; result: independent republic, federal written Constitution, slavery persists. Haitian (1791–1804) — leaders: Toussaint Louverture, Jean-Jacques Dessalines; causes: brutal slavery, French Revolution ideals; result: slavery abolished, independence 1804, first Black republic. Latin American (1810–1820s) — leaders: Creoles like Simón Bolívar and José de San Martín; causes: Creole exclusion from power, Napoleon's invasion of Spain, Enlightenment ideas; result: independent republics often dominated by elites and caudillos. Score 4 = every cell accurate; 3 = 1–2 errors; 2 = several gaps; 1 = incomplete.

days.guide: Read the preamble and the opening of the grievances aloud. The student highlights phrases that echo Locke and writes the Lockean idea beside each. Check understanding with the question(s) below; on document days the student must name the source (author, date, purpose) in the answer.

questions.q: Which phrase echoes Locke's natural rights?
questions.a: 'Unalienable Rights, that among these are Life, Liberty and the pursuit of Happiness' (Locke: life, liberty, property).

questions.q: Which phrase echoes Locke's idea of consent and revolution?
questions.a: Governments derive 'their just powers from the consent of the governed,' and the people may 'alter or to abolish' a destructive government.

days.guide: Discuss what made the American Revolution distinctive: a written constitution, federalism dividing power between national and state governments, and a Bill of Rights. The student writes a paragraph on one distinctive feature and its influence abroad.

questions.q: What is federalism?
questions.a: A system dividing power between a national government and state governments.

days.guide: Read about the Haitian Revolution (1791 uprising, Toussaint Louverture, independence in 1804). Analyze the 1801 constitution excerpt: what did it abolish, and what power did it give Toussaint? Check understanding with the question(s) below; on document days the student must name the source (author, date, purpose) in the answer.

questions.q: What did the 1801 constitution declare about slavery?
questions.a: Slavery was abolished forever — there could be no slaves in the territory.

questions.q: Why was the Haitian Revolution so significant?
questions.a: It was the only successful slave revolt to create a nation — the first independent Black republic — and it alarmed slaveholding societies throughout the Americas.

days.guide: Source the Jamaica Letter (Bolívar, 1815, written in exile to a British audience). The student identifies Enlightenment ideas and Creole grievances. Check understanding with the question(s) below; on document days the student must name the source (author, date, purpose) in the answer.

questions.q: What grievance does Bolívar raise for Creoles?
questions.a: Spain excluded American-born Creoles from high offices and trade, treating them as subordinates despite their wealth and education.

questions.q: Why might Bolívar write to a British reader?
questions.a: To win British sympathy and support for Spanish American independence.

days.guide: The student completes the comparison chart for the three revolutions (leaders, causes, ideas, results, who was included/excluded). Score with the assessment key. Check understanding with the question(s) below; on document days the student must name the source (author, date, purpose) in the answer.

questions.q: Which event in Europe helped trigger Latin American independence movements?
questions.a: Napoleon's invasion of Spain (1808), which weakened Spanish control over its colonies.

weeks.prep: The 1789 cartoon of a Third Estate peasant carrying a clergyman and nobleman; Declaration of the Rights of Man and of the Citizen (1789); Olympe de Gouges's Declaration of the Rights of Woman (1791) excerpt; Robespierre's 'On the Principles of Political Morality' (February 1794) excerpt; map of Napoleon's empire (1812). Prepare a 5–6 document DBQ set from these sources.
misconceptions: Seeing the Revolution as one event. It moved through phases: moderate (1789–91), radical/Terror (1792–94), Directory (1795–99), Napoleon (1799–1815).
Viewing Napoleon only as a conqueror. He also spread legal equality (Napoleonic Code) while limiting liberty.
weeks.assessment_key: DBQ rubric (4-point per row): Thesis — directly answers the question with a defensible claim; Evidence — uses at least 4 documents accurately plus outside knowledge; Sourcing — explains author, purpose, audience or context for at least 2 documents; Analysis — groups documents and explains how they support the claim; Writing — organized, clear. 17–20 = proficient. Strong thesis example: 'The Revolution partly achieved its goals: it ended feudal privilege and spread the idea of rights through the Declaration and Napoleonic Code, but the Terror and Napoleon's dictatorship betrayed liberty, and women were excluded, as de Gouges protested.'

days.guide: Analyze the cartoon with the student: who is carrying whom, and what does it say? Then list causes of the Revolution: unequal estates and taxes, royal debt (including from aiding the American Revolution), bread prices, and Enlightenment ideas.

questions.q: What does the cartoon of the peasant carrying the clergy and noble mean?
questions.a: The Third Estate bore the burden of taxes and labor while the privileged First and Second Estates paid little.

questions.q: Name two economic causes of the French Revolution.
questions.a: Royal debt from wars (including the American Revolution) and rising bread prices after poor harvests, with an unfair tax system.

days.guide: Read selected articles of the Declaration of the Rights of Man and de Gouges's response side by side. The student charts how de Gouges rewrites each article. Check understanding with the question(s) below; on document days the student must name the source (author, date, purpose) in the answer.

questions.q: What does Article 1 of the Declaration of the Rights of Man state?
questions.a: Men are born and remain free and equal in rights.

questions.q: What was de Gouges's main argument?
questions.a: Women are born free and equal to men in rights; if a woman can mount the scaffold (be executed), she must also have the right to mount the speaker's rostrum.

days.guide: Read Robespierre's speech excerpt and source it (February 1794, to the National Convention, during war and the Terror). The student evaluates his justification of terror. Check understanding with the question(s) below; on document days the student must name the source (author, date, purpose) in the answer.

questions.q: How does Robespierre connect virtue and terror?
questions.a: He says virtue without terror is powerless and terror without virtue is fatal; terror is 'prompt, severe, inflexible justice' that flows from virtue.

questions.q: About how many people were officially executed during the Terror?
questions.a: About 17,000 official executions (with many more deaths in prison and in civil war).

days.guide: The student makes a T-chart of Napoleon's achievements (Napoleonic Code, Concordat, Bank of France, merit-based careers, public schools) and abuses (dictatorship, censorship, wars, restoring slavery in the colonies in 1802). Map his empire at its 1812 height, then explain the Congress of Vienna's goals.

questions.q: What were the goals of the Congress of Vienna (1814–1815)?
questions.a: Restore a balance of power, return legitimate monarchs, and contain France to prevent future revolutions and wars (led by Metternich).

questions.q: What did the Napoleonic Code establish?
questions.a: Equality of male citizens before the law, religious toleration, and protection of property — but it limited women's rights.

days.guide: Give the DBQ: Did the French Revolution achieve its goals? Allow 10 minutes to read documents and plan, 40 minutes to write. Score with the DBQ rubric. Check understanding with the question(s) below; on document days the student must name the source (author, date, purpose) in the answer.

questions.q: What were the Revolution's stated goals?
questions.a: 'Liberty, equality, fraternity' — ending privilege, securing rights, and creating government by the people.

weeks.prep: Maps of British coalfields, rivers and ports; images of the spinning jenny, water frame, Watt steam engine and early railways (e.g., Stephenson's Rocket). A textile mill case study (e.g., Arkwright's Cromford Mill).
misconceptions: Thinking the Industrial Revolution began with factories. It began with agricultural changes that freed labor and grew the population.
Crediting James Watt with inventing the steam engine. Newcomen built an earlier engine (1712); Watt greatly improved its efficiency (patent 1769).
weeks.assessment_key: Quiz (answers): 1) Enclosure → fencing common lands into private farms, pushing small farmers to cities. 2) Crop rotation → alternating crops (e.g., turnips, clover) to restore soil instead of leaving fields fallow. 3) Five factors favoring Britain → coal and iron, rivers and ports, colonies/markets, capital and banks, stable government and navy (also labor supply). 4) Spinning jenny → Hargreaves, spun many threads at once. 5) Water frame → Arkwright, water-powered spinning, led to factories. 6) Watt → improved steam engine efficiency. 7) First major passenger railway → Liverpool–Manchester (1830).

days.guide: Explain enclosure and new methods (Jethro Tull's seed drill, crop rotation with turnips and clover). The student draws a cause-effect chain from these changes to population growth and a workforce for factories.

questions.q: How did enclosure contribute to industrialization?
questions.a: It made farming more efficient but pushed many small farmers off the land, creating a labor force that moved to cities and factories.

questions.q: Why did crop rotation increase food supply?
questions.a: Planting crops like turnips and clover restored soil nutrients, so fields didn't need to lie fallow and fed more livestock.

days.guide: The student maps Britain's coal and iron deposits, navigable rivers and major ports, then lists five factors favoring early industrialization. Check understanding with the question(s) below; on document days the student must name the source (author, date, purpose) in the answer.

questions.q: Why were rivers important to early industry?
questions.a: They provided water power for mills and cheap transport for heavy goods like coal.

days.guide: The student builds an illustrated chart: invention, inventor, date, what it did, and its effect (flying shuttle 1733, spinning jenny c. 1764, water frame 1769, Watt's improved steam engine 1769/1776, power loom 1785, Stephenson's railways 1825–1830).

questions.q: Why was the steam engine so important?
questions.a: It provided reliable power anywhere, not just near rivers, driving factories, locomotives and steamships.

days.guide: Define land, labor, capital and entrepreneurship. Apply them to a textile mill case study: the student identifies each factor in Arkwright's mill. Check understanding with the question(s) below; on document days the student must name the source (author, date, purpose) in the answer.

questions.q: In a textile mill, give an example of capital and of entrepreneurship.
questions.a: Capital: the building and machines (and money to buy them). Entrepreneurship: the owner (e.g., Richard Arkwright) organizing resources and taking the risk.

days.guide: Give the quiz from the assessment key. Review answers, and have the student explain any missed item using their chart. Check understanding with the question(s) below; on document days the student must name the source (author, date, purpose) in the answer.

questions.q: What were the 'factors of production' Britain had in abundance?
questions.a: Land with natural resources (coal, iron), labor (displaced farmers), capital (banks and investors), and entrepreneurs.

weeks.prep: Sadler Committee testimony (1832; e.g., Elizabeth Bentley), Engels, The Condition of the Working Class in England (1845) excerpt on Manchester, Dickens, Hard Times Book I ch. 5 ('The Key-note,' Coketown) from Gutenberg. Parent note: testimony describes beatings and injuries of children.
misconceptions: Assuming reforms happened quickly. Change was gradual: 1833 Factory Act, 1842 Mines Act, 1847 Ten Hours Act.
Thinking only men worked in factories. Women and children were a large part of the textile workforce.
weeks.assessment_key: Historical letter rubric (4-point): 4 = written in the voice of an 1833 factory worker; cites at least three specific details from the Sadler testimony, Engels or Dickens (e.g., 14–16 hour days, beatings by overlookers, injuries, polluted housing); makes a clear request (shorter hours, limits on child labor, inspectors); historically accurate; 3 = good but fewer specifics; 2 = generic; 1 = inaccurate. Reform timeline: Reform Act 1832; Factory Act 1833 (no children under 9 in textile mills; ages 9–13 limited to 9 hours a day; inspectors); Slavery Abolition Act 1833; Mines Act 1842; Ten Hours Act 1847; legalization of unions (Combination Acts repealed 1824–25).

days.guide: Source the Sadler Committee (1832, a parliamentary inquiry by reformers). The student reads testimony and annotates conditions: hours, age, punishments, injuries. Check understanding with the question(s) below; on document days the student must name the source (author, date, purpose) in the answer.

questions.q: What conditions did child workers describe to the Sadler Committee?
questions.a: Very long days (often 5 or 6 a.m. to 8 or 9 p.m. in busy times), beatings by overlookers when tired, injuries and deformities.

questions.q: Why must historians consider the Committee's purpose?
questions.a: Sadler was a reformer pushing a ten-hour bill, so he chose witnesses who supported reform; testimony is valuable but may emphasize the worst cases.

days.guide: Read Engels's description of Manchester. The student lists five details about housing, sanitation and pollution and compares them to a modern city. Check understanding with the question(s) below; on document days the student must name the source (author, date, purpose) in the answer.

questions.q: What did Engels observe about Manchester's working-class districts?
questions.a: Crowded, filthy housing, open sewage, polluted rivers and air, and poverty hidden away from middle-class streets.

days.guide: Read the Coketown chapter. The student identifies Dickens's criticism of industrial sameness and pollution. Check understanding with the question(s) below; on document days the student must name the source (author, date, purpose) in the answer.

questions.q: How does Dickens describe Coketown?
questions.a: A town of red brick blackened by smoke, with machinery, tall chimneys, a black canal, a river purple with dye, and streets and people all alike.

questions.q: What is Dickens criticizing?
questions.a: The dehumanizing sameness and ugliness of industrial life, where people become like machines.

days.guide: The student creates a timeline of reforms 1824–1847 and notes women's roles in industry and reform movements. Check understanding with the question(s) below; on document days the student must name the source (author, date, purpose) in the answer.

questions.q: What did the Factory Act of 1833 do?
questions.a: Banned children under 9 from textile mills, limited hours for children 9–13, and created factory inspectors.

days.guide: The student writes a letter to Parliament as a factory worker in 1833 using at least three pieces of evidence. Score with the rubric. Check understanding with the question(s) below; on document days the student must name the source (author, date, purpose) in the answer.

questions.q: What would a worker likely ask Parliament for in 1833?
questions.a: Shorter working hours (a ten-hour day), limits on child labor, and safer conditions.

weeks.prep: Adam Smith, Wealth of Nations (1776) excerpts: pin factory (Book I ch. 1), 'butcher, brewer, baker' and 'invisible hand' (Book IV ch. 2); The Communist Manifesto (1848) Section I excerpt; reading on Robert Owen's New Lanark. Prepare the Unit 3 test.
misconceptions: Equating Marx's communism with any government program. Marx called for workers to overthrow capitalism and abolish private ownership of the means of production.
Thinking Smith opposed all government. He supported defense, justice and some public works.
weeks.assessment_key: Unit 3 test (sample answers): 1) Smith's 'invisible hand' → individuals pursuing self-interest in a free market unintentionally benefit society. 2) Division of labor in the pin factory → 10 workers specializing made about 48,000 pins a day. 3) Marx's view of history → 'the history of all hitherto existing society is the history of class struggles' (bourgeoisie vs. proletariat). 4) Robert Owen → reformer who ran New Lanark mill with shorter hours, schools, and decent housing. 5) Meiji Japan → government-led industrialization after 1868. 6) Germany → rapid industrialization after unification (1871), steel and chemicals. 7) Source-analysis: identify author, purpose and bias of a given excerpt (2 points each).

days.guide: Read the pin factory and 'butcher, brewer, baker' passages. The student summarizes Smith's arguments for the division of labor and free markets in a paragraph. Check understanding with the question(s) below; on document days the student must name the source (author, date, purpose) in the answer.

questions.q: What did Smith's pin factory example show?
questions.a: Division of labor: 10 workers each specializing in a step made about 48,000 pins a day, far more than they could make alone.

questions.q: Explain 'It is not from the benevolence of the butcher, the brewer, or the baker that we expect our dinner.'
questions.a: Sellers serve us out of their own self-interest, and that self-interest, through trade, benefits everyone.

days.guide: Source the Manifesto (1848, Marx and Engels, for the Communist League amid revolutions). The student summarizes its critique and predicted outcome. Check understanding with the question(s) below; on document days the student must name the source (author, date, purpose) in the answer.

questions.q: What do Marx and Engels predict will happen to capitalism?
questions.a: Workers (proletariat) will overthrow the bourgeoisie in revolution, abolish private property in the means of production, and create a classless society.

questions.q: What is the famous closing call?
questions.a: 'Workers of the world, unite!' — they have nothing to lose but their chains.

days.guide: Read about Robert Owen's New Lanark. The student builds a chart comparing responses to industrialization: laissez-faire (Smith), utopian socialism (Owen), communism (Marx), and reform/unions. Check understanding with the question(s) below; on document days the student must name the source (author, date, purpose) in the answer.

questions.q: How did Robert Owen run New Lanark differently?
