questions.a: He shortened hours, refused to employ very young children, built schools and decent housing, and showed a mill could profit while treating workers better.

days.guide: Compare Germany, Meiji Japan and the U.S. in a chart: start date, role of government, key industries. Check understanding with the question(s) below; on document days the student must name the source (author, date, purpose) in the answer.

questions.q: How did Japan's industrialization differ from Britain's?
questions.a: It was led by the Meiji government, which built railroads and factories and then sold them to private firms (zaibatsu), and it came much later (after 1868).

days.guide: Give the Unit 3 test from the assessment key, including the source-analysis section. Check understanding with the question(s) below; on document days the student must name the source (author, date, purpose) in the answer.

questions.q: Why did the U.S. industrialize rapidly after the Civil War?
questions.a: Abundant resources, railroads, immigrant labor, capital and inventions.

weeks.prep: A blank world map, colored pencils, a 1914 reference map (Khan Academy or an atlas). Kipling's 'The White Man's Burden' (1899) and Henry Labouchère's 'The Brown Man's Burden' (1899). Three imperialist cartoons (e.g., 'The Rhodes Colossus').
misconceptions: Seeing imperialism as only economic. Motives included nationalism, Social Darwinism, religion, and strategic bases.
Thinking all of Africa was colonized by 1914. Ethiopia and Liberia remained independent.
weeks.assessment_key: Map key: Britain — India, Canada, Australia, Egypt, South Africa, Nigeria, Kenya, Malaya, Burma; France — Algeria, French West Africa, Madagascar, Indochina; Germany — Togo, Cameroon, German Southwest Africa (Namibia), German East Africa (Tanzania); Belgium — Congo; Netherlands — Dutch East Indies (Indonesia); Russia — Central Asia, Siberia; Japan — Korea, Taiwan; U.S. — Philippines, Hawaii, Puerto Rico, Guam. Quiz (answers): 1) Social Darwinism → the false idea that 'survival of the fittest' applied to nations and races, used to justify conquest. 2) Two economic motives → raw materials, new markets. 3) Independent African nations in 1914 → Ethiopia, Liberia. 4) Kipling's purpose → urge the U.S. to colonize the Philippines as a 'civilizing' duty. 5) Rhodes Colossus → Cecil Rhodes straddling Africa from Cape to Cairo.

days.guide: Give the student cards with examples (rubber in the Congo, Suez Canal, 'civilizing mission,' missionaries, coaling stations). They sort them under raw materials, markets, nationalism, Social Darwinism, and missionary/religious motives.

questions.q: Why did industrial nations want colonies for raw materials?
questions.a: Factories needed rubber, cotton, palm oil, minerals and other resources not available at home.

questions.q: What is Social Darwinism?
questions.a: A false application of 'survival of the fittest' to societies and races, used to justify domination of other peoples.

days.guide: The student colors a 1914 map by empire using a reference map and adds a legend. Check understanding with the question(s) below; on document days the student must name the source (author, date, purpose) in the answer.

questions.q: Which two African countries were independent in 1914?
questions.a: Ethiopia and Liberia.

days.guide: Read 'The White Man's Burden' and 'The Brown Man's Burden.' The student sources each and analyzes the perspectives. Check understanding with the question(s) below; on document days the student must name the source (author, date, purpose) in the answer.

questions.q: What does Kipling mean by 'the White Man's burden'?
questions.a: The claimed duty of white Westerners to 'civilize' colonized peoples — a paternalistic, racist justification for empire.

questions.q: How does 'The Brown Man's Burden' respond?
questions.a: It satirizes Kipling, exposing the violence and greed behind imperialism and the burden placed on colonized people.

days.guide: Model the cartoon analysis worksheet (symbols, labels, exaggeration, message, point of view) on one cartoon. The student analyzes three. Check understanding with the question(s) below; on document days the student must name the source (author, date, purpose) in the answer.

questions.q: In 'The Rhodes Colossus,' what does Rhodes straddling Africa represent?
questions.a: British ambition to control Africa from Cape Town to Cairo.

days.guide: Give the quiz from the assessment key and check the map. Check understanding with the question(s) below; on document days the student must name the source (author, date, purpose) in the answer.

questions.q: Why did Belgium's King Leopold II want the Congo?
questions.a: For its wealth — especially ivory and later rubber.

weeks.prep: A map of African states and societies before 1880 (e.g., Ethiopia, Asante, Sokoto Caliphate, Zulu kingdom, Buganda); Berlin Conference General Act excerpt; Congo Free State photographs (preview: images of mutilated people) and Casement Report summary; readings on Adwa, the Herero, and the Zulu. Link to Things Fall Apart from English.
misconceptions: Viewing pre-colonial Africa as empty or without states. Many complex kingdoms and trade networks existed.
Assuming colonial borders followed ethnic lines. Many split groups or joined rivals.
weeks.assessment_key: Paragraph rubric (sourcing): 4 = claim comparing colonizer and colonized perspectives; cites at least two documents with author, date and purpose (e.g., Berlin Conference Act — European diplomats, 1885, to regulate colonization; Casement Report — British consul, 1904, exposing abuses); explains how perspective shapes each; 3 = sources one document well; 2 = summary; 1 = no evidence.

days.guide: Study a map of Africa before 1880. The student lists five states or societies with one fact each. Check understanding with the question(s) below; on document days the student must name the source (author, date, purpose) in the answer.

questions.q: Name two African states that existed before the Scramble.
questions.a: Ethiopia, the Asante (Ashanti) kingdom, the Sokoto Caliphate, the Zulu kingdom, or Buganda.

days.guide: Read about the Berlin Conference (1884–85). The student draws modern borders over ethnic regions and notes where groups are split. Check understanding with the question(s) below; on document days the student must name the source (author, date, purpose) in the answer.

questions.q: Who attended the Berlin Conference?
questions.a: European powers (and the U.S.) — no African representatives.

questions.q: What principle did the conference set?
questions.a: 'Effective occupation' — a power had to control territory to claim it.

days.guide: Examine photographs and the Casement Report on the Congo. Discuss how forced labor and quotas led to atrocities. Check understanding with the question(s) below; on document days the student must name the source (author, date, purpose) in the answer.

questions.q: What abuses occurred in the Congo Free State?
questions.a: Forced labor for rubber quotas, hostage-taking, mutilation (cutting off hands), and millions of deaths.

questions.q: What happened after the Casement Report (1904)?
questions.a: International outrage forced Leopold to give up the Congo to Belgium in 1908.

days.guide: Compare Ethiopia's victory at Adwa (1896) with the Herero (1904–08) and Zulu (1879) resistance. Check understanding with the question(s) below; on document days the student must name the source (author, date, purpose) in the answer.

questions.q: Why did Ethiopia win at Adwa?
questions.a: Emperor Menelik II modernized his army with modern rifles and artillery and had a large, united force.

questions.q: What happened to the Herero?
questions.a: German forces killed most of the Herero in the first genocide of the 20th century.

days.guide: The student writes a document-based paragraph on colonizer vs. colonized perspectives. Score with the rubric. Check understanding with the question(s) below; on document days the student must name the source (author, date, purpose) in the answer.

questions.q: Why is sourcing important for colonial documents?
questions.a: Colonizers' documents often justify rule, while colonized people's voices may be missing or recorded by outsiders.

weeks.prep: Macaulay's 'Minute on Indian Education' (1835), Dadabhai Naoroji's 'drain of wealth' excerpt (Poverty and Un-British Rule in India, 1901), Emilio Aguinaldo's proclamation (1898/1899). Map of Southeast Asia.
misconceptions: Thinking the British government ruled India from the start. The East India Company ruled until 1858.
Overlooking that Siam stayed independent.
weeks.assessment_key: Quiz (answers): 1) East India Company → British trading company that gained control of India after Plassey (1757). 2) Cause of the 1857 rebellion → rumors of cartridges greased with cow and pig fat, plus resentment of British rule. 3) Result → British Crown took direct control (the Raj, 1858). 4) Macaulay's goal → create a class of Indians 'English in taste, in opinions, in morals and in intellect.' 5) Naoroji's argument → Britain drained India's wealth. 6) Siam → stayed independent as a buffer. 7) Aguinaldo → declared Philippine independence (1898), fought the U.S. (1899–1902).

days.guide: Draw a timeline from the East India Company's charter (1600) through the Battle of Plassey (1757) to the 1857 rebellion and the Government of India Act (1858). Explain how a trading company became a ruling power, then have the student write two causes and two results of 1857.

questions.q: What sparked the 1857 rebellion?
questions.a: Rumors that new rifle cartridges were greased with cow and pig fat, offending Hindus and Muslims.

questions.q: What changed after 1857?
questions.a: The British government took direct control of India (the Raj).

days.guide: Source each document first: Macaulay (British official, 1835, arguing for English-language education) and Naoroji (Indian nationalist economist, 1901). The student builds a two-column chart of each author's claims and evidence, then writes which argument is more convincing and why.

questions.q: What did Macaulay claim about Indian literature?
questions.a: That 'a single shelf of a good European library was worth the whole native literature of India and Arabia.'

questions.q: What was Naoroji's 'drain of wealth' argument?
questions.a: That Britain extracted India's wealth through taxes, salaries and trade, impoverishing India.

days.guide: On a blank map of Southeast Asia, the student shades French Indochina (Vietnam, Laos, Cambodia), the Dutch East Indies (Indonesia), British Burma and Malaya, the U.S. Philippines, and independent Siam (Thailand). Discuss why Siam stayed free.

questions.q: Why did Siam remain independent?
questions.a: It served as a buffer between British and French colonies, and its kings modernized.

days.guide: Explain the Spanish-American War (1898) and the Treaty of Paris, in which the U.S. bought the Philippines for $20 million. Read Aguinaldo's proclamation and a short anti-imperialist statement (e.g., Mark Twain or the Anti-Imperialist League); the student lists arguments for and against annexation.

questions.q: What happened after the U.S. annexed the Philippines?
questions.a: Filipinos led by Aguinaldo fought the Philippine-American War (1899–1902).

days.guide: Give the quiz from the assessment key without notes (about 20 minutes). Grade it together; for each missed item the student finds the answer in their notes and writes a one-sentence correction.

questions.q: What colonial power ruled Indonesia?
questions.a: The Netherlands (Dutch East Indies).

weeks.prep: Commissioner Lin Zexu's letter to Queen Victoria (1839), Sun Yat-sen's Three Principles of the People excerpt, readings on Meiji Japan and the Panama Canal/Roosevelt Corollary (1904). Assemble a 5–6 document DBQ set on responses to imperialism (e.g., Lin's letter, Aguinaldo, Menelik at Adwa, Naoroji, Sun Yat-sen, a Boxer poster).
misconceptions: Seeing colonized peoples as passive. Responses ranged from armed resistance to reform, modernization and nationalism.
Thinking Japan only resisted imperialism. After modernizing, Japan became an imperial power itself.
weeks.assessment_key: DBQ rubric (4-point per row): Thesis — directly answers the question with a defensible claim; Evidence — uses at least 4 documents accurately plus outside knowledge; Sourcing — explains author, purpose, audience or context for at least 2 documents; Analysis — groups documents and explains how they support the claim; Writing — organized, clear. 17–20 = proficient. Strong thesis example: 'Colonized peoples responded to imperialism through armed resistance (Boxers, Ethiopia at Adwa), modernization and reform (Self-Strengthening, Meiji Japan), and nationalist movements (Sun Yat-sen, Naoroji).'

days.guide: Source Lin's letter (1839, an imperial official writing to Queen Victoria to stop the opium trade). The student lists his arguments and predicts Britain's response. Check understanding with the question(s) below; on document days the student must name the source (author, date, purpose) in the answer.

questions.q: What is Lin Zexu's main argument?
questions.a: Opium is banned in Britain because it is harmful, so Britain should not sell it to China; he appeals to Victoria's conscience.

questions.q: What were the results of the First Opium War (1839–1842)?
questions.a: Britain won; the Treaty of Nanjing gave Britain Hong Kong, opened five treaty ports, and required an indemnity.

days.guide: The student charts the Taiping Rebellion (1850–64), Self-Strengthening Movement (1860s–90s), Boxer Rebellion (1899–1901), and 1911 Revolution: who, goal, result. Check understanding with the question(s) below; on document days the student must name the source (author, date, purpose) in the answer.

questions.q: What did the Boxers want?
questions.a: To expel foreigners and Christian influence from China.

questions.q: What were Sun Yat-sen's Three Principles?
questions.a: Nationalism, democracy (people's rights), and people's livelihood.

days.guide: Compare Meiji modernization with Japan's expansion (Taiwan 1895, Korea 1910). The student explains the irony. Check understanding with the question(s) below; on document days the student must name the source (author, date, purpose) in the answer.

questions.q: How did Japan avoid colonization?
questions.a: After Perry's arrival (1853), the Meiji government (1868) rapidly modernized industry, military and education on Western models.

questions.q: Which territories did Japan take by 1910?
questions.a: Taiwan (1895) and Korea (annexed 1910).

days.guide: Read about economic imperialism in Latin America, the Panama Canal (opened 1914) and the Roosevelt Corollary. Check understanding with the question(s) below; on document days the student must name the source (author, date, purpose) in the answer.

questions.q: What did the Roosevelt Corollary (1904) claim?
questions.a: The U.S. could act as an 'international police power' in Latin America to keep European powers out.

days.guide: Give the DBQ: How did colonized peoples respond to imperialism? Allow 10 minutes planning, 40 writing. Check understanding with the question(s) below; on document days the student must name the source (author, date, purpose) in the answer.

questions.q: Name three types of response to imperialism.
questions.a: Armed resistance, modernization/reform, and nationalist movements.

weeks.prep: Austria-Hungary's ultimatum to Serbia (July 23, 1914) and the 'Willy–Nicky' telegrams (July 29–August 1, 1914) — available from the Avalon Project or BYU WWI Document Archive. Map of 1914 alliances.
misconceptions: Believing the assassination alone caused the war. It was the spark; the MAIN causes made a local crisis a world war.
Thinking Italy fought with Germany. Italy was in the Triple Alliance but joined the Allies in 1915.
weeks.assessment_key: Quiz (answers): 1) MAIN → militarism, alliances, imperialism, nationalism. 2) Triple Entente → France, Russia, Britain; Triple Alliance → Germany, Austria-Hungary, Italy. 3) Assassination → Archduke Franz Ferdinand and Sophie, June 28, 1914, Sarajevo, by Gavrilo Princip (Black Hand). 4) 'Blank check' → Germany's promise of unconditional support to Austria-Hungary. 5) Order of declarations → Austria on Serbia (July 28), Germany on Russia (Aug 1), Germany on France (Aug 3), Britain on Germany (Aug 4). 6) Why Britain entered → Germany invaded neutral Belgium. Debate notes: full credit for three cited pieces of evidence and a rebuttal.

days.guide: Draw a web with 'WWI' in the center and four bubbles: militarism, alliances, imperialism, nationalism. The student adds at least two specific examples to each (e.g., Anglo-German naval race; Triple Entente; Moroccan crises; Pan-Slavism) and draws arrows showing how causes connect.

questions.q: Give an example of militarism before 1914.
questions.a: The Anglo-German naval race (dreadnoughts) or mass conscript armies and war plans like the Schlieffen Plan.

questions.q: How did alliances turn a local conflict into a world war?
questions.a: Each country was bound to defend its partners, so the Austria-Serbia conflict pulled in Russia, Germany, France and Britain.

days.guide: Read two short accounts of the assassination in Sarajevo (June 28, 1914). The student builds a dated timeline of the July Crisis from the assassination to Britain's declaration of war on August 4, marking each alliance obligation that pulled a country in.

questions.q: Who assassinated Franz Ferdinand?
questions.a: Gavrilo Princip, a Bosnian Serb nationalist linked to the Black Hand.

questions.q: Why did Britain declare war?
questions.a: Germany invaded neutral Belgium as part of the Schlieffen Plan.

days.guide: Source the documents: Austria-Hungary's ultimatum (July 23, 1914) and telegrams between Kaiser Wilhelm II and Tsar Nicholas II (July 29–August 1). The student summarizes each leader's position and identifies where each blames the other.

questions.q: What did Austria's ultimatum demand?
questions.a: That Serbia suppress anti-Austrian groups and allow Austrian officials to take part in the investigation inside Serbia — demands meant to be hard to accept.

days.guide: Assign the student a nation (Germany, Austria-Hungary, Russia, Serbia, France or Britain) to blame and have them prepare three pieces of evidence; you argue another side. After a 15-minute debate, the student writes debate notes summarizing the strongest evidence on each side.

questions.q: What evidence suggests Germany bears major responsibility?
questions.a: The 'blank check' to Austria and the Schlieffen Plan invasion of Belgium.

days.guide: Give the quiz from the assessment key without notes (about 20 minutes). Grade it together; for each missed item the student finds the answer in their notes and writes a one-sentence correction.

questions.q: What was the Schlieffen Plan?
questions.a: Germany's plan to defeat France quickly through Belgium, then turn to Russia.

weeks.prep: WWI map, Library of Congress WWI posters from three nations, soldier letters (Library of Congress Veterans History or BYU archive), Zimmermann Telegram (archives.gov).
misconceptions: Thinking the Western Front moved a lot. It was largely a stalemate of trenches from late 1914 to 1918.
Forgetting other fronts (Eastern, Ottoman/Gallipoli).
weeks.assessment_key: Quiz (answers): 1) First Battle of the Marne (1914) → stopped the German advance on Paris; led to trench warfare. 2) Verdun (1916) → long French-German battle of attrition. 3) Somme (July 1, 1916) → about 57,000 British casualties on the first day. 4) Gallipoli (1915–16) → failed Allied attempt to take the Dardanelles; heavy ANZAC losses. 5) Zimmermann Telegram → Germany proposed an alliance with Mexico, offering Texas, New Mexico, Arizona. 6) Why the U.S. entered (April 1917) → unrestricted submarine warfare and the telegram. 7) Russia's exit → Treaty of Brest-Litovsk (March 1918). Poster analysis: full credit for identifying the nation, audience, emotional appeal and message for three posters.

days.guide: On a map of Europe and the Middle East, the student draws the Western Front (Belgium to Switzerland), the Eastern Front, and the Ottoman fronts, and labels the Marne (1914), Verdun (1916), the Somme (1916) and Gallipoli (1915–16) with one fact each.

questions.q: Why did trench warfare develop?
questions.a: After the Marne, both sides dug in; machine guns and artillery made attacks so deadly that neither side could break through.

days.guide: Read two or three soldier letters from the Library of Congress or a WWI archive. The student lists details of trench life and finds matching images in the poems from English class (e.g., Owen's 'Dulce et Decorum Est').

questions.q: What details of trench life appear in letters and poems?
questions.a: Mud, rats, lice, trench foot, constant shelling, poison gas, and fear.

days.guide: Show propaganda posters from three nations (e.g., U.S., Britain, Germany). For each, the student identifies audience, emotional appeal, symbols and message, and explains what 'total war' required of civilians. Check understanding with the question(s) below; on document days the student must name the source (author, date, purpose) in the answer.

questions.q: What is total war?
questions.a: A war in which nations mobilize their entire economies and populations.

days.guide: Source the Zimmermann Telegram (January 1917, German Foreign Secretary to the ambassador in Mexico, intercepted by Britain). The student explains why it angered Americans, then writes a paragraph on how Russia's exit (Brest-Litovsk, March 1918) and U.S. entry (April 1917) changed the war.

questions.q: What did the Zimmermann Telegram propose?
questions.a: A German-Mexican alliance; Mexico would regain Texas, New Mexico and Arizona.

days.guide: Give the quiz from the assessment key without notes (about 20 minutes). Grade it together; for each missed item the student finds the answer in their notes and writes a one-sentence correction. Then score the poster analysis.

questions.q: When did the armistice take effect?
questions.a: November 11, 1918.

weeks.prep: Readings on the Armenian Genocide (1915) from a reputable source (e.g., Armenian National Institute, USHMM, Facing History). Ambassador Henry Morgenthau's account. Parent preview: descriptions of mass killings and death marches.
misconceptions: Thinking the deportations were wartime relocation. They were a deliberate campaign of mass murder.
Assuming 'genocide' means any mass death. It requires intent to destroy a group.
weeks.assessment_key: Reflection rubric (4-point): explains why remembering genocide matters; uses evidence (Morgenthau's account; Lemkin's definition); connects to the Armenian American community in California; thoughtful. Source analysis: Morgenthau — U.S. ambassador to the Ottoman Empire 1913–16, eyewitness reports; purpose to inform U.S. government and public.

days.guide: Read background on Armenians as a Christian minority in the Ottoman Empire and the 1915 events (arrests of April 24, deportations into the Syrian desert). The student builds a short timeline and notes the wartime context the government used as cover.

questions.q: When did the Armenian Genocide begin?
questions.a: April 24, 1915, with the arrest of Armenian leaders in Constantinople.

questions.q: About how many Armenians were killed?
questions.a: About 1 million to 1.5 million.

days.guide: Source Ambassador Henry Morgenthau (U.S. ambassador to the Ottoman Empire, 1913–1916, writing to the State Department and later in his memoir). The student reads his account and one survivor testimony and lists what each reveals about intent and method.

questions.q: What did Morgenthau conclude?
questions.a: That the deportations were a death warrant for a whole race — a deliberate campaign.

days.guide: Read Raphael Lemkin's definition and the UN Genocide Convention (1948). The student makes a chart matching each element of the legal definition to evidence from 1915. Check understanding with the question(s) below; on document days the student must name the source (author, date, purpose) in the answer.

questions.q: Who coined 'genocide'?
questions.a: Raphael Lemkin, in 1944.

questions.q: What is the UN definition?
questions.a: Acts committed with intent to destroy, in whole or part, a national, ethnic, racial or religious group.

days.guide: Give the student casualty data for major WWI nations. They make a bar graph of military deaths by country and discuss the 1918 influenza, which killed an estimated 50 million people worldwide — more than the war.

questions.q: About how many soldiers died in WWI?
questions.a: About 9–10 million.

days.guide: The student writes a one-page reflection on why remembering genocide matters, using Morgenthau or survivor testimony and Lemkin's definition as evidence. Discuss California's large Armenian American community (Fresno, Glendale) and April 24 commemorations.

questions.q: Why does California have a large Armenian community?
questions.a: Many survivors' descendants settled in Fresno and Los Angeles.

weeks.prep: Wilson's Fourteen Points (January 8, 1918; archives.gov), Treaty of Versailles Article 231 and key terms, Keynes's Economic Consequences of the Peace (1919) excerpt, maps of Europe and the Middle East in 1914 and 1923, Dada images and Remarque's All Quiet on the Western Front quotes. Prepare the Unit 5 test.
misconceptions: Thinking the Fourteen Points became the treaty. Most were dropped; the treaty punished Germany.
Believing the U.S. joined the League of Nations. The Senate rejected the treaty and the League.
weeks.assessment_key: Unit 5 test (sample answers): 1) MAIN causes. 2) Marne → led to trench stalemate. 3) Zimmermann Telegram → German offer to Mexico. 4) Armenian Genocide → 1915, Ottoman government, about 1–1.5 million killed. 5) Fourteen Points → open diplomacy, freedom of the seas, free trade, arms reduction, self-determination, League of Nations. 6) Article 231 → Germany accepts responsibility for causing all loss and damage (war guilt). 7) Treaty terms → reparations, army limited to 100,000, no air force, Rhineland demilitarized, Alsace-Lorraine to France, colonies lost. 8) New nations → Poland, Czechoslovakia, Yugoslavia, Austria, Hungary, Finland, Estonia, Latvia, Lithuania. 9) Mandates → Syria and Lebanon (France); Iraq, Palestine, Transjordan (Britain). Document analysis: source and interpret Keynes (British economist warning harsh reparations would ruin Germany and Europe).

days.guide: Read the Fourteen Points together. The student summarizes each in a few words and ranks the five most important with reasons. Check understanding with the question(s) below; on document days the student must name the source (author, date, purpose) in the answer.

questions.q: What was Wilson's fourteenth point?
questions.a: A general association of nations — the League of Nations — to guarantee independence and territorial integrity.

questions.q: What does 'self-determination' mean?
questions.a: The right of national groups to choose their own government.

days.guide: Assign roles: Wilson (just peace, League), Clemenceau (punish Germany, security for France), Lloyd George (punish but keep Germany as trading partner), Orlando (territory for Italy). Negotiate terms, then compare to the actual treaty (signed June 28, 1919).

questions.q: What did Clemenceau want?
questions.a: Harsh terms — reparations, a weakened German military, and security for France.

questions.q: What does Article 231 say?
questions.a: Germany accepts responsibility for causing all the loss and damage of the war (the 'war guilt clause').

days.guide: Place 1914 and 1923 maps side by side. The student lists empires that disappeared, new nations in Eastern Europe, and League mandates in the Middle East, then predicts one problem new borders might cause.

questions.q: Which empires collapsed after WWI?
questions.a: The German, Austro-Hungarian, Russian and Ottoman Empires.

questions.q: What were mandates?
questions.a: Former Ottoman and German territories administered by Britain or France under the League of Nations, supposedly until ready for independence.

days.guide: Show two Dada artworks (e.g., Duchamp's 'Fountain' or Hannah Höch's collage) and read Remarque quotes from All Quiet on the Western Front. The student explains in a paragraph why postwar artists and writers rejected old ideals.

questions.q: What did Remarque mean by a generation 'destroyed by the war'?
questions.a: Even survivors were physically and psychologically damaged and lost faith in old ideals.

days.guide: Give the Unit 5 test from the assessment key, including the Keynes document analysis (about 50 minutes). Grade together and have the student correct missed items with notes. Check understanding with the question(s) below; on document days the student must name the source (author, date, purpose) in the answer.

questions.q: What did Keynes predict about the treaty?
questions.a: Harsh reparations would ruin Germany's economy, hurt all of Europe, and could lead to future conflict.

weeks.prep: Lenin's April Theses excerpt (1917), Soviet propaganda posters (five-year plans, collectivization), Holodomor survivor testimony (preview: descriptions of starvation), doctored Soviet photographs (e.g., Yezhov removed from a photo with Stalin).
misconceptions: Confusing the February and October Revolutions. February ended the tsar; October brought the Bolsheviks to power.
Thinking Stalin's policies were economically successful at no cost. Industrial output rose, but millions died.
weeks.assessment_key: Quiz (answers): 1) February 1917 → Tsar Nicholas II abdicates; Provisional Government forms. 2) April Theses → 'Peace, Land, Bread'; 'All power to the soviets.' 3) October 1917 → Bolsheviks seize power. 4) War Communism → state control of industry and grain requisitioning during the civil war (1918–21). 5) NEP (1921) → allowed some private trade. 6) Collectivization → peasants forced into collective farms; kulaks targeted. 7) Holodomor → 1932–33 man-made famine in Ukraine, millions died (about 3.5–5 million). 8) Great Purge → 1936–38, about 750,000 executed. Photo analysis: full credit for identifying the alteration, its purpose, and what it reveals about Stalin's regime.

days.guide: Draw a two-column chart: February 1917 (bread riots, soldiers mutiny, Tsar abdicates, Provisional Government) and October 1917 (Bolsheviks seize power). Read the April Theses excerpt; the student explains why Lenin's slogans appealed to workers, peasants and soldiers.

questions.q: What did Lenin promise in the April Theses?
questions.a: 'Peace, Land, Bread' and 'All power to the soviets.'

questions.q: Why was the Provisional Government unpopular?
questions.a: It kept Russia in WWI and delayed land reform.

days.guide: Explain the Civil War (1918–21) between Bolshevik Reds and anti-Bolshevik Whites, War Communism's grain seizures, and Lenin's retreat to the NEP in 1921. The student writes a cause-effect chain from War Communism to the NEP.

questions.q: Why did Lenin introduce the NEP?
questions.a: War Communism had wrecked the economy; the NEP allowed some private trade.

days.guide: Show two Soviet posters about five-year plans and collectivization. The student identifies the message and compares it with data on industrial growth and peasant resistance (slaughtering livestock, kulak deportations). Check understanding with the question(s) below; on document days the student must name the source (author, date, purpose) in the answer.

questions.q: What were the goals of the five-year plans?
questions.a: Rapid industrialization — steel, coal, machinery.

days.guide: Read a Holodomor survivor testimony (preview first) and a short reading on the Great Purge. Then show a doctored photo pair (Stalin with and without Yezhov); the student explains what was altered and why.

questions.q: What was the Holodomor?
questions.a: A man-made famine in Ukraine in 1932–33 caused by collectivization and grain seizures.

days.guide: Give the quiz from the assessment key without notes (about 20 minutes). Grade it together; for each missed item the student finds the answer in their notes and writes a one-sentence correction. Then check the photo analysis.

questions.q: Why did Stalin doctor photographs?
questions.a: To erase purged officials from history.

weeks.prep: Review notes; prepare the semester exam: multiple choice, a map section, a short document set, and a short essay.
misconceptions: Memorizing dates without understanding causes and effects.
Skipping sourcing on document questions.
weeks.assessment_key: Semester exam (sample answers): 1) Locke's natural rights → life, liberty, property. 2) Montesquieu → separation of powers. 3) Haiti → first Black republic, 1804. 4) Napoleonic Code → legal equality for men. 5) Factory Act 1833 → limited child labor. 6) Berlin Conference → divided Africa without Africans. 7) MAIN causes. 8) Article 231 → war guilt. 9) April Theses → 'Peace, Land, Bread.' Essay rubric (4-point): thesis, evidence, sourcing, analysis.

days.guide: The student builds a review chart of the American, Haitian, French, Latin American and Russian revolutions: causes, key ideas, leaders and outcomes. Quiz orally by covering a column. Check understanding with the question(s) below; on document days the student must name the source (author, date, purpose) in the answer.

questions.q: Compare the goals of the American and French Revolutions.
questions.a: Both sought rights and government by consent; the French also sought to end feudal privilege.

days.guide: The student makes flashcards for industrialization and imperialism (terms on front, definition and an example on back) and answers five cause-effect questions in writing. Check understanding with the question(s) below; on document days the student must name the source (author, date, purpose) in the answer.

questions.q: What caused the Scramble for Africa?
questions.a: Industrial demand for raw materials, nationalism and new technology.

days.guide: Give a short timed document set on WWI (three or four documents, 30 minutes). Review answers together, checking that each response sources the document. Check understanding with the question(s) below; on document days the student must name the source (author, date, purpose) in the answer.

questions.q: What should every document answer include?
questions.a: Sourcing, the document's main idea, and its connection to the question.

days.guide: Give the semester exam from the assessment key (about 90 minutes, can split across the morning). Grade with the key and rubric. Check understanding with the question(s) below; on document days the student must name the source (author, date, purpose) in the answer.

questions.q: What was the war guilt clause?
questions.a: Article 231 of the Treaty of Versailles.

days.guide: Return the exam; the student corrects each error with a one-sentence explanation. Then they choose one historical thinking skill to improve next semester (sourcing, contextualization, corroboration or close reading) and write how they'll practice it.

questions.q: Name a historical thinking skill.
questions.a: Sourcing, contextualization, corroboration, or close reading.

weeks.prep: Unemployment data 1929–1933 (Germany, Britain, U.S.), Mussolini's 'The Doctrine of Fascism' (1932) excerpt, USHMM pages on Nazi propaganda and the Nuremberg Laws, 1923 hyperinflation photographs. Prepare the Unit 6 test and a blank totalitarian-regimes comparison chart.
misconceptions: Thinking Hitler seized power in a coup. He was appointed chancellor legally (January 1933), then used the Reichstag fire and Enabling Act to destroy democracy.
Treating fascism and communism as the same. Both were totalitarian, but fascism was ultra-nationalist and kept private property; communism aimed at a classless society and state ownership.
weeks.assessment_key: Unit 6 test (sample answers): 1) Peak unemployment → Germany about 30% (6 million registered, 1932), U.S. about 25% (1933), Britain about 20%. 2) Fascism's core ideas → extreme nationalism, the state above the individual ('Everything within the state, nothing outside the state, nothing against the state'), glorification of war, anti-communism, anti-liberalism, a single leader. 3) Hitler appointed chancellor → January 30, 1933. 4) Reichstag fire → February 27, 1933; used to suspend civil liberties. 5) Enabling Act → March 1933, let Hitler make laws without the Reichstag. 6) Nuremberg Laws (1935) → stripped Jews of citizenship and banned marriage between Jews and non-Jews. Comparison chart (Stalin, Mussolini, Hitler): leader, ideology, economic system, methods of control (secret police, propaganda, censorship, terror), targets.

days.guide: The student graphs unemployment for Germany, Britain and the U.S. 1929–1933 and explains how economic crisis made extremist promises appealing. Check understanding with the question(s) below; on document days the student must name the source (author, date, purpose) in the answer.

questions.q: Why did the Great Depression help extremist parties?
questions.a: Mass unemployment and despair made people lose faith in democratic governments and turn to leaders promising jobs, order and national pride.

days.guide: Source the Doctrine of Fascism (1932, Mussolini and Giovanni Gentile). The student lists fascism's core ideas. Check understanding with the question(s) below; on document days the student must name the source (author, date, purpose) in the answer.

questions.q: What is fascism's view of the individual and the state?
questions.a: The individual exists for the state: 'Everything within the state, nothing outside the state, nothing against the state.'

questions.q: When and how did Mussolini come to power?
questions.a: 1922, after the March on Rome, when the king appointed him prime minister.

days.guide: Trace the Weimar crises (Versailles, 1923 hyperinflation, Depression), the 1932–33 elections, Hitler's appointment, the Reichstag fire and the Enabling Act on a timeline. Check understanding with the question(s) below; on document days the student must name the source (author, date, purpose) in the answer.

questions.q: How did Hitler use the Reichstag fire?
questions.a: He blamed communists and had emergency decrees suspend civil liberties, then arrested opponents.

questions.q: What did the Enabling Act do?
questions.a: Allowed Hitler's cabinet to pass laws without the Reichstag — effectively creating a dictatorship.

days.guide: Analyze Nazi propaganda and the Nuremberg Laws using USHMM sources. Check understanding with the question(s) below; on document days the student must name the source (author, date, purpose) in the answer.

questions.q: What did the Nuremberg Laws (1935) do?
questions.a: Stripped German Jews of citizenship and banned marriage and relationships between Jews and non-Jews.

days.guide: The student completes the totalitarian regimes comparison chart, then takes the Unit 6 test. Check understanding with the question(s) below; on document days the student must name the source (author, date, purpose) in the answer.

questions.q: Name three methods totalitarian regimes used to control people.
questions.a: Secret police, propaganda, censorship, terror and purges, and control of education and youth groups.

weeks.prep: Chamberlain's 'peace for our time' statement (September 30, 1938), Churchill's Commons speech on Munich (October 5, 1938), maps of 1930s aggression, readings on Nanjing (preview: mass killing and sexual violence), U.S. Neutrality Acts summary, Nazi-Soviet Pact.
misconceptions: Judging appeasement only with hindsight. In 1938 many Britons feared another world war and believed Germany had legitimate grievances.
Forgetting Asia. Japan's aggression began in Manchuria in 1931.
weeks.assessment_key: Debate rubric (4-point): clear position; at least three pieces of evidence (e.g., British unpreparedness, public fear of war, Dominions' reluctance vs. Hitler's broken promises, Czechoslovakia's defenses lost, Churchill's warnings); rebuttal; civil delivery. Exit ticket answer: 'Appeasement was the policy of giving in to an aggressor's demands to avoid war; at Munich, Britain and France allowed Germany to annex the Sudetenland.'

days.guide: On a map of East Asia, the student marks Manchuria (1931) and the invasion of China (1937). Read a short account of the Nanjing massacre (preview first) and discuss how the League of Nations' failure encouraged further aggression.

questions.q: What happened at Nanjing (1937–38)?
questions.a: Japanese troops massacred tens of thousands to an estimated 200,000–300,000 Chinese civilians and prisoners and committed mass rapes.

questions.q: How did the League of Nations respond to Manchuria?
questions.a: It condemned Japan, and Japan simply left the League — showing the League's weakness.

days.guide: The student maps Ethiopia (1935), the Rhineland (1936), Anschluss (1938) and the Sudetenland (1938). Check understanding with the question(s) below; on document days the student must name the source (author, date, purpose) in the answer.

questions.q: Which treaty did Hitler violate by remilitarizing the Rhineland?
questions.a: The Treaty of Versailles (and Locarno).

days.guide: Source both speeches (Chamberlain returning from Munich, September 30, 1938; Churchill in the House of Commons, October 5, 1938). The student charts each speaker's claims and evidence and predicts which view events proved right.

questions.q: What did Chamberlain claim after Munich?
questions.a: 'Peace for our time.'

questions.q: How did Churchill describe Munich?
questions.a: 'A total and unmitigated defeat.'

days.guide: Analyze the U.S. Neutrality Acts and the Nazi-Soviet Pact (August 1939). Check understanding with the question(s) below; on document days the student must name the source (author, date, purpose) in the answer.

questions.q: What did the Nazi-Soviet Pact secretly include?
questions.a: A plan to divide Poland and Eastern Europe between Germany and the USSR.

days.guide: Hold a 15-minute debate on whether appeasement could have been reasonable in 1938; the student argues one side with three pieces of evidence, then switches. End with the exit ticket in the assessment key.

questions.q: What event ended appeasement?
questions.a: Germany's seizure of the rest of Czechoslovakia (March 1939) and invasion of Poland (September 1, 1939).

weeks.prep: WWII maps of Europe and the Pacific, FDR's 'Day of Infamy' speech audio (December 8, 1941), Eisenhower's D-Day Order of the Day and his unused 'in case of failure' note (National Archives / Eisenhower Library).
misconceptions: Seeing the war as won mainly on the Western Front. The Eastern Front saw most German casualties.
Thinking Pearl Harbor caused U.S. entry into the European war directly. Germany declared war on the U.S. on December 11, 1941.
weeks.assessment_key: Quiz (answers): 1) Blitzkrieg → 'lightning war' using tanks and aircraft. 2) Battle of Britain (1940) → RAF stopped Germany's air campaign, preventing invasion. 3) Operation Barbarossa → German invasion of the USSR, June 22, 1941. 4) Stalingrad → German 6th Army surrendered February 1943; turning point in the East. 5) Pearl Harbor → December 7, 1941. 6) Midway (June 1942) → U.S. sank four Japanese carriers; Pacific turning point. 7) Island hopping → capturing key islands while bypassing others. 8) D-Day → June 6, 1944, Normandy. 9) V-E Day → May 8, 1945.

days.guide: The student maps Axis conquests 1939–1941 (Poland, Denmark, Norway, Low Countries, France, Balkans, invasion of the USSR) and explains blitzkrieg. Read a short account of the Battle of Britain and discuss why it mattered.

questions.q: Why was the Battle of Britain significant?
questions.a: The RAF prevented German air superiority, so Hitler postponed invading Britain.

days.guide: Read a short account of Stalingrad (August 1942–February 1943) and look at a map of the Eastern Front. The student writes a paragraph explaining why it was a turning point using two pieces of evidence.

questions.q: Why was Stalingrad a turning point?
questions.a: Germany lost an entire army, and the Soviets began pushing west.

days.guide: Play FDR's 'Day of Infamy' speech (about 7 minutes). The student notes its rhetoric, then maps Pearl Harbor, Midway and the island-hopping route toward Japan. Check understanding with the question(s) below; on document days the student must name the source (author, date, purpose) in the answer.

questions.q: What phrase did FDR use?
questions.a: 'A date which will live in infamy.'

questions.q: Why was Midway a turning point?
questions.a: The U.S. sank four Japanese aircraft carriers.

days.guide: Read Eisenhower's Order of the Day ('You are about to embark upon the Great Crusade') and his unused failure note. The student compares tone and purpose and explains what the note reveals about leadership.

questions.q: What did Eisenhower's unused note say?
questions.a: The landings failed and 'if any blame or fault attaches to the attempt it is mine alone.'

days.guide: Give the quiz from the assessment key without notes (about 20 minutes). Grade it together; for each missed item the student finds the answer in their notes and writes a one-sentence correction.

questions.q: When did Japan surrender?
questions.a: August 15, 1945 (formally signed September 2, 1945).

weeks.prep: USHMM primary sources (photographs, documents), Wannsee Conference minutes excerpt (January 20, 1942), survivor testimony (USC Shoah Foundation IWitness). Parent preview: graphic content; allow processing time and coordinate with Night in English.
misconceptions: Seeing the Holocaust as sudden. It escalated step by step from 1933 discrimination to 1941–45 mass murder.
Assuming victims did not resist. Resistance included armed uprisings, smuggling and preserving culture.
weeks.assessment_key: Testimony response rubric (4-point): summarizes the survivor's experience accurately; connects to specific events in Night; reflects on the importance of testimony; uses respectful language.

days.guide: Using USHMM sources, the student builds a timeline from the April 1933 boycott through the Nuremberg Laws (1935) to Kristallnacht (November 9–10, 1938), noting how persecution escalated step by step.

questions.q: What happened on Kristallnacht?
questions.a: Nazi-organized attacks destroyed synagogues and Jewish businesses; about 30,000 Jewish men were sent to camps.

days.guide: Show ghetto photographs (e.g., Warsaw or Łódź) and a short Einsatzgruppen report excerpt from USHMM (preview first). The student sources each and describes what it shows about conditions and policy.

questions.q: Who were the Einsatzgruppen?
questions.a: Mobile killing units that shot Jews and others in the occupied USSR after June 1941.

days.guide: Read the Wannsee Conference (January 20, 1942) minutes excerpt. The student underlines euphemisms and rewrites each in plain language, then explains why officials used such language. Check understanding with the question(s) below; on document days the student must name the source (author, date, purpose) in the answer.

questions.q: What euphemisms appear in the Wannsee minutes?
questions.a: 'Final Solution,' 'evacuation to the East,' 'treated accordingly.'

days.guide: The student researches the Warsaw Ghetto Uprising (April–May 1943) and two rescuers or rescue efforts (Danish rescue of about 7,000 Jews; Chiune Sugihara's visas). They write a paragraph on forms of resistance and rescue.

questions.q: What happened in Denmark in 1943?
questions.a: Danes ferried about 7,000 Jews to safety in Sweden.

questions.q: Who was Chiune Sugihara?
questions.a: A Japanese diplomat in Lithuania who issued thousands of visas to Jewish refugees.

days.guide: Watch a survivor testimony on IWitness (about 10–15 minutes). The student writes a one-page response connecting specific moments to Night from English class. Allow time to talk. Check understanding with the question(s) below; on document days the student must name the source (author, date, purpose) in the answer.

questions.q: How many Jews were murdered in the Holocaust?
questions.a: About 6 million.

weeks.prep: Executive Order 9066 (February 19, 1942), Truman's statement on Hiroshima (August 6, 1945), the Franck Report (June 1945) excerpt, a Hiroshima survivor account (e.g., from John Hersey's Hiroshima), WWII casualty data by country. Parent preview: survivor accounts describe severe burns and death.
misconceptions: Thinking only soldiers died in WWII. Most deaths were civilians.
Presenting the atomic bomb decision as having only one side.
weeks.assessment_key: Seminar rubric (4-point): clear position; uses four documents accurately (Truman's statement, the Franck Report, a survivor account, casualty data or an invasion estimate); considers alternatives (demonstration, blockade, waiting for Soviet entry, modifying surrender terms); responds to others.

days.guide: Compare home fronts in the U.S., Britain, USSR and Japan (rationing, women's work, propaganda). Read Executive Order 9066 and a Japanese American incarceration account; the student explains the constitutional issues.

questions.q: What did EO 9066 lead to?
questions.a: The forced removal and incarceration of about 120,000 Japanese Americans, most of them U.S. citizens.

questions.q: How did the U.S. later respond?
questions.a: The Civil Liberties Act of 1988 apologized and paid $20,000 to each surviving incarceree.

days.guide: Source Truman's statement (August 6, 1945) and the Franck Report (June 1945, scientists' recommendation). The student charts arguments for using the bomb and alternatives proposed. Check understanding with the question(s) below; on document days the student must name the source (author, date, purpose) in the answer.

questions.q: What did the Franck Report recommend?
questions.a: A demonstration of the bomb on an uninhabited area before using it on a city.

days.guide: Read a Hiroshima survivor account (e.g., from John Hersey's Hiroshima) aloud together; preview first. The student writes what the source adds that official statements leave out. Check understanding with the question(s) below; on document days the student must name the source (author, date, purpose) in the answer.

questions.q: About how many died in Hiroshima by the end of 1945?

days.guide: Give casualty data by country. The student graphs military and civilian deaths and explains why China and the USSR suffered so heavily. Check understanding with the question(s) below; on document days the student must name the source (author, date, purpose) in the answer.

questions.q: Which country suffered the most deaths?
questions.a: The Soviet Union (about 24–27 million).

days.guide: Hold a 20-minute seminar: Was the atomic bombing justified? The student uses four documents and considers alternatives. Score with the seminar rubric. Check understanding with the question(s) below; on document days the student must name the source (author, date, purpose) in the answer.

questions.q: When were the bombs dropped?
questions.a: August 6 (Hiroshima) and August 9 (Nagasaki), 1945.

weeks.prep: DBQ document set on the causes of WWII (Versailles terms, hyperinflation photo, Depression data, Mein Kampf excerpt on living space, Chamberlain's statement, Nazi-Soviet Pact), readings on Nuremberg trials. Prepare the Unit 7 test.
misconceptions: Writing a DBQ that summarizes documents one by one. Group documents by argument.
Thinking Nuremberg tried only top Nazis. Later trials tried doctors, judges and others.
weeks.assessment_key: DBQ rubric (4-point per row): Thesis — directly answers the question with a defensible claim; Evidence — uses at least 4 documents accurately plus outside knowledge; Sourcing — explains author, purpose, audience or context for at least 2 documents; Analysis — groups documents and explains how they support the claim; Writing — organized, clear. 17–20 = proficient. Unit 7 test (sample answers): Pearl Harbor, Stalingrad, Midway, D-Day, Wannsee, Kristallnacht, EO 9066, Hiroshima; Nuremberg charges — conspiracy, crimes against peace, war crimes, crimes against humanity; 'following orders' was not accepted as a defense.

days.guide: Give the DBQ document set on the causes of WWII. The student sources each document and groups them into categories (economic, political, diplomatic) and drafts a thesis. Check understanding with the question(s) below; on document days the student must name the source (author, date, purpose) in the answer.

questions.q: How should DBQ documents be grouped?
questions.a: By argument or theme (e.g., economic, political, diplomatic).

days.guide: The student writes the DBQ essay in a timed session (about 50 minutes). Score with the DBQ rubric. Check understanding with the question(s) below; on document days the student must name the source (author, date, purpose) in the answer.

questions.q: What makes a strong DBQ thesis?
questions.a: A specific, arguable claim that answers the question and previews categories.

days.guide: Read about the Nuremberg trials (1945–46). The student lists the four charges and explains why 'crimes against humanity' was a new legal idea. Check understanding with the question(s) below; on document days the student must name the source (author, date, purpose) in the answer.

questions.q: What were the Nuremberg charges?
questions.a: Conspiracy, crimes against peace, war crimes and crimes against humanity.

days.guide: The student reviews WWII terms with flashcards and a matching game. Quiz orally on terms that were missed. Check understanding with the question(s) below; on document days the student must name the source (author, date, purpose) in the answer.

questions.q: Define appeasement.
questions.a: Giving in to an aggressor's demands to avoid war.

days.guide: Give the Unit 7 test from the assessment key. Grade together and correct missed items. Check understanding with the question(s) below; on document days the student must name the source (author, date, purpose) in the answer.

questions.q: Why was 'following orders' rejected at Nuremberg?
questions.a: Individuals are responsible for crimes even if ordered.

weeks.prep: Churchill's 'Iron Curtain' speech (March 5, 1946), Stalin's response, Truman Doctrine speech (March 12, 1947), Marshall Plan summary, UN Charter preamble, alliance maps.
misconceptions: Thinking the Cold War began only in 1947. Tensions grew from Yalta and 1945–46.
Confusing containment with rollback.
weeks.assessment_key: Quiz (answers): 1) Yalta → February 1945, divided Germany into zones, promised free elections in Eastern Europe, USSR to join the war against Japan. 2) UN Charter → signed June 26, 1945 in San Francisco. 3) Iron Curtain → 'From Stettin in the Baltic to Trieste in the Adriatic.' 4) Truman Doctrine → support free peoples resisting subjugation (Greece, Turkey). 5) Marshall Plan → about $13 billion for European recovery. 6) NATO → 1949; Warsaw Pact → 1955.

days.guide: Read a summary of the Yalta Conference (February 1945) and the UN Charter preamble. The student lists what each of the Big Three wanted and what was agreed. Check understanding with the question(s) below; on document days the student must name the source (author, date, purpose) in the answer.

questions.q: Where was the UN Charter signed?
questions.a: San Francisco, June 26, 1945.

days.guide: Source Churchill's 'Iron Curtain' speech (March 5, 1946, Fulton, Missouri) and Stalin's response. The student compares claims. Check understanding with the question(s) below; on document days the student must name the source (author, date, purpose) in the answer.

questions.q: Where did Churchill say the Iron Curtain ran?
questions.a: From Stettin in the Baltic to Trieste in the Adriatic.

days.guide: Read the Truman Doctrine speech excerpt and a Marshall Plan summary. The student explains containment and how each policy supported it. Check understanding with the question(s) below; on document days the student must name the source (author, date, purpose) in the answer.

questions.q: What was containment?
questions.a: Preventing the spread of communism.

days.guide: The student maps NATO, the Warsaw Pact and SEATO members with a legend. Discuss why alliances formed. Check understanding with the question(s) below; on document days the student must name the source (author, date, purpose) in the answer.

questions.q: Name three founding NATO members.
questions.a: U.S., Canada, Britain, France (any three of the 12).

days.guide: Give the quiz from the assessment key without notes (about 20 minutes). Grade it together; for each missed item the student finds the answer in their notes and writes a one-sentence correction.

questions.q: What was the Berlin Airlift?
questions.a: U.S. and British planes supplied West Berlin during the Soviet blockade (1948–49).

weeks.prep: Excerpts of Mao's Quotations ('Little Red Book'), Cultural Revolution posters, Red Scarf Girl (Ji-li Jiang) excerpt, famine data for the Great Leap Forward, Korean War map.
misconceptions: Thinking China's communists won quickly. The civil war lasted decades.
Assuming Deng abandoned communism. He kept one-party rule while allowing markets.
weeks.assessment_key: Comparison chart (Mao vs. Deng): Mao — collectivization, communes, Great Leap Forward (1958–62, famine killed an estimated 30–45 million), Cultural Revolution (1966–76), ideology first. Deng — reforms from 1978, household responsibility system, special economic zones (Shenzhen), foreign investment, rapid growth, but one-party rule and Tiananmen Square crackdown (1989).

days.guide: Trace the Nationalist–Communist conflict from the 1920s through the Long March (1934–35) to the Communist victory in 1949. The student builds a timeline. Check understanding with the question(s) below; on document days the student must name the source (author, date, purpose) in the answer.

questions.q: What was the Long March?
questions.a: A 1934–35 retreat of about 6,000 miles by the Communists; it made Mao the leader.

days.guide: The student maps the Korean War's phases (North invasion 1950, Inchon, Chinese entry, stalemate, 1953 armistice). Check understanding with the question(s) below; on document days the student must name the source (author, date, purpose) in the answer.

questions.q: How did the Korean War end?
questions.a: With an armistice in 1953 near the 38th parallel.

days.guide: Read about the Great Leap Forward and look at famine data. The student explains how policy caused famine. Check understanding with the question(s) below; on document days the student must name the source (author, date, purpose) in the answer.

questions.q: What was the Great Leap Forward?
questions.a: Mao's 1958–62 plan for rapid industrialization; it caused a famine killing tens of millions.

days.guide: Show Cultural Revolution posters and read a Red Scarf Girl excerpt. The student analyzes the propaganda and the memoir's perspective. Check understanding with the question(s) below; on document days the student must name the source (author, date, purpose) in the answer.

questions.q: Who were the Red Guards?
questions.a: Young people who attacked 'class enemies' during the Cultural Revolution.

days.guide: The student completes the Mao vs. Deng comparison chart from the assessment key. Check understanding with the question(s) below; on document days the student must name the source (author, date, purpose) in the answer.

questions.q: What were special economic zones?
questions.a: Areas open to foreign investment and markets, like Shenzhen.

weeks.prep: Gandhi's letter to Lord Irwin (March 2, 1930), Nehru's 'Tryst with Destiny' (August 14–15, 1947), Nkrumah's independence speech (March 6, 1957), the Balfour Declaration (November 2, 1917), apartheid law summaries.
misconceptions: Thinking decolonization was peaceful everywhere. India's partition and Algeria's war were very violent.
Seeing apartheid as just informal segregation. It was a legal system.
weeks.assessment_key: Quiz (answers): 1) Salt March → 1930, Gandhi's 240-mile march to protest the salt tax. 2) Indian independence → August 15, 1947, with partition into India and Pakistan. 3) Partition → about 1 million killed, 10–15 million displaced. 4) Ghana → first sub-Saharan colony to gain independence (1957), led by Nkrumah. 5) Balfour Declaration → British support for 'a national home for the Jewish people' in Palestine while protecting non-Jewish communities' rights. 6) Israel → founded May 14, 1948. 7) Apartheid laws → Population Registration Act, Group Areas Act, pass laws. 8) Mandela → imprisoned 1964–1990, president 1994.

days.guide: Read Gandhi's letter to Lord Irwin and Nehru's 'Tryst with Destiny.' The student analyzes nonviolent strategy and partition's consequences. Check understanding with the question(s) below; on document days the student must name the source (author, date, purpose) in the answer.

questions.q: What did Nehru say at midnight?
questions.a: 'At the stroke of the midnight hour, when the world sleeps, India will awake to life and freedom.'

days.guide: Read Nkrumah's 1957 speech. The student maps African independence dates by decade. Check understanding with the question(s) below; on document days the student must name the source (author, date, purpose) in the answer.

questions.q: Why is 1960 called the 'Year of Africa'?
questions.a: Seventeen African nations gained independence.

days.guide: Read the Balfour Declaration. Discuss how the Holocaust increased support for Israel and the rise of Arab nationalism. Check understanding with the question(s) below; on document days the student must name the source (author, date, purpose) in the answer.

questions.q: How did the Holocaust affect support for Israel?
questions.a: It increased international support for a Jewish state.

days.guide: Read apartheid laws summaries. The student traces Mandela's struggle from the ANC to prison to presidency. Check understanding with the question(s) below; on document days the student must name the source (author, date, purpose) in the answer.

questions.q: What was the Group Areas Act?
questions.a: It assigned racial groups to separate residential areas.

days.guide: Give the quiz from the assessment key without notes (about 20 minutes). Grade it together; for each missed item the student finds the answer in their notes and writes a one-sentence correction.

questions.q: Who led Ghana to independence?
questions.a: Kwame Nkrumah.

weeks.prep: Nuclear stockpile data (e.g., Federation of American Scientists or Our World in Data), JFK's October 22, 1962 address (JFK Library), summaries of Khrushchev's October 26 and 27 letters, photographs of Budapest 1956 and Prague 1968, Solidarity's 21 demands (August 1980).
misconceptions: Thinking the Cuban Missile Crisis ended with a one-sided Soviet retreat. The U.S. pledged not to invade Cuba and secretly agreed to remove missiles from Turkey.
Assuming Eastern Europeans accepted Soviet control. Uprisings recurred in 1953, 1956, 1968 and 1980.
weeks.assessment_key: Short constructed responses (answers): 1) Stockpiles → U.S. peaked around 31,000 warheads (1967); USSR peaked around 40,000 (mid-1980s). 2) Cuban Missile Crisis resolution → USSR removed missiles from Cuba; U.S. promised not to invade Cuba and secretly removed Jupiter missiles from Turkey. 3) Hungary 1956 → reform government under Imre Nagy crushed by Soviet tanks. 4) Prague Spring 1968 → Dubček's 'socialism with a human face' ended by Warsaw Pact invasion. 5) Vietnam as Cold War conflict → U.S. fought to contain communism (domino theory); North Vietnam supported by USSR and China; Saigon fell 1975. 6) Solidarity → independent trade union led by Lech Wałęsa; demands included free unions, the right to strike, freedom of speech, release of political prisoners. Score 2 points each for accuracy and explanation.

days.guide: The student graphs U.S. and Soviet stockpiles 1945–1990 and explains MAD (mutually assured destruction). Check understanding with the question(s) below; on document days the student must name the source (author, date, purpose) in the answer.

questions.q: What does 'mutually assured destruction' mean?
questions.a: Both sides had enough nuclear weapons to destroy each other, so neither could win a nuclear war — which deterred attack.

days.guide: Listen to JFK's address and read summaries of Khrushchev's letters. The student explains how the crisis was resolved. Check understanding with the question(s) below; on document days the student must name the source (author, date, purpose) in the answer.

questions.q: What did JFK announce on October 22, 1962?
questions.a: Soviet missiles in Cuba and a naval 'quarantine' (blockade) of Cuba.

questions.q: How was the crisis resolved?
questions.a: The USSR removed its missiles; the U.S. promised not to invade Cuba and secretly agreed to remove missiles from Turkey.

days.guide: The student builds a chart comparing East Germany 1953, Hungary 1956 and Prague 1968: causes, demands, Soviet response. Check understanding with the question(s) below; on document days the student must name the source (author, date, purpose) in the answer.

questions.q: What was the Prague Spring?
questions.a: Alexander Dubček's 1968 reforms ('socialism with a human face'), crushed by a Warsaw Pact invasion in August 1968.

days.guide: Read a short summary of the Vietnam War. The student explains it as a Cold War conflict. Check understanding with the question(s) below; on document days the student must name the source (author, date, purpose) in the answer.

questions.q: What was the domino theory?
questions.a: The belief that if one country fell to communism, neighbors would follow.

days.guide: Read Solidarity's 21 demands. The student explains which demands challenged communist rule. Check understanding with the question(s) below; on document days the student must name the source (author, date, purpose) in the answer.

questions.q: Who led Solidarity?
questions.a: Lech Wałęsa, an electrician at the Gdańsk shipyard.

weeks.prep: Soviet economic data (growth rates, consumer shortages), Reagan's 'Tear Down This Wall' (June 12, 1987), photos of the Berlin Wall's fall (November 9, 1989), Gorbachev's resignation speech (December 25, 1991). Prepare the Unit 8 test.
misconceptions: Crediting a single person for the end of the Cold War. Economic failure, Gorbachev's reforms, Western pressure and popular movements all mattered.
Thinking the USSR and Eastern bloc collapsed at once. Eastern Europe broke away in 1989; the USSR dissolved in December 1991.
weeks.assessment_key: Unit 8 test (sample answers): 1) Iron Curtain, containment, Marshall Plan, NATO. 2) Korean War → armistice 1953. 3) Great Leap Forward → famine. 4) Cuban Missile Crisis → October 1962. 5) Glasnost → openness; perestroika → economic restructuring. 6) Berlin Wall fell → November 9, 1989. 7) USSR dissolved → December 1991. DBQ short essay rubric (4-point): thesis on why the Cold War ended, three documents, sourcing, analysis.

days.guide: Show Soviet economic data and photos of shortages. The student explains command economy weaknesses. Check understanding with the question(s) below; on document days the student must name the source (author, date, purpose) in the answer.

questions.q: What problems did the Soviet command economy face?
questions.a: Inefficiency, shortages of consumer goods, low quality, and stagnating growth.

days.guide: Explain glasnost and perestroika. The student predicts their effects. Check understanding with the question(s) below; on document days the student must name the source (author, date, purpose) in the answer.

questions.q: What were glasnost and perestroika?
questions.a: Glasnost: openness, more free speech. Perestroika: restructuring the economy with limited market reforms.

days.guide: Watch Reagan's Berlin speech excerpt and photos of 1989. The student explains the significance. Check understanding with the question(s) below; on document days the student must name the source (author, date, purpose) in the answer.

questions.q: What did Reagan say at the Brandenburg Gate?
questions.a: 'Mr. Gorbachev, tear down this wall!'

days.guide: Read Gorbachev's resignation speech. The student lists reasons for the Soviet collapse. Check understanding with the question(s) below; on document days the student must name the source (author, date, purpose) in the answer.

questions.q: Name three reasons the USSR collapsed.
questions.a: Economic stagnation, costs of the arms race and Afghanistan war, nationalist movements, and reforms that unleashed criticism.

days.guide: Give the Unit 8 test from the assessment key, including the DBQ short essay. Check understanding with the question(s) below; on document days the student must name the source (author, date, purpose) in the answer.

questions.q: When did the USSR dissolve?
questions.a: December 1991.

weeks.prep: Maps of Middle East oil reserves, water sources and religious groups; balanced readings on the Israeli-Palestinian conflict (e.g., BBC, Council on Foreign Relations backgrounders).
misconceptions: Seeing the region as uniform. It includes Arabs, Persians, Turks, Kurds and Jews; Sunni and Shia Muslims, Christians and others.
Thinking conflicts are ancient and unchangeable. Many stem from 20th-century events.
weeks.assessment_key: Written analysis rubric (4-point): evaluates two countries' trends toward or away from freedom and democracy, uses specific evidence (e.g., Tunisia after the Arab Spring, Iran after 1979, Israel's parliamentary democracy), considers multiple perspectives, organized.

days.guide: The student maps oil reserves, major rivers and religious groups in the Middle East. Check understanding with the question(s) below; on document days the student must name the source (author, date, purpose) in the answer.

questions.q: Which Middle Eastern country has the largest proven oil reserves?
questions.a: Saudi Arabia (among Middle Eastern countries).

days.guide: The student builds a timeline of key events from 1948 to the Arab Spring. Check understanding with the question(s) below; on document days the student must name the source (author, date, purpose) in the answer.

questions.q: What happened in 1979 in Iran?
questions.a: The Islamic Revolution overthrew the Shah; Ayatollah Khomeini took power.

questions.q: What territories did Israel capture in 1967?
questions.a: The West Bank, Gaza, East Jerusalem, the Golan Heights and the Sinai.

days.guide: Read balanced perspectives on the Israeli-Palestinian conflict. The student identifies key issues from each perspective. Check understanding with the question(s) below; on document days the student must name the source (author, date, purpose) in the answer.

questions.q: Name the key issues.
questions.a: Borders, Jerusalem, refugees, security, and settlements.

days.guide: The student evaluates trends toward or away from democracy in two countries using evidence. Check understanding with the question(s) below; on document days the student must name the source (author, date, purpose) in the answer.

questions.q: Where did the Arab Spring begin?
questions.a: Tunisia, December 2010.

days.guide: The student writes a short written analysis. Score with the rubric. Check understanding with the question(s) below; on document days the student must name the source (author, date, purpose) in the answer.

questions.q: What triggered the 1990–91 Gulf War?
questions.a: Iraq's invasion of Kuwait.

weeks.prep: Mandela's inaugural speech (May 10, 1994), readings on the Truth and Reconciliation Commission, the Rwandan genocide (preview: mass killing), Mexican Constitution of 1917 excerpt, readings on Chile or Brazil.
misconceptions: Seeing reconciliation as forgetting. The TRC exchanged amnesty for full public truth-telling.
Thinking Mexico was a democracy throughout the 20th century. The PRI held power from 1929 to 2000.
weeks.assessment_key: Comparison outline rubric (4-point): thesis comparing two nations' paths; three points with evidence (e.g., South Africa's TRC; Mexico's PRI era ending 2000; Chile's Pinochet dictatorship 1973–1990 and return to democracy); counterpoint; clear structure.

days.guide: Read Mandela's inaugural speech and about the TRC. The student analyzes its approach to justice. Check understanding with the question(s) below; on document days the student must name the source (author, date, purpose) in the answer.

questions.q: What did Mandela promise at his inauguration?
questions.a: 'Never, never and never again shall it be that this beautiful land will again experience the oppression of one by another.'

questions.q: What did the TRC do?
questions.a: Heard testimony on apartheid-era crimes and offered amnesty for full disclosure.

days.guide: Study the 1994 Rwandan genocide and recovery. The student explains causes and recovery efforts. Check understanding with the question(s) below; on document days the student must name the source (author, date, purpose) in the answer.

questions.q: About how many people were killed in the Rwandan genocide?
questions.a: About 800,000, mostly Tutsi, in about 100 days.

days.guide: Trace Mexico from the PRI era to the 2000 election and NAFTA/USMCA. Check understanding with the question(s) below; on document days the student must name the source (author, date, purpose) in the answer.

questions.q: When did the PRI lose the presidency?
questions.a: In 2000, to Vicente Fox.

days.guide: The student researches Chile or Brazil and compares its path. Check understanding with the question(s) below; on document days the student must name the source (author, date, purpose) in the answer.

questions.q: What happened in Chile in 1973?
questions.a: General Pinochet overthrew President Allende.

days.guide: The student writes a comparison essay outline. Score with the rubric. Check understanding with the question(s) below; on document days the student must name the source (author, date, purpose) in the answer.

questions.q: What does Article 27 of the 1917 Mexican Constitution do?
questions.a: Declares land and subsoil resources the property of the nation.

weeks.prep: Library databases (public library card), CIA World Factbook, World Bank Open Data, Freedom House 'Freedom in the World' scores, UNDP Human Development Index. A research report template.
misconceptions: Using one source type only. Require statistics, at least two primary sources (a speech, constitution or interview) and a scholarly or news source.
Confusing correlation with causation (e.g., 'higher literacy caused democracy'). Teach the student to say 'is associated with' unless evidence shows cause.
weeks.assessment_key: Research report rubric (4-point each): Research question — focused on freedom and development in one nation; Data — at least three indicators (e.g., GDP per capita, literacy rate, life expectancy, Freedom House score) with sources and years; Primary sources — two, accurately sourced; Analysis — explains how history (colonialism, revolution, Cold War) shaped current conditions and distinguishes correlation from causation; Visual — accurate, labeled; Citations — MLA; Presentation — 5 minutes, clear. 22–28 = proficient.

days.guide: Brainstorm nations studied this year (e.g., India, Ghana, South Africa, Mexico, South Korea, Poland). The student picks one and drafts a research question about freedom and development, then revises it to be specific and answerable.

questions.q: Make this question more focused: 'What is Ghana like?'
questions.a: For example: 'How has Ghana's history since independence in 1957 shaped its democracy and economic growth today?'

days.guide: Show the student how to find indicators in the World Factbook, World Bank and Freedom House, recording the year of each figure. The student also finds two primary sources and sources each.

questions.q: What does GDP per capita measure, and what does it miss?
questions.a: Average economic output per person; it doesn't show inequality, or how wealth is distributed.

questions.q: What does a Freedom House score measure?
questions.a: Political rights and civil liberties in a country (rated Free, Partly Free or Not Free).

days.guide: The student drafts the 1,000-word report from an outline: background history, current data, primary-source evidence, analysis, conclusion. Check that every statistic has a citation. Check understanding with the question(s) below; on document days the student must name the source (author, date, purpose) in the answer.

questions.q: Why include the year with every statistic?
questions.a: Data change over time; the year lets readers judge how current and comparable the figure is.

days.guide: Help the student choose a visual: a line graph for change over time, a bar chart for comparisons, or a map. They build it with a title, labeled axes and a source line.

questions.q: Which chart best shows a country's literacy rate from 1960 to 2020?
questions.a: A line graph, because it shows change over time.

days.guide: The student presents for 5 minutes and answers questions. Score the report and presentation with the rubric. Check understanding with the question(s) below; on document days the student must name the source (author, date, purpose) in the answer.

questions.q: What should the conclusion of the presentation answer?
questions.a: The research question — a clear claim about freedom and development supported by the key evidence.

weeks.prep: World Bank or Our World in Data trade figures, 20 household products with country-of-origin labels, a blank world map. Readings on the WTO, IMF and EU; a short history of Silicon Valley.
misconceptions: Thinking globalization benefits everyone equally. Consumers gain cheaper goods while some workers and regions lose jobs.
Confusing the WTO (trade rules), IMF (financial stability and emergency loans) and World Bank (development loans).
weeks.assessment_key: Map: full credit for 20 products correctly plotted with a legend and two observations (e.g., many electronics from China, produce from Mexico). Quiz (answers): 1) WTO → created 1995 (from GATT, 1947); sets trade rules and settles trade disputes. 2) IMF → created 1944 at Bretton Woods; stabilizes currencies and lends to countries in financial crisis. 3) EU → economic and political union of European nations with a single market; the euro adopted 1999 (coins/notes 2002). 4) Information revolution milestones → satellites (Sputnik 1957), personal computers (1970s–80s), ARPANET (1969), World Wide Web (Tim Berners-Lee, 1989–91). 5) Silicon Valley → Santa Clara Valley region of California; Hewlett-Packard, Intel, Apple, Google. 6) One benefit and one cost of globalization → cheaper goods / job losses in manufacturing regions.

days.guide: The student checks labels on 20 household products and records the country of origin, then plots them on a world map. Discuss patterns and why goods come from where they do.

questions.q: Why are many electronics assembled in East Asia?
questions.a: Lower labor costs, large manufacturing capacity, skilled workforces and established supply chains.

days.guide: Read short descriptions of the WTO, IMF and EU. The student makes a three-column chart: purpose, year founded, one example of its role. Check understanding with the question(s) below; on document days the student must name the source (author, date, purpose) in the answer.

questions.q: What is the difference between the IMF and the WTO?
questions.a: The IMF stabilizes the global financial system and lends to countries in crisis; the WTO sets rules for international trade and settles trade disputes.
