days.guide: The student builds a timeline of the information revolution (TV, satellites, computers, ARPANET, the Web, smartphones) and connects it to Silicon Valley companies in California. Check understanding with the question(s) below; on document days the student must name the source (author, date, purpose) in the answer.

questions.q: Who created the World Wide Web?
questions.a: Tim Berners-Lee at CERN, 1989–1991.

questions.q: Why is Silicon Valley important to the information revolution?
questions.a: Companies there (Intel, Apple, HP, Google) developed key chips, computers and internet services.

days.guide: Give the student data for two countries (e.g., China's poverty rate falling, and manufacturing job losses in a U.S. region). The student identifies winners and losers of globalization. Check understanding with the question(s) below; on document days the student must name the source (author, date, purpose) in the answer.

questions.q: Name one group that has gained and one that has lost from globalization.
questions.a: Gained: consumers (cheaper goods) or workers in new export industries. Lost: workers in industries moved overseas.

days.guide: Give the quiz from the assessment key and check the map. Check understanding with the question(s) below; on document days the student must name the source (author, date, purpose) in the answer.

questions.q: What is outsourcing?
questions.a: Moving production or services to another company or country, often to lower costs.

weeks.prep: UN Sustainable Development Goals (sdgs.un.org), UNHCR Global Trends data, news sources on COVID-19 responses, the Universal Declaration of Human Rights. Op-ed examples from a newspaper.
misconceptions: Thinking global problems can be solved by one country alone. Climate, migration and pandemics cross borders.
Writing an op-ed that is all opinion. Strong op-eds use data and address counterarguments.
weeks.assessment_key: Op-ed rubric (4-point each): Position — clear and specific on a global challenge; Evidence — at least three facts or data points with sources (e.g., UNHCR, WHO, UN); Counterargument — acknowledged and answered; Call to action — realistic; Style — about 600 words, engaging, organized. 16–20 = proficient.

days.guide: Read the list of 17 SDGs together. The student chooses one, reads its targets and progress data, and summarizes why it matters. Check understanding with the question(s) below; on document days the student must name the source (author, date, purpose) in the answer.

questions.q: How many Sustainable Development Goals are there, and what is the deadline?
questions.a: 17 goals, adopted by the UN in 2015, with a target date of 2030.

days.guide: Examine UNHCR data and read two refugee stories. The student explains push and pull factors. Check understanding with the question(s) below; on document days the student must name the source (author, date, purpose) in the answer.

questions.q: What is the difference between a refugee and a migrant?
questions.a: A refugee is forced to flee persecution, war or violence and is protected under international law; a migrant may move for many reasons, including work or family.

questions.q: Give a push factor and a pull factor.
questions.a: Push: war or persecution. Pull: safety or job opportunities.

days.guide: Compare responses to COVID-19 in two or three countries (lockdowns, testing, vaccines). The student evaluates one strength and one weakness of each. Check understanding with the question(s) below; on document days the student must name the source (author, date, purpose) in the answer.

questions.q: When did the WHO declare COVID-19 a pandemic?

days.guide: Choose a current human-rights issue from the news. The student identifies which UDHR articles apply and explains the connection. Check understanding with the question(s) below; on document days the student must name the source (author, date, purpose) in the answer.

questions.q: When was the UDHR adopted, and who led its drafting?
questions.a: December 10, 1948; Eleanor Roosevelt chaired the drafting committee.

days.guide: Read a model op-ed. The student writes a 600-word op-ed on a global challenge with evidence and a call to action. Score with the rubric. Check understanding with the question(s) below; on document days the student must name the source (author, date, purpose) in the answer.

questions.q: What is an op-ed?
questions.a: An opinion essay published opposite the editorial page, arguing a position with evidence.

weeks.prep: Review packet, blank world and Europe maps, a timed document set, and a practice final modeled on the final exam (multiple choice, map, DBQ).
misconceptions: Memorizing isolated facts without themes. Organize review around democracy, nationalism, imperialism, industrialization and conflict.
Skipping map practice; maps carry real points on the final.
weeks.assessment_key: Practice final (sample answers): 1) Locke → natural rights; consent of the governed. 2) Haiti → independence 1804. 3) Factory Act 1833 → limited child labor. 4) Berlin Conference → 1884–85, divided Africa. 5) Article 231 → war guilt. 6) Enabling Act → Hitler's dictatorship (1933). 7) Truman Doctrine → containment (1947). 8) India's independence → 1947 with partition. 9) Berlin Wall → fell November 9, 1989. Map items: locate Sarajevo, the Somme, Stalingrad, Normandy, Hiroshima, Berlin, the Suez Canal, Korea's 38th parallel. Essay: score with the DBQ rubric. DBQ rubric (4-point per row): Thesis — directly answers the question with a defensible claim; Evidence — uses at least 4 documents accurately plus outside knowledge; Sourcing — explains author, purpose, audience or context for at least 2 documents; Analysis — groups documents and explains how they support the claim; Writing — organized, clear. 17–20 = proficient.

days.guide: The student builds a thematic timeline with five colored strands: democracy, nationalism, imperialism, industrialization, global conflict. Each strand needs at least five events from Weeks 1–34. Check understanding with the question(s) below; on document days the student must name the source (author, date, purpose) in the answer.

questions.q: Trace democracy from the course's start to its end in three events.
questions.a: Athenian democracy / Locke and the Enlightenment → the American and French Revolutions → post-1989 democratization in Eastern Europe or South Africa's 1994 election.

days.guide: Give a blank map review: the student labels key places from each unit, then checks against an atlas. Check understanding with the question(s) below; on document days the student must name the source (author, date, purpose) in the answer.

questions.q: Where is the Suez Canal, and why was it important?
questions.a: In Egypt, linking the Mediterranean and Red Seas; it shortened the route between Europe and Asia and was vital to the British Empire.

days.guide: Give a timed document set (40 minutes). Review sourcing and corroboration. Check understanding with the question(s) below; on document days the student must name the source (author, date, purpose) in the answer.

questions.q: What is corroboration?
questions.a: Comparing multiple sources to see where they agree or disagree, to judge reliability.

days.guide: Hold a seminar: What is the most important turning point of the modern era? Each participant defends one with three pieces of evidence. Check understanding with the question(s) below; on document days the student must name the source (author, date, purpose) in the answer.

questions.q: Make a case for the Industrial Revolution as the key turning point.
questions.a: It transformed how people work and live, created modern cities and classes, drove imperialism for raw materials and markets, and enabled the industrial warfare of the 20th century.

days.guide: Give the practice final under timed conditions and grade it together. The student lists the three weakest topics for Week 36 review. Check understanding with the question(s) below; on document days the student must name the source (author, date, purpose) in the answer.

questions.q: What was decided at the Berlin Conference?
questions.a: European powers set rules for claiming African territory (1884–85), without African participation.

weeks.prep: The student's notes and practice-final error list; prepare the two-part final exam (Part 1 multiple choice and map; Part 2 timed DBQ, e.g., 'What caused the end of European empires after 1945?').
misconceptions: Cramming new material instead of fixing known weaknesses.
Misreading the DBQ prompt — underline the task verbs and time period.
weeks.assessment_key: Final exam key: Part 1 — multiple-choice and map items drawn from the course (sample: Montesquieu → separation of powers; Napoleonic Code → legal equality; Sadler Report → child labor; Adwa → Ethiopia defeats Italy 1896; Zimmermann Telegram → Germany-Mexico offer; Holodomor → Ukraine famine 1932–33; Munich → appeasement 1938; Stalingrad → Eastern Front turning point; Marshall Plan → European recovery; Nkrumah → Ghana 1957; glasnost → openness). Part 2 — DBQ rubric (4-point per row): Thesis — directly answers the question with a defensible claim; Evidence — uses at least 4 documents accurately plus outside knowledge; Sourcing — explains author, purpose, audience or context for at least 2 documents; Analysis — groups documents and explains how they support the claim; Writing — organized, clear. 17–20 = proficient. Reflection rubric: 3 = connects at least two historical topics to specific current events with insight; 2 = general connections; 1 = minimal.

days.guide: Using the practice-final error list, the student reviews the three weakest topics with flashcards and one practice question each. Quiz orally at the end. Check understanding with the question(s) below; on document days the student must name the source (author, date, purpose) in the answer.

questions.q: Explain one topic you missed on the practice final in your own words.
questions.a: Answers vary; a good answer corrects the error with specific evidence (e.g., 'The Treaty of Versailles was signed in 1919, not 1918; the armistice was November 11, 1918').

days.guide: Give Part 1 of the final: multiple choice and map (about 60 minutes). Check understanding with the question(s) below; on document days the student must name the source (author, date, purpose) in the answer.

questions.q: Where was the Western Front in WWI?
questions.a: A line of trenches across Belgium and northeastern France from the North Sea to Switzerland.

days.guide: Give Part 2: the timed DBQ (about 60 minutes with 10 minutes to plan). Score with the DBQ rubric. Check understanding with the question(s) below; on document days the student must name the source (author, date, purpose) in the answer.

questions.q: What four things must a strong DBQ include?
questions.a: A thesis, evidence from documents and outside knowledge, sourcing, and analysis that connects evidence to the thesis.

days.guide: Return the exam. The student corrects every error and writes a one-sentence explanation for each. Check understanding with the question(s) below; on document days the student must name the source (author, date, purpose) in the answer.

questions.q: Why write explanations for corrections?
questions.a: Explaining why an answer is right builds understanding and prevents repeating the mistake.

days.guide: The student writes a one-page reflection on how studying history changed their view of current events, with two specific examples. Check understanding with the question(s) below; on document days the student must name the source (author, date, purpose) in the answer.

questions.q: Give an example of how history explains a current event.
questions.a: For example, borders drawn at the Berlin Conference or by post-WWI mandates help explain some conflicts in Africa and the Middle East today.

MATH.overview: Geometry is taught in 60-minute lessons: a short demonstration, guided examples worked together, then independent practice from Khan Academy, CK-12 or Illustrative Mathematics with GeoGebra for constructions. Proof is the heart of the course — require a marked diagram and a reason for every statement, and have the student explain proofs aloud. Grade each Friday check together, log errors, and revisit weak skills before the unit test.

weeks.prep: Gather compass, straightedge, protractor and a notebook for a vocabulary/theorem log. Preview Khan Academy 'Geometry foundations' videos. Write the 7 vocabulary words on cards.
misconceptions: Students treat a line and a segment as the same thing. Insist on notation: line AB has arrows on both ends and no length; segment AB has endpoints and a length.
Reading a protractor from the wrong scale (getting 130° for a 50° angle). Have the student first decide 'acute or obtuse?' before reading the number.
weeks.assessment_key: Quiz items and answers: 1) Define a ray using only undefined terms — part of a line that starts at one point and extends forever in one direction through another point. 2) B is between A and C; AB = 2x + 3, BC = x + 1, AC = 19. Find x and AB — 3x + 4 = 19, x = 5, AB = 13. 3) D is in the interior of ∠ABC; m∠ABD = (3x + 5)°, m∠DBC = 2x°, m∠ABC = 75°. Find x — 5x + 5 = 75, x = 14. 4) Complement and supplement of 38° — 52° and 142°. 5) Vertical angles measure (4x − 10)° and (2x + 30)°. Find each — x = 20, each 70°. 6) A linear pair measures (5x + 10)° and (3x + 10)° — x = 20; 110° and 70°. Score 1 point each; 5–6 = mastery, 3–4 = reteach angle equations.

days.guide: Explain that point, line and plane are 'undefined' — we describe them but every other term is built from them. Model sketching and labeling each (point A, line AB or line ℓ, plane ABC or plane M), then have the student write definitions of segment, ray and angle using only those words. Check that each definition mentions points and lines only.

questions.q: Using only undefined terms, define a segment.
questions.a: A segment AB is the part of a line consisting of two points A and B and all the points between them.

questions.q: How many points determine a plane, and what condition must they meet?
questions.a: Three points that are not on the same line (noncollinear) determine exactly one plane.

days.guide: Draw a number line and show AB + BC = AC when B is between A and C; distance is the absolute value of the difference of coordinates. Work one algebra example together, then assign the 10 problems, checking that the student substitutes x back to find the actual lengths asked.

questions.q: On a number line A is at −3 and C is at 9. What is AC, and where is the midpoint?
questions.a: AC = |9 − (−3)| = 12; the midpoint is at 3.

questions.q: B is between A and C. AB = 3x − 1, BC = 2x + 4, AC = 23. Find x and BC.

days.guide: Model placing the protractor's center on the vertex and the zero line on one ray, then reading the scale that starts at 0 on that ray. Classify angles as acute, right, obtuse or straight, then solve angle-addition equations together before independent practice.

questions.q: m∠PQS = (3x + 5)°, m∠SQR = (x + 15)°, and m∠PQR = 100°. Find x and m∠PQS.
Classify a 90°, a 135° and a 180° angle.
questions.a: Right, obtuse, straight.

days.guide: Define each pair with a quick sketch: complementary sum to 90°, supplementary to 180°, vertical angles are congruent, a linear pair is adjacent and supplementary. Have the student label a diagram of two intersecting lines and then write and solve an equation for each problem.

questions.q: Two angles are complementary. One is 4 times the other. Find both.
questions.a: x + 4x = 90 → x = 18; the angles are 18° and 72°.

questions.q: Two lines intersect and one angle is 47°. Give the other three angles.
questions.a: 133°, 47° (its vertical angle), and 133°.

days.guide: Give the quiz in the assessment key without notes (about 25 minutes). Grade together, and have the student redo any missed item and explain the error aloud.

questions.q: Are all linear pairs supplementary? Are all supplementary angles linear pairs?
questions.a: Yes, every linear pair is supplementary. No — supplementary angles need not be adjacent, so they are not always a linear pair.

weeks.prep: Compass (one that locks is easiest), straightedge, patty paper or tracing paper, and GeoGebra (geogebra.org/geometry) open on a device. Practice the four constructions yourself first so you can demonstrate them.
misconceptions: Changing the compass width in the middle of a construction. Explain that every step relies on 'same radius means same distance.'
Using the ruler's markings to measure. In a construction the straightedge only draws lines; lengths are copied with the compass.
weeks.assessment_key: Performance check (3 constructions from memory, observe each): Perpendicular bisector — arcs from both endpoints with the same radius larger than half the segment; line through the two intersections. Angle bisector — arc from vertex hits both sides; equal arcs from those two points meet; ray from vertex through that point. Parallel through a point — draw a transversal through P and copy the angle at P (corresponding angles). Rubric per construction: 3 = accurate with no erased re-dos and a correct 'why' (equal radii make congruent segments/triangles); 2 = accurate but explanation vague; 1 = steps out of order or radius changed; 0 = not attempted.

days.guide: Demonstrate copying a segment (set compass to AB, swing from a new point) and copying an angle (arc on original, same arc on new ray, then copy the chord width). The student does each twice and writes numbered steps.

questions.q: When copying an angle, why do you set the compass to the distance between where the arc crosses the two sides?
questions.a: That distance is the third side of a triangle; copying it makes the two triangles congruent by SSS, so the angles are congruent.

days.guide: Model the perpendicular bisector and angle bisector, then have the student fold patty paper (segment endpoint onto endpoint; one side of the angle onto the other) to see the fold lands on the constructed line.

questions.q: Why must the compass opening be more than half the segment for a perpendicular bisector?
questions.a: Otherwise the arcs from the two endpoints do not intersect.

questions.q: Every point on a perpendicular bisector has what property?
questions.a: It is equidistant from the two endpoints of the segment.

days.guide: Show the perpendicular through a point (on or off the line) by marking two points on the line equidistant from P and bisecting. For a parallel line, draw a transversal through P and copy the angle. The student does both and labels the congruent angles.

questions.q: Which angle relationship justifies the parallel-line construction?
questions.a: Congruent corresponding angles: if corresponding angles are congruent, the lines are parallel.

days.guide: Have the student use GeoGebra's circle-with-center-through-point and intersect tools (not the built-in bisector button) to rebuild each construction, then drag the original points. A correct construction stays correct when dragged.

questions.q: Why does a correct GeoGebra construction keep working when you drag the points?
questions.a: Because it is built from relationships (circles of equal radius, intersections), not from fixed measurements.

days.guide: Run the performance check in the assessment key: the student performs three constructions from memory and explains each aloud. Score with the rubric.

questions.q: Explain why the angle-bisector construction works.
questions.a: The arc from the vertex gives two equal segments on the sides, the two equal arcs give two more equal segments, and the shared ray is common; the two triangles are congruent by SSS, so the two angles at the vertex are congruent.

weeks.prep: Graph paper, compass, calculator. Review the Pythagorean theorem with the student before Day 2. Prepare the Unit 1 test items listed in the assessment key.
misconceptions: Subtracting coordinates in mixed order in the distance formula. Remind the student squaring removes sign, but both differences must be in the same order (x2 − x1 and y2 − y1).
For partitioning, using the ratio 2:3 as the fraction 2/3. The point is 2/5 of the way, because the whole has 2 + 3 = 5 parts.
weeks.assessment_key: Unit 1 test (sample items with answers): 1) Midpoint of (−4, 7) and (6, −1) → (1, 3). 2) M(2, 5) is the midpoint of AB with A(−1, 8); find B → (5, 2). 3) Distance from (−2, 1) to (4, 9) → √(36 + 64) = 10. 4) Point 1/4 of the way from A(0, 0) to B(8, 12) → (2, 3). 5) Complement of 27° → 63°. 6) Construction: perpendicular bisector of a given segment (graded with the Week 2 rubric). 7) Explain why the inscribed hexagon construction uses the radius as the side length → a regular hexagon is six equilateral triangles whose sides equal the radius. Mastery: 80% or better.

days.guide: Show that the midpoint averages the coordinates, using a segment on graph paper. Practice finding midpoints, then the reverse problem: given a midpoint and one endpoint, find the other by 'stepping' the same change again.

questions.q: Find the midpoint of (2, −3) and (8, 5).
M(4, 1) is the midpoint of AB and A = (1, −2). Find B.
questions.a: From A to M is +3 in x and +3 in y, so B = (7, 4).

days.guide: Draw a segment on the grid, build a right triangle under it, and use a² + b² = c² to derive d = √((x2 − x1)² + (y2 − y1)²). Then have the student find the perimeter of a polygon given by vertices.

questions.q: Find the distance from (1, 2) to (7, 10).
Find the perimeter of the triangle with vertices (0, 0), (3, 0), (0, 4).
questions.a: Sides 3, 4 and 5, so the perimeter is 12.

days.guide: Explain that a 2:3 ratio splits the segment into 5 equal parts, so the point is 2/5 of the way from A. Compute A + (2/5)(B − A) in each coordinate, and check by graphing.

questions.q: Find the point dividing A(0, 0) to B(10, 5) in a 2:3 ratio from A.
questions.a: 2/5 of the change (10, 5) is (4, 2), so the point is (4, 2).

questions.q: Find the point 1/3 of the way from (−3, 6) to (9, 0).
questions.a: Change is (12, −6); 1/3 is (4, −2); the point is (1, 4).

days.guide: Construct the hexagon by marking the radius six times around the circle; connect every other vertex for the equilateral triangle. For the square, draw a diameter, construct its perpendicular bisector to get a second diameter, and connect the four endpoints.

questions.q: Why can you step the radius around a circle exactly six times?
questions.a: Each chord equal to the radius forms an equilateral triangle with the center, giving a 60° central angle; 360° ÷ 60° = 6.

questions.q: How do you inscribe a square in a circle?
questions.a: Draw two perpendicular diameters and connect their four endpoints.

days.guide: Give the Unit 1 test from the assessment key (about 50 minutes, compass allowed). Grade together and log missed skills for review. Allow no notes (formula sheet only if stated); about 30–50 minutes. Grade it together right away: the student reworks every missed item and explains the error aloud, and you note any skill to revisit next week.

questions.q: What does the midpoint formula have in common with an average?
questions.a: Each coordinate of the midpoint is the average (mean) of the two endpoints' coordinates.

weeks.prep: Graph paper, patty paper, colored pencils, GeoGebra. Read through the reflection rules so you can check quickly: over x-axis (x, −y); y-axis (−x, y); y = x (y, x); y = −x (−y, −x).
misconceptions: Mixing up reflections over the x-axis and y-axis. Reflecting over the x-axis keeps x the same and negates y — the figure flips up/down across the x-axis.
Thinking a stretch is a rigid motion because the shape 'looks the same.' Measure: rigid motions preserve every length and angle.
weeks.assessment_key: Quiz with answers: 1) Translate (2, 4) by (x, y) → (x + 3, y − 5) → (5, −1). 2) Write the rule that moves (1, 1) to (−2, 6) → (x, y) → (x − 3, y + 5), vector ⟨−3, 5⟩. 3) Reflect (3, −2) over the x-axis → (3, 2); y-axis → (−3, −2); y = x → (−2, 3); y = −x → (2, −3). 4) A(1, 2) maps to A'(5, 2) by a reflection; name the line → x = 3. 5) Is (x, y) → (2x, y) a rigid motion? → No, it changes horizontal lengths. Score out of 8 points (item 3 = 4 points).

days.guide: Plot a triangle and apply (x, y) → (x + 2, y), then (x, y) → (2x, y). Have the student measure sides and angles in each image and decide which preserve distance and angle; introduce 'rigid motion' and the idea of a transformation as a function from points to points.

questions.q: Does (x, y) → (x, 3y) preserve distance? Explain.
questions.a: No. Vertical distances triple, so lengths change (it is a stretch, not a rigid motion).

questions.q: What two things does every rigid motion preserve?
questions.a: Distance (segment lengths) and angle measure.

days.guide: Model translating a quadrilateral using a rule and using vector notation ⟨a, b⟩. Then the student translates figures and writes the rule from a pre-image and image pair.

questions.q: Translate (−1, 4) by the vector ⟨3, −5⟩.
A(2, 3) maps to A'(−1, 7). Write the translation rule.

days.guide: Reflect a triangle over each axis and over y = x and y = −x on graph paper, recording coordinates in a table so the student discovers each rule.

questions.q: Reflect (4, −1) over y = x and over y = −x.
Reflect (−3, 5) over the y-axis.

days.guide: Trace a figure and its reflection on patty paper, connect each point to its image, and fold to show the mirror line meets every connecting segment at 90° at its midpoint. The student writes the definition of a reflection in their own words.

questions.q: State the definition of a reflection across line ℓ.
questions.a: Each point P maps to P' so that ℓ is the perpendicular bisector of PP' (points on ℓ map to themselves).

questions.q: A(2, 1) reflects to A'(2, 7). What is the line of reflection?
questions.a: y = 4, the perpendicular bisector of the segment from (2, 1) to (2, 7).

days.guide: Give the quiz in the assessment key. Have the student check reflection answers by plotting. Allow no notes (formula sheet only if stated); about 30–50 minutes. Grade it together right away: the student reworks every missed item and explains the error aloud, and you note any skill to revisit next week.

questions.q: Which reflection rule swaps the coordinates?
questions.a: Reflection over y = x: (x, y) → (y, x).

weeks.prep: Protractor, patty paper, compass, phone camera for Day 4, GeoGebra. Memorize the counterclockwise rotation rules about the origin: 90° (−y, x), 180° (−x, −y), 270° (y, −x).
misconceptions: Rotating clockwise when the problem says 90° (positive rotations are counterclockwise). Have the student turn the paper to check direction.
Saying a rectangle has 4 lines of symmetry (its diagonals are not lines of symmetry unless it is a square).
weeks.assessment_key: Quiz with answers: 1) Rotate (2, 5) 90° counterclockwise about the origin → (−5, 2). 2) Rotate (−3, 1) 180° → (3, −1). 3) Rotate (4, −2) 270° counterclockwise → (−2, −4). 4) Lines of symmetry and rotational symmetry: regular pentagon → 5 lines, 72° rotations; rectangle (non-square) → 2 lines, 180°; rhombus (non-square) → 2 lines (diagonals), 180°; square → 4 lines, 90°. Photo set rubric: 3 = three objects, each symmetry correctly named (line count and/or rotation angle); 2 = one error; 1 = symmetries named vaguely; 0 = missing.

days.guide: Rotate a triangle 90° about the origin with patty paper (pin at origin, turn counterclockwise) and record coordinates in a table to find each rule.

questions.q: Rotate (3, 1) 90° counterclockwise about the origin.
What is the rule for a 180° rotation about the origin?

days.guide: Model rotating about point P: draw segment from P to each vertex, use the protractor to make the rotation angle at P, and use the compass to keep the same distance. The student rotates a triangle 60° about a non-origin point.

questions.q: When rotating point A about P, what must be equal for A and its image A'?
questions.a: PA = PA' (same distance from the center), and m∠APA' equals the rotation angle.

questions.q: Rotate (5, 2) 180° about P(1, 1).
questions.a: Shift so P is the origin: (4, 1) → (−4, −1); shift back: (−3, 0).

days.guide: Use cut-out shapes to find lines of symmetry by folding and rotation symmetry by turning in place. Summarize in a table for regular polygons: an n-gon has n lines and rotations by multiples of 360°/n.

questions.q: What rotations carry a regular hexagon onto itself?
How many lines of symmetry does a non-square rhombus have?
questions.a: Two — its diagonals.

days.guide: The student photographs three symmetric objects at home and writes the line and/or rotational symmetry of each. Discuss one together to model precise wording.

questions.q: A hubcap with 5 identical spokes has what rotational symmetry?
questions.a: 72° (and multiples of 72°); it also has 5 lines of symmetry if each spoke is itself symmetric.

days.guide: Give the quiz and score the photo set using the assessment key. Allow no notes (formula sheet only if stated); about 30–50 minutes. Grade it together right away: the student reworks every missed item and explains the error aloud, and you note any skill to revisit next week.

questions.q: Rotate (0, 4) 270° counterclockwise about the origin.

weeks.prep: Graph paper, colored pencils, scissors, tape, cardstock for tessellation; GeoGebra. Look up a few M.C. Escher tessellations to show the student.
misconceptions: Assuming order doesn't matter in compositions. Show a translation then reflection versus the reverse can give different images.
Forgetting that two reflections over parallel lines give a translation of twice the distance between the lines.
weeks.assessment_key: Quiz: 1) Translate (1, 2) by ⟨3, 0⟩ then reflect over the y-axis → (−4, 2); reverse order → (2, 2) — different. 2) Reflect over x = 1 then x = 4 → equivalent to a translation 6 units right. 3) Reflect over two lines meeting at 35° → rotation of 70° about their intersection. 4) Give a sequence mapping triangle A(1, 1), B(3, 1), C(1, 2) to A'(−1, −1), B'(−3, −1), C'(−1, −2) → a 180° rotation about the origin (or reflect over the x-axis then y-axis). Tessellation rubric: 4 = tiles fit without gaps/overlaps, correct transformation named and explained, neat color; 3 = tiles fit, explanation minor gaps; 2 = gaps or wrong transformation named; 1 = incomplete.

days.guide: Have the student translate a triangle and then reflect it, and then do the steps in the reverse order. Compare final images and discuss that compositions are applied one after another like functions.

questions.q: Point (2, 3): translate by ⟨0, −5⟩, then reflect over the x-axis. Where does it end up?
questions.a: (2, −2) after translating, then (2, 2) after reflecting.

days.guide: In GeoGebra reflect a figure over x = 1 and then x = 4; measure the shift (6 units = twice the distance). Then reflect over two lines meeting at 40° and measure the rotation (80°).

questions.q: Two reflections over intersecting lines that meet at 50° equal what single transformation?
questions.a: A rotation of 100° about the intersection point.

days.guide: Model working backward: compare orientation (a flip means a reflection is needed), then match one vertex with a translation or rotation. The student writes sequences for the 8 problems and checks by performing them.

questions.q: If the image has the opposite orientation (clockwise vs. counterclockwise labels), what must the sequence include?
questions.a: An odd number of reflections.

days.guide: Show how to cut a piece from one side of a square and tape it to the opposite side (translation) or rotate it about a corner (rotation). The student traces the tile repeatedly to fill a page and colors it.

questions.q: Why does a modified square still tessellate?
questions.a: Whatever is removed from one side is added to the matching side, so the tiles still fit together without gaps or overlaps.

days.guide: Give the quiz and have the student explain their tessellation aloud: which transformation, and why it fills the plane. Allow no notes (formula sheet only if stated); about 30–50 minutes. Grade it together right away: the student reworks every missed item and explains the error aloud, and you note any skill to revisit next week.

questions.q: Can every composition of rigid motions be described as a single rigid motion?
questions.a: Yes — a composition of rigid motions is itself a rigid motion (a translation, rotation, reflection or glide reflection).

weeks.prep: Patty paper, straws or paper strips cut to lengths (e.g., 4, 5, 6, 7, 9 inches), brads or tape, protractor, GeoGebra. Prepare the Unit 2 test from the assessment key.
misconceptions: Believing SSA or AAA proves congruence. Build counterexamples with straws: AAA gives same shape different sizes; SSA can give two different triangles.
Writing congruence statements with vertices in the wrong order. The order must match corresponding parts: △ABC ≅ △DEF means A↔D, B↔E, C↔F.
weeks.assessment_key: Unit 2 test with answers: 1) Rotate (−2, 5) 90° counterclockwise → (−5, −2). 2) Reflect (4, 1) over y = −x → (−1, −4). 3) Lines of symmetry of a regular octagon → 8. 4) △PQR ≅ △XYZ; list corresponding parts → PQ ≅ XY, QR ≅ YZ, PR ≅ XZ, ∠P ≅ ∠X, ∠Q ≅ ∠Y, ∠R ≅ ∠Z. 5) Which are valid criteria: SSS, SAS, ASA, SSA, AAA → SSS, SAS, ASA (and AAS); not SSA or AAA. 6) Short answer: explain with rigid motions why two triangles with SAS are congruent → translate to match the included vertex, rotate to align one side, the equal side lengths make endpoints match, reflect if needed; the equal included angle makes the second side lie on the same ray and its equal length makes the endpoints coincide, so all three vertices match. 7) Write a sequence mapping one given figure to another (any correct sequence). Mastery 80%.

days.guide: Define congruent figures as figures related by a rigid motion. For each pair, the student uses patty paper to try to map one onto the other and names the motion or explains why none exists (different side lengths).

questions.q: Two triangles have the same angles but different side lengths. Are they congruent?
questions.a: No — no rigid motion maps one onto the other because rigid motions preserve length.

days.guide: Model writing △ABC ≅ △DEF so that matching vertices are in the same order, then listing six pairs of congruent parts. Introduce CPCTC.

questions.q: If △JKL ≅ △RST, which angle is congruent to ∠K and which side to LJ?
questions.a: ∠K ≅ ∠S, and LJ ≅ TR.

days.guide: Give the student sets of straws and challenge them to build two different triangles for each case. SSS, SAS, ASA always produce one triangle; AAA and SSA may not.

questions.q: Why does AAA not prove triangles congruent?
questions.a: Triangles can have the same angles but be different sizes (similar, not congruent).

questions.q: Show SSA can fail.
questions.a: With sides 5 and 7 and a 30° angle not between them, the side of length 5 can swing to two different positions, making two different triangles.

days.guide: Talk through the argument together using patty paper, then the student writes a paragraph: map the included angle's vertex, rotate to line up one side, use equal lengths and equal angle to land the other vertices.

questions.q: In SAS, why must the angle be the included angle?
questions.a: The angle between the two sides fixes the direction of both sides from the common vertex; a non-included angle does not lock the triangle in place.

days.guide: Give the Unit 2 test from the assessment key; review errors together. Allow no notes (formula sheet only if stated); about 30–50 minutes. Grade it together right away: the student reworks every missed item and explains the error aloud, and you note any skill to revisit next week.

questions.q: Name the four triangle congruence shortcuts for general triangles.
questions.a: SSS, SAS, ASA and AAS.

weeks.prep: Notebook. Prepare examples of conditional statements from everyday life (ads, rules). Know these logic terms: converse (swap), inverse (negate both), contrapositive (swap and negate).
misconceptions: Thinking the converse of a true statement is always true. Use 'If it's a dog, then it's a mammal' — its converse is false.
Confusing the Law of Detachment with affirming the conclusion. Knowing q is true does not let you conclude p.
weeks.assessment_key: Quiz with answers: 1) Find a counterexample to 'All prime numbers are odd' → 2. 2) Write 'Right angles are congruent' in if-then form → If two angles are right angles, then they are congruent. 3) For 'If a figure is a square, then it is a rectangle': converse (If a rectangle, then a square) false; inverse (If not a square, then not a rectangle) false; contrapositive (If not a rectangle, then not a square) true. 4) 'If it rains, the game is canceled. It rains.' → The game is canceled (Detachment). 5) 'If A then B; if B then C' → If A then C (Syllogism). 6) Two-column proof: 3(x − 2) = 15 → x − 2 = 5 or 3x − 6 = 15 (Distributive), 3x = 21 (Addition Prop.), x = 7 (Division Prop.). Score 1 point per item; item 3 and 6 worth 3.

days.guide: Show a pattern (sums of consecutive odd numbers: 1, 4, 9, 16) and have the student make a conjecture (inductive), then show how a counterexample disproves a false conjecture. Contrast with deductive reasoning from definitions.

questions.q: Conjecture: 'The square of any number is greater than the number.' Give a counterexample.
Is a conjecture from many examples proven?
questions.a: No — inductive reasoning suggests a conjecture but only a deductive proof establishes it.

days.guide: Model rewriting statements in if-then form and then generating converse, inverse and contrapositive; the student marks each true or false with a counterexample when false. Note the contrapositive always has the same truth value as the original.

questions.q: Write the contrapositive of 'If two angles are vertical, then they are congruent.' Is it true?
questions.a: If two angles are not congruent, then they are not vertical angles. True.

questions.q: Write the converse of 'If x = 3, then x² = 9.' Is it true?
questions.a: If x² = 9, then x = 3. False, since x could be −3.

days.guide: Introduce the Law of Detachment (if p→q and p, then q) and the Law of Syllogism (p→q and q→r gives p→r) with silly and real examples, and have the student decide whether conclusions are valid.

questions.q: 'If you finish chores, you get screen time. You got screen time.' Can you conclude you finished chores?
questions.a: No — that is affirming the conclusion; screen time could have another cause.

questions.q: 'If a shape is a square, it has four right angles. If a shape has four right angles, it is a rectangle.' What follows?
questions.a: If a shape is a square, it is a rectangle (Law of Syllogism).

days.guide: Model a two-column proof that solves 2x + 5 = 17 with a reason for every step (Given, Subtraction Prop. of Equality, Division Prop.). The student writes proofs for 4–5 equations, including one with the Distributive Property.

questions.q: Give the reasons: 5x − 4 = 21 → 5x = 25 → x = 5.
questions.a: Given; Addition Property of Equality; Division Property of Equality.

days.guide: Give the quiz from the assessment key. Allow no notes (formula sheet only if stated); about 30–50 minutes. Grade it together right away: the student reworks every missed item and explains the error aloud, and you note any skill to revisit next week.

questions.q: Which statement is logically equivalent to a conditional: its converse, inverse, or contrapositive?
questions.a: Its contrapositive.

weeks.prep: GeoGebra and protractor. Make a theorem reference sheet listing postulates the student may cite: Linear Pair Postulate, Corresponding Angles Postulate, and the definitions of congruent and supplementary angles.
misconceptions: Citing a theorem's converse when using the theorem (e.g., using 'if lines are parallel...' to prove lines parallel). Ask, 'What do you know, and what are you trying to prove?'
Assuming all angle pairs formed by a transversal are congruent; consecutive (same-side) interior angles are supplementary.
weeks.assessment_key: Proof quiz: Proof 1 (vertical angles congruent) — Statements/reasons: ∠1 and ∠2 are a linear pair, ∠2 and ∠3 are a linear pair (definition/diagram); m∠1 + m∠2 = 180, m∠2 + m∠3 = 180 (Linear Pair Postulate); m∠1 + m∠2 = m∠2 + m∠3 (Substitution); m∠1 = m∠3 (Subtraction); ∠1 ≅ ∠3 (def. of congruent). Proof 2 (lines parallel ⇒ alternate interior congruent) — ℓ ∥ m (Given); ∠1 ≅ ∠5 corresponding (Corresponding Angles Postulate); ∠5 ≅ ∠3 vertical (Vertical Angles Theorem); ∠1 ≅ ∠3 (Transitive). Rubric each proof: 4 = every statement valid with correct reason, logical order; 3 = one missing/incorrect reason; 2 = key step missing; 1 = statements without reasons.

days.guide: Label two intersecting lines with ∠1–∠4. Model the proof statement by statement, then have the student write it again from a blank page.

questions.q: What postulate gives m∠1 + m∠2 = 180° when they form a linear pair?
questions.a: The Linear Pair Postulate (angles that form a linear pair are supplementary).

days.guide: In GeoGebra draw two parallel lines and a transversal; measure all 8 angles and drag the transversal. The student records which pairs stay congruent and which stay supplementary.

questions.q: Two parallel lines are cut by a transversal; one angle is 65°. Name the measure of its alternate interior, corresponding, and same-side interior angles.
questions.a: Alternate interior 65°, corresponding 65°, same-side interior 115°.

days.guide: Prove alternate interior angles congruent using the corresponding angles postulate and vertical angles. The student then proves same-side interior angles are supplementary.

questions.q: Outline why same-side interior angles are supplementary.
questions.a: One of them forms a linear pair with an angle that is congruent (alternate interior) to the other, so their measures add to 180°.

days.guide: Explain converses: congruent corresponding, alternate interior, or alternate exterior angles (or supplementary same-side interior) prove lines parallel. Solve algebra problems where the student finds x that makes lines parallel.

questions.q: Alternate interior angles are (3x + 10)° and (5x − 30)°. What x makes the lines parallel, and what is each angle?
questions.a: 3x + 10 = 5x − 30 → x = 20; each angle is 70°.

questions.q: Same-side interior angles are (2x)° and (x + 30)°. For what x are the lines parallel?

days.guide: Give the two-proof quiz from the assessment key; the student works independently with the theorem reference sheet. Allow no notes (formula sheet only if stated); about 30–50 minutes. Grade it together right away: the student reworks every missed item and explains the error aloud, and you note any skill to revisit next week.

questions.q: What is the difference between a postulate and a theorem?
questions.a: A postulate is accepted without proof; a theorem is proven from definitions, postulates and earlier theorems.

weeks.prep: Patty paper, scissors, paper triangles to tear, GeoGebra, graph paper. Review what centroid, incenter and circumcenter are.
misconceptions: Confusing which segments meet at which center. Memory aid: medians → centroid; angle bisectors → incenter (center of inscribed circle); perpendicular bisectors → circumcenter.
Thinking the exterior angle equals the adjacent interior angle. The exterior angle equals the sum of the two remote interior angles.
weeks.assessment_key: Quiz with answers: 1) Two angles of a triangle are 48° and 77°; the third → 55°. 2) Remote interior angles 40° and 65°; the exterior angle → 105°. 3) An isosceles triangle's vertex angle is 40°; base angles → 70° each. 4) A midsegment is parallel to a side of length 18; its length → 9. 5) Median from vertex A is 12 long; distance from A to the centroid → 8. 6) Which center is equidistant from the three vertices? → circumcenter. From the three sides? → incenter. 7) Short proof: triangle angle sum using a line through one vertex parallel to the opposite side (alternate interior angles + straight angle = 180°).

days.guide: Have the student tear the three corners of a paper triangle and line them up to form a straight angle. Then model the formal proof: draw a line through one vertex parallel to the opposite side and use alternate interior angles. Apply the Exterior Angle Theorem.

questions.q: A triangle has angles (2x)°, (3x)° and (4x)°. Find each angle.
An exterior angle measures 130° and one remote interior angle is 55°. Find the other remote interior angle.

days.guide: Fold an isosceles triangle along its line of symmetry to show base angles match. Then write the proof: draw the bisector of the vertex angle and use SAS to get congruent triangles, so the base angles are congruent by CPCTC.

questions.q: In isosceles △ABC with AB = AC, m∠B = 52°. Find m∠A.

days.guide: Place a triangle at A(0, 0), B(2a, 0), C(2b, 2c). Find the midpoints of AC and BC, then show the segment joining them has slope 0 (parallel to AB) and length a, half of AB.

questions.q: In the coordinate proof, why use 2a, 2b, 2c instead of a, b, c?
questions.a: So the midpoints come out without fractions: midpoints (b, c) and (a + b, c).

questions.q: A midsegment of a triangle is 7.5 cm. How long is the parallel side?
questions.a: 15 cm.

days.guide: Construct medians, angle bisectors and perpendicular bisectors of one triangle each (or in GeoGebra) and locate the centroid, incenter and circumcenter. Balance the cardboard triangle on a pencil at the centroid.

questions.q: Which point of concurrency is the center of the circle that passes through all three vertices?
questions.a: The circumcenter (intersection of the perpendicular bisectors).

questions.q: The centroid divides each median in what ratio?
questions.a: 2:1, with the longer part from the vertex to the centroid.

days.guide: Give the quiz in the assessment key. Allow no notes (formula sheet only if stated); about 30–50 minutes. Grade it together right away: the student reworks every missed item and explains the error aloud, and you note any skill to revisit next week.

questions.q: Where is the circumcenter of a right triangle?
questions.a: At the midpoint of the hypotenuse.

weeks.prep: Print or draw proof templates (two columns, numbered). Make a list of reasons: Given, Reflexive Property, Vertical Angles Theorem, definitions of midpoint/bisector, alternate interior angles, SSS, SAS, ASA, AAS, HL, CPCTC.
misconceptions: Using CPCTC before proving the triangles congruent. CPCTC can only be used after a congruence statement.
Forgetting the shared side (Reflexive Property) or vertical angles in a diagram. Teach the student to mark the diagram with every given, then look for 'free' parts.
weeks.assessment_key: Unit 3 test key: 1) Contrapositive of 'If an angle measures 30°, it is acute' → If an angle is not acute, then it does not measure 30° (true). 2) Lines parallel; alternate interior angles (4x + 6)° and (6x − 20)° → x = 13, 58°. 3) Proof: Given AB ≅ CB and D the midpoint of AC, prove △ABD ≅ △CBD → AD ≅ CD (def. midpoint), BD ≅ BD (Reflexive), SSS. 4) Proof: Given AB ∥ DC and AB ≅ DC (quadrilateral ABCD with diagonal AC), prove △ABC ≅ △CDA → ∠BAC ≅ ∠DCA (alternate interior), AC ≅ CA (Reflexive), SAS. 5) Then prove BC ≅ DA → CPCTC. 6) Which criterion: two angles and a non-included side → AAS; right triangles with congruent hypotenuses and one leg → HL. Proof rubric as in Week 9 (4-point scale).

days.guide: Model one SSS and one SAS proof, marking the diagram with tick marks and arcs first. The student writes the other two, saying the reason for each line aloud.

questions.q: Given: M is the midpoint of AB, and PM ⊥ AB. Prove △PMA ≅ △PMB. Which criterion?
questions.a: SAS: AM ≅ BM (midpoint), ∠PMA ≅ ∠PMB (both right angles), PM ≅ PM (Reflexive).

days.guide: Introduce AAS (it follows from ASA because the third angles match) and HL for right triangles. Show again why SSA fails except in the HL case.

questions.q: Two right triangles have congruent hypotenuses and one pair of congruent legs. Are they congruent? Why?
questions.a: Yes, by HL (Hypotenuse-Leg).

questions.q: Two triangles share two angles and a side that is not between them. Which criterion applies?
questions.a: AAS.

days.guide: Model a proof that ends by proving a segment or angle congruent: first prove the triangles congruent, then write CPCTC. The student does three such proofs.

questions.q: In a proof, AC and BD bisect each other at E. What triangles can be proven congruent and what follows?
questions.a: △AEB ≅ △CED by SAS (bisected segments and vertical angles), so AB ≅ CD by CPCTC (and ∠A ≅ ∠C, which makes AB ∥ CD).

days.guide: Have the student trace the overlapping figure and redraw the two triangles separately, transferring the given marks. Then complete two proofs.

questions.q: Why redraw overlapping triangles separately?
questions.a: To see clearly which sides and angles correspond and which part (often a shared angle or side) belongs to both.

days.guide: Give the Unit 3 test from the assessment key; allow the reasons list but not worked examples. Allow no notes (formula sheet only if stated); about 30–50 minutes. Grade it together right away: the student reworks every missed item and explains the error aloud, and you note any skill to revisit next week.

questions.q: Can you use HL on triangles that are not right triangles?
questions.a: No — HL applies only to right triangles.

weeks.prep: GeoGebra, graph paper. Prepare cut-out quadrilaterals (or GeoGebra files) for the parallelogram tests.
misconceptions: Using (n − 2)·180 for each interior angle rather than the sum. Divide by n for one angle of a regular polygon.
Thinking a quadrilateral with one pair of parallel sides and the other pair congruent must be a parallelogram (an isosceles trapezoid is a counterexample).
weeks.assessment_key: Quiz with answers: 1) Sum of interior angles of a hexagon → 720°. 2) Each interior angle of a regular octagon → 135°; each exterior → 45°. 3) A regular polygon has exterior angles of 24°; number of sides → 15. 4) In parallelogram ABCD, m∠A = 65°; find ∠B, ∠C, ∠D → 115°, 65°, 115°. 5) Diagonals of parallelogram bisect each other; AE = 3x − 2, EC = x + 8 → x = 5, AC = 26. 6) Is a quadrilateral with both pairs of opposite angles congruent a parallelogram? → Yes. 7) Short proof: opposite sides of a parallelogram are congruent (draw diagonal; alternate interior angles; ASA; CPCTC).

days.guide: Have the student split polygons into triangles from one vertex to find the pattern (n − 2)·180°. Then compute interior and exterior angles of regular polygons, noting exterior angles always sum to 360°.

questions.q: Find the interior angle sum of a decagon and one interior angle of a regular decagon.
Each exterior angle of a regular polygon is 30°. How many sides?

days.guide: Draw diagonal AC in parallelogram ABCD. Use the parallel sides to find two pairs of alternate interior angles, AC as a shared side, ASA for congruent triangles, and CPCTC for opposite sides.

questions.q: In parallelogram ABCD, AB = 2x + 3 and CD = 5x − 9. Find AB.
Consecutive angles of a parallelogram are (3y)° and (2y + 30)°. Find y.
questions.a: They are supplementary: 5y + 30 = 180 → y = 30.

days.guide: Prove that the diagonals bisect each other using the triangles formed at the intersection (ASA with alternate interior angles and opposite sides). The student practices algebra problems with diagonals.

questions.q: Diagonals of parallelogram PQRS meet at T. PT = x + 4, TR = 2x − 1. Find PR.

days.guide: List the five tests: both pairs opposite sides parallel; both pairs opposite sides congruent; both pairs opposite angles congruent; diagonals bisect each other; one pair of sides both parallel and congruent. The student decides for several given quadrilaterals and cites the test.

questions.q: Quadrilateral has vertices (0, 0), (4, 1), (5, 4), (1, 3). Is it a parallelogram?
questions.a: Yes: slopes of opposite sides are 1/4 and 1/4, and 3 and 3, so both pairs are parallel ; also the diagonals share the midpoint (2.5, 2).

days.guide: Give the quiz in the assessment key. Allow no notes (formula sheet only if stated); about 30–50 minutes. Grade it together right away: the student reworks every missed item and explains the error aloud, and you note any skill to revisit next week.

questions.q: Must a parallelogram's diagonals be congruent?
questions.a: No — only in a rectangle.

weeks.prep: GeoGebra, paper for a large Venn diagram/hierarchy, colored pencils.
misconceptions: Thinking a square is not a rectangle or rhombus. Use definitions: a square has four right angles (rectangle) and four congruent sides (rhombus).
Thinking kite diagonals bisect each other. Only one diagonal is bisected (the one between the vertices where unequal sides meet); they are perpendicular.
weeks.assessment_key: Quiz with answers: 1) Rectangle diagonals AC = 3x + 4, BD = 5x − 8 → x = 6, each 22. 2) Rhombus with diagonals 10 and 24 → side = √(5² + 12²) = 13. 3) In a rhombus, m∠ABD = 35° where BD is a diagonal → m∠ABC = 70°. 4) Trapezoid bases 10 and 16 → midsegment 13. 5) Kite diagonals → perpendicular, one bisects the other. 6) True/False: every square is a rhombus (T); every rhombus is a square (F); every rectangle is a parallelogram (T); a trapezoid is a parallelogram (F, under the exclusive definition). Hierarchy rubric: 3 = quadrilateral → parallelogram/trapezoid/kite; parallelogram → rectangle and rhombus; square in both; each placement justified by a definition; 2 = one misplacement; 1 = several.

days.guide: Have the student prove rectangle diagonals congruent with SAS (two right angles, opposite sides congruent, shared side). Solve algebra problems using equal diagonals.

questions.q: Rectangle ABCD has diagonal AC = 2x + 6 and BD = 4x − 10. Find x and AC.

days.guide: Prove rhombus diagonals are perpendicular using SSS on the four small triangles, and that they bisect the vertex angles. Practice problems combining the Pythagorean theorem with diagonals.

questions.q: A rhombus has diagonals 12 and 16. Find a side length.
questions.a: Half-diagonals 6 and 8, so side = 10.

questions.q: Why is every square a rhombus?
questions.a: A square has four congruent sides, which is the definition of a rhombus.

days.guide: In GeoGebra, measure a trapezoid's midsegment and compare to the bases; measure the diagonals of a kite. The student writes conjectures.

questions.q: A trapezoid's midsegment is 11 and one base is 8. Find the other base.
Name a property of an isosceles trapezoid's diagonals.
questions.a: They are congruent.

days.guide: Build the hierarchy diagram together, asking 'Is every ___ a ___?' for each link. The student justifies each placement with a definition.

questions.q: Is every rectangle a square? Is every square a rectangle?
questions.a: No; yes.

days.guide: Give the quiz in the assessment key and check the hierarchy diagram. Allow no notes (formula sheet only if stated); about 30–50 minutes. Grade it together right away: the student reworks every missed item and explains the error aloud, and you note any skill to revisit next week.

questions.q: Which quadrilaterals have perpendicular diagonals?
questions.a: Rhombi (including squares) and kites.

weeks.prep: Graph paper, Desmos, calculator. Prepare the Unit 4 test from the assessment key.
misconceptions: Making the perpendicular slope only negative or only reciprocal. Both: slope 2/3 → −3/2.
Using a single property to classify (e.g., 4 equal sides ⇒ square). Students must also show right angles (perpendicular slopes) to prove a square.
weeks.assessment_key: Unit 4 test with answers: 1) Slope of the line through (1, 2) and (4, 8) → 2; perpendicular slope → −1/2. 2) Line parallel to y = 2x + 1 through (3, 4) → y = 2x − 2. 3) Line perpendicular to y = 2x + 1 through (3, 4) → y = −½x + 5.5. 4) Prove A(0, 0), B(4, 0), C(4, 3), D(0, 3) is a rectangle → opposite sides parallel (slopes 0, 0, undefined, undefined) and adjacent sides perpendicular (horizontal and vertical). 5) Classify P(0, 0), Q(3, 4), R(8, 4), S(5, 0) → all sides 5, diagonals PR = √80 and QS = √20 unequal → rhombus, not a square. 6) Area of triangle (0, 0), (6, 0), (2, 5) → 15. 7) Exterior angle of a regular pentagon → 72°. Mastery 80%.

days.guide: Rotate a line 90° in GeoGebra or on graph paper: a slope triangle with run a and rise b becomes run −b and rise a, so m becomes −a/b. Have the student verify with several examples.

questions.q: Line ℓ has slope 3/4. Give the slope of a parallel line and a perpendicular line.
questions.a: Parallel 3/4; perpendicular −4/3.

days.guide: Model writing lines in point-slope form, then converting to slope-intercept. The student writes several and checks with Desmos.

questions.q: Write the line parallel to y = −3x + 2 through (1, 5).
Write the line perpendicular to y = ½x − 4 through (2, 1).

days.guide: Show the checklist: compute all side lengths (distance) and slopes. Rectangle: parallelogram + perpendicular sides; rhombus: 4 equal sides; square: both. The student classifies several quadrilaterals with full justification.

questions.a: Slopes AB = 1/3, BC = −3, CD = 1/3, DA = −3, so adjacent sides are perpendicular; lengths all √10. It is a square.

days.guide: For an irregular polygon, show the 'box' method: draw a rectangle around it and subtract right triangles, or split it into triangles. The student finds areas of three polygons.

questions.q: Find the area of the triangle with vertices (1, 1), (5, 1), (3, 6).
questions.a: Base 4, height 5, area = ½·4·5 = 10.

days.guide: Give the Unit 4 test from the assessment key. Allow no notes (formula sheet only if stated); about 30–50 minutes. Grade it together right away: the student reworks every missed item and explains the error aloud, and you note any skill to revisit next week.

questions.q: How do you show two segments are perpendicular on the coordinate plane?
questions.a: Show their slopes are negative reciprocals (product −1), or one is horizontal and the other vertical.

weeks.prep: Ruler, graph paper, GeoGebra, colored pencils.
misconceptions: Measuring the scale factor from the original vertex to the image vertex instead of from the center. All distances in a dilation are measured from the center.
Applying (kx, ky) when the center is not the origin. Subtract the center, scale, then add the center back.
weeks.assessment_key: Quiz with answers: 1) Dilate (4, −2) by k = ½ about the origin → (2, −1). 2) Dilate (3, 4) by k = 2 about (1, 1) → (5, 7). 3) A segment of length 6 is dilated by k = 1.5 → 9. 4) A dilation maps line y = 2x + 3 (not through the center at origin) by k = 2 → y = 2x + 6, a parallel line. 5) A'(6, 9) is the image of A(2, 3) about the origin; k → 3. 6) Describe a similarity transformation mapping △ABC with A(0, 0), B(2, 0), C(0, 1) to A'(1, 1), B'(5, 1), C'(1, 3) → dilate by 2 about the origin, then translate ⟨1, 1⟩.

days.guide: Choose a center O outside a triangle. The student measures OA, multiplies by 2 (and ½), and marks A' on ray OA; repeat for B and C. Compare side lengths and angles of image and pre-image.

questions.q: If OA = 3 cm and the scale factor is 2, how far is A' from O?
questions.a: 6 cm, on ray OA.

questions.q: Does a dilation preserve angle measure? Side length?
questions.a: Angle measure yes; side lengths are multiplied by k.

days.guide: In GeoGebra dilate a line not through the center and a line through the center. The student observes the first is parallel and the second maps to itself, and lengths scale by k.

questions.q: What happens to a line through the center of dilation?
questions.a: It maps onto itself.

days.guide: Practice the origin rule (kx, ky), then dilations about another center (subtract center, scale, add back).

questions.q: Dilate (−6, 3) by k = 1/3 about the origin.
Dilate (5, 2) by k = 3 about (2, 0).

days.guide: Define similarity as a dilation followed by rigid motions. Given pairs of similar figures, the student finds the scale factor from corresponding sides and then the motions.

questions.q: Two similar triangles have corresponding sides 4 and 10. What is the scale factor from small to large?

days.guide: Give the quiz in the assessment key. Allow no notes (formula sheet only if stated); about 30–50 minutes. Grade it together right away: the student reworks every missed item and explains the error aloud, and you note any skill to revisit next week.

questions.q: If k is between 0 and 1, is the dilation an enlargement or reduction?
questions.a: A reduction.

weeks.prep: Small mirror, tape measure, a sunny day for shadows (Day 3), notebook for lab report. Pick a tree or flagpole outdoors.
misconceptions: Mismatching corresponding sides in proportions. Write the similarity statement first, then set up ratios in the same order.
Thinking SSA works for similarity. Valid criteria: AA, SSS~, SAS~ (with the included angle).
weeks.assessment_key: Quiz with answers: 1) △ABC has angles 50° and 60°; △DEF has 60° and 70°. Similar? → Yes, AA (third angles 70° and 50°). 2) Sides 6, 8, 10 and 9, 12, 15 → similar SSS~, k = 1.5. 3) △ABC ~ △DEF, AB = 8, DE = 12, BC = 10; EF → 15. 4) Sides 4 and 6 with included 40°, and 6 and 9 with included 40° → similar by SAS~. Lab report rubric: 4 = diagram, measurements with units, proportions correctly set up, both methods computed, comparison and error sources discussed; 3 = minor calculation slips; 2 = only one method or missing diagram; 1 = incomplete.

days.guide: Explain: dilate one triangle so a side matches; with two equal angle pairs, the dilated copy is congruent to the other by ASA, so the triangles are similar. The student finds missing sides in AA-similar triangles.

questions.q: Two triangles each have a 35° angle and a 90° angle. Are they similar?
questions.a: Yes, by AA.

days.guide: Model checking SSS~ (all side ratios equal) and SAS~ (two side ratios equal and included angles congruent). The student writes similarity statements in correct order.

questions.q: Are triangles with sides 5, 7, 9 and 10, 14, 17 similar?

days.guide: Mirror method: place a mirror on the ground, step back until you see the treetop, measure eye height and both distances. Shadow method: measure your shadow and the tree's shadow at the same time. Set up proportions for each.

questions.q: Eye height 1.6 m, you stand 2 m from the mirror, the mirror is 10 m from the tree. Tree height?
A 1.8 m person casts a 1.2 m shadow; a tree casts a 6 m shadow. Tree height?

days.guide: Model one similarity proof (e.g., parallel line creating AA through corresponding angles). The student writes a second proof independently.

questions.q: In △ABC, DE ∥ BC with D on AB and E on AC. Why is △ADE ~ △ABC?
questions.a: ∠A is shared and ∠ADE ≅ ∠ABC (corresponding angles), so AA similarity.

days.guide: Give the quiz and collect the lab report; score both with the assessment key. Allow no notes (formula sheet only if stated); about 30–50 minutes. Grade it together right away: the student reworks every missed item and explains the error aloud, and you note any skill to revisit next week.

questions.q: If two triangles are similar with scale factor 3, how do their perimeters compare?
questions.a: The larger perimeter is 3 times the smaller.

weeks.prep: GeoGebra, centimeter cubes or sugar cubes (Day 5), graph paper.
misconceptions: Setting up side-splitter proportions using the whole side in one ratio and a part in the other inconsistently. Use part/part = part/part.
Assuming area scales by k (not k²). Build 2×2×2 cubes from unit cubes to see area ×4 and volume ×8.
weeks.assessment_key: Exit tickets with answers: Day 1) AD = 4, DB = 6, AE = 5, DE ∥ BC → EC = 7.5. Day 2) Angle bisector from A in triangle with AB = 6, AC = 9, BC = 10 → BD = 4, DC = 6. Day 3) Altitude to hypotenuse splits it into 4 and 9 → altitude 6. Day 5) Scale factor 3 → perimeter ×3, area ×9, volume ×27. Proof write-up rubric (Pythagorean theorem via similar triangles): 4 = states the three similar triangles, writes a/c = x/a and b/c = y/b, gets a² = cx and b² = cy, adds to a² + b² = c(x + y) = c²; 3 = one step unjustified; 2 = similarity named but algebra incomplete; 1 = only the statement.

days.guide: Use AA similarity of △ADE and △ABC (DE ∥ BC) to derive AD/DB = AE/EC. The student solves several side-splitter problems.

questions.q: DE ∥ BC, AD = 4, DB = 6, AE = 5. Find EC.

days.guide: State the theorem: an angle bisector divides the opposite side in the same ratio as the adjacent sides. Work examples and have the student check in GeoGebra.

questions.q: In △ABC, AD bisects ∠A, AB = 6, AC = 9, BC = 10. Find BD and DC.

days.guide: Draw the altitude to the hypotenuse and cut out the three triangles to show they are similar. Derive the geometric mean relationships: altitude² = product of hypotenuse segments; each leg² = hypotenuse × adjacent segment.

questions.q: The altitude to the hypotenuse divides it into segments of 4 and 9. Find the altitude.
Hypotenuse 13 is split into 4 and 9 (with 4 adjacent to leg a). Find a.

days.guide: Use the three similar triangles to prove a² + b² = c², then show a dissection (four copies of the triangle inside a square). The student writes the similarity proof.

questions.q: In the similarity proof, the hypotenuse is split into x and y. What does a² + b² equal?
questions.a: cx + cy = c(x + y) = c·c = c².

days.guide: Build cubes of side 1, 2 and 3 from unit cubes; record perimeter of one face, surface area and volume in a table. The student generalizes to k, k², k³.

questions.q: A model car is scaled by 1/20. Its paint area compares how to the real car's?
questions.a: (1/20)² = 1/400 of the real paint area.

weeks.prep: Assemble a review packet (Khan Academy unit tests or CK-12 practice) covering Units 1–5, plus the semester exam described in the assessment key. Have compass, protractor, calculator.
misconceptions: Rushing proofs without marking the diagram. Require marking givens first on every review proof.
Over-relying on memorized rules for rotations without sketching. Encourage a quick sketch to check every coordinate answer.
weeks.assessment_key: Semester 1 exam (sample items, 1 point unless noted): 1) Midpoint of (−2, 8) and (6, 0) → (2, 4). 2) Distance (−1, −1) to (5, 7) → 10. 3) Rotate (3, −4) 90° counterclockwise → (4, 3). 4) Reflect (5, 2) over y = x → (2, 5). 5) Supplement of 3x when x = 25 → 105°. 6) Interior angle of a regular 12-gon → 150°. 7) Rhombus diagonals 10 and 24 → side 13. 8) Line ⊥ to y = −4x + 1 through (0, 3) → y = ¼x + 3. 9) △ABC ~ △DEF, AB = 5, DE = 15, AC = 7 → DF = 21. 10) Shadow problem: 2 m pole, 3 m shadow; building shadow 30 m → 20 m. 11) Proof (4 pts): parallelogram opposite sides congruent. 12) Proof (4 pts): given AB ≅ AD and AC bisects ∠BAD, prove △ABC ≅ △ADC (SAS with reflexive AC). Grade: 90%+ A, 80% B, 70% C.

days.guide: Work mixed transformation and congruence problems; the student works first, and you check each set of 5 before continuing.

questions.q: Rotate (−1, 6) 180° about the origin, then reflect over the x-axis.

days.guide: The student completes four proofs from Units 3–4 with the reasons list; discuss one aloud as if teaching it to you.

questions.q: In parallelogram ABCD, what reason justifies ∠BAC ≅ ∠DCA when AC is a diagonal?
questions.a: AB ∥ DC, so they are alternate interior angles (congruent).

days.guide: Mixed similarity practice including side splitter and indirect measurement problems.

questions.q: A 6-ft person casts a 4-ft shadow when a flagpole casts a 22-ft shadow. How tall is the pole?

days.guide: Give the semester exam (about 90 minutes) from the assessment key. No notes; calculator and tools allowed. Allow no notes (formula sheet only if stated); about 30–50 minutes. Grade it together right away: the student reworks every missed item and explains the error aloud, and you note any skill to revisit next week.

questions.q: (Self-check after exam) Which topic felt hardest, and what's one problem type to review?
questions.a: Answers vary; the student names a specific skill (e.g., overlapping-triangle proofs).

days.guide: Return the graded exam. For each missed item the student writes what went wrong and redoes the problem correctly.

questions.q: What is the difference between a careless error and a concept error?
questions.a: A careless error is a slip (arithmetic, sign) on a skill you know; a concept error is misunderstanding the idea, which needs reteaching.

weeks.prep: Square tiles or graph paper, scientific calculator. Know √2 ≈ 1.414 and √3 ≈ 1.732.
misconceptions: Using a² + b² = c² with c as a leg. The hypotenuse (longest side, opposite the right angle) is always c.
Mixing up the 30-60-90 ratios: the short leg is opposite 30°, the hypotenuse is twice the short leg, the long leg is short leg × √3.
weeks.assessment_key: Quiz with answers: 1) Legs 9 and 12 → hypotenuse 15. 2) Ladder 13 ft, base 5 ft from wall → reaches 12 ft. 3) Classify 6, 8, 11 → 121 > 100 → obtuse. 4) 7, 24, 25 → right. 5) 45-45-90 with leg 5 → hypotenuse 5√2 ≈ 7.07. 6) 45-45-90 with hypotenuse 10 → legs 5√2 ≈ 7.07. 7) 30-60-90 with short leg 4 → long leg 4√3 ≈ 6.93, hypotenuse 8. 8) 30-60-90 with hypotenuse 14 → short leg 7, long leg 7√3 ≈ 12.12.

days.guide: Review the theorem with a tile square-on-each-side model, then solve applied problems: draw a sketch, label the right angle and hypotenuse, write the equation.

questions.q: A 13-ft ladder's base is 5 ft from a wall. How high up the wall does it reach?
A TV screen is 32 in wide and 18 in tall. What is the diagonal?

days.guide: Teach: if c² = a² + b² right; c² > a² + b² obtuse; c² < a² + b² acute (c longest). The student classifies a list of triangles.

questions.q: Classify a triangle with sides 6, 8, 11.
Classify sides 5, 6, 7.

days.guide: Draw a square with side 1 and its diagonal: √(1 + 1) = √2. Generalize to leg x → hypotenuse x√2, and practice both directions.

questions.q: A square has side 8. Find its diagonal.
A 45-45-90 triangle has hypotenuse 6. Find a leg.

days.guide: Cut an equilateral triangle of side 2 in half: short leg 1, hypotenuse 2, long leg √3. Generalize and practice.

questions.q: In a 30-60-90 triangle the long leg is 9. Find the short leg and hypotenuse.
questions.a: Short leg 9/√3 = 3√3 ≈ 5.20; hypotenuse 6√3 ≈ 10.39.

questions.q: Find the height of an equilateral triangle with side 10.

days.guide: Give the quiz in the assessment key. Allow no notes (formula sheet only if stated); about 30–50 minutes. Grade it together right away: the student reworks every missed item and explains the error aloud, and you note any skill to revisit next week.

questions.q: Is a triangle with sides 8, 15, 17 a right triangle?

weeks.prep: Protractor, ruler, scientific calculator set to DEGREE mode (check this first!).
misconceptions: Calculator in radian mode. sin 30 should be 0.5; if it shows −0.988, switch to degrees.
Labeling 'opposite' and 'adjacent' without reference to an angle. They depend on which acute angle you are using.
weeks.assessment_key: Quiz with answers: 1) Right triangle with legs 3 (opposite A) and 4, hypotenuse 5: sin A = 3/5, cos A = 4/5, tan A = 3/4. 2) sin 35° ≈ 0.574, cos 35° ≈ 0.819, tan 35° ≈ 0.700. 3) If sin x = 0.6, what is cos(90° − x)? → 0.6. 4) Solve sin(2x + 10)° = cos(x + 20)° → 3x + 30 = 90, x = 20. 5) Hypotenuse 20, angle 40°, opposite side → 20 sin 40° ≈ 12.86. 6) Adjacent 15, angle 28°, opposite → 15 tan 28° ≈ 7.98. 7) Opposite 7, angle 50°, hypotenuse → 7/sin 50° ≈ 9.14.

days.guide: The student draws three right triangles of different sizes with a 35° angle, measures sides, and computes opposite/hypotenuse, adjacent/hypotenuse, opposite/adjacent. Discuss why the ratios match (AA similarity).

questions.q: Why are the side ratios the same for every right triangle with a 35° angle?
questions.a: All such triangles are similar by AA, so corresponding side ratios are equal.

days.guide: Teach SOH-CAH-TOA, label sides relative to an angle, and check values on the calculator.

questions.q: In right △ABC with right angle C, AC = 12, BC = 5, AB = 13. Find sin A, cos A, tan A.

days.guide: Show that the opposite side of one acute angle is the adjacent side of the other, so sin x = cos(90° − x). Solve equations using this.

questions.q: cos 72° equals the sine of which angle?
questions.a: sin 18°.

questions.q: Solve sin(x + 15)° = cos(2x)°.

days.guide: Model the steps: label, choose the ratio that uses the known side and the unknown, set up an equation, and solve (note when the unknown is in the denominator). The student completes 12 problems.

questions.q: Angle 40°, hypotenuse 20. Find the opposite side.
Angle 55°, adjacent 10. Find the hypotenuse.

days.guide: Give the quiz in the assessment key. Allow no notes (formula sheet only if stated); about 30–50 minutes. Grade it together right away: the student reworks every missed item and explains the error aloud, and you note any skill to revisit next week.

questions.q: Can the sine of an acute angle be greater than 1? Why?
questions.a: No — the opposite side is always shorter than the hypotenuse.

weeks.prep: Clinometer materials: protractor, straw, string, a washer or nut, tape. Tape measure. Pick a building or tree with flat ground in front. Look up ADA ramp rule: maximum slope 1:12.
misconceptions: Forgetting to add eye height in the clinometer lab. The trig calculation gives height above eye level.

Reading the clinometer angle directly when the string shows the complement. Depending on construction, the angle of elevation may be 90° minus the reading; test with a level line (should read 0° elevation).
weeks.assessment_key: Quiz with answers: 1) Opposite 5, adjacent 12 → angle tan⁻¹(5/12) ≈ 22.6°. 2) Solve right triangle with legs 7 and 10 → hypotenuse ≈ 12.21, angles ≈ 35.0° and 55.0°. 3) Angle of elevation 35° from 50 ft away, eye height 5 ft → 50 tan 35° + 5 ≈ 40.0 ft. 4) ADA ramp (1:12) rising 30 in → 360 in = 30 ft run; angle ≈ 4.76°. 5) A ship sails 40 km at bearing that makes 30° east of north; distance east → 40 sin 30° = 20 km. Lab report rubric: 4 = diagram with angle, distance, eye height; correct tan calculation; final height with units; 2+ error sources; 3 = minor slips; 2 = eye height omitted or wrong ratio; 1 = incomplete.

days.guide: Introduce sin⁻¹, cos⁻¹, tan⁻¹ as 'what angle has this ratio?' Model completely solving a right triangle (all sides and angles).

questions.q: Legs 7 and 10. Find the angle opposite the 7.
Hypotenuse 10, one leg 6. Find the angle opposite the 6.

days.guide: Build the clinometer: tape a straw along the protractor's straight edge, hang the weighted string from the center hole. Test: sighting a level line should give 0° elevation. Make a conversion note if the string reads 90°.

questions.q: Your clinometer string reads 60° on the protractor (measured from the straw's side). What is the angle of elevation?
questions.a: 90° − 60° = 30° (for a design where level reads 90°).

days.guide: Outside, the student measures distance to the base, sights the top, records the angle and eye height, and repeats 3 times to average. Compute height = d·tan θ + eye height and write the lab report.

questions.q: Standing 40 ft from a tree with angle of elevation 32° and eye height 5 ft, how tall is the tree?

days.guide: Work ADA ramp problems (1 in rise per 12 in run maximum) and navigation problems using sketches.

questions.q: A porch is 24 inches high. What minimum ramp length (horizontal run) meets ADA?
A plane descends at 3° and is 1,500 ft high. How far horizontally until touchdown?
questions.a: 1500/tan 3° ≈ 28,600 ft (about 5.4 miles).

days.guide: Give the quiz in the assessment key. Allow no notes (formula sheet only if stated); about 30–50 minutes. Grade it together right away: the student reworks every missed item and explains the error aloud, and you note any skill to revisit next week.

questions.q: Which inverse function do you use if you know the opposite and hypotenuse?
questions.a: Inverse sine, sin⁻¹(opposite/hypotenuse).

weeks.prep: Scientific calculator in degree mode; Unit 6 test from the assessment key. Review the formulas: Area = ½ab sin C; a/sin A = b/sin B = c/sin C; c² = a² + b² − 2ab cos C.
misconceptions: Using the Law of Sines for SAS or SSS (it needs an angle-opposite-side pair). Choose Law of Cosines for SAS and SSS.
Missing the second solution in the SSA ambiguous case. If sin B gives angle B, also check 180° − B.
weeks.assessment_key: Unit 6 test with answers: 1) sin 52° ≈ 0.788. 2) Right triangle angle 25°, hypotenuse 30 → opposite ≈ 12.68. 3) Angle of elevation for a 6 ft rise over 20 ft → tan⁻¹(0.3) ≈ 16.7°. 4) Area with a = 8, b = 10, C = 30° → 20. 5) A = 40°, B = 60°, a = 10 → b ≈ 13.47. 6) a = 7, b = 8, C = 60° → c = √57 ≈ 7.55. 7) Sides 5, 7, 8 → angle opposite 7 = 60°. 8) SSA: a = 6, b = 8, A = 30° → sin B = 0.667, B ≈ 41.8° or 138.2° (two triangles). Mastery 80%.

days.guide: Draw an oblique triangle, drop the altitude from B to side b; h = a sin C, so Area = ½ab sin C. The student applies it to several triangles.

questions.q: Find the area of a triangle with sides 8 and 10 and included angle 30°.
Sides 12 and 15 with included 110°. Area?

days.guide: Derive the Law of Sines from two expressions for the same altitude. Solve AAS/ASA problems, then show SSA can give 0, 1, or 2 triangles.

questions.q: a = 6, b = 8, A = 30°. How many triangles?
questions.a: sin B = 8 sin 30°/6 ≈ 0.667 → B ≈ 41.8° or 138.2°; both work (138.2 + 30 < 180), so two triangles.

days.guide: Derive the Law of Cosines by placing C at the origin and using the distance formula (or the altitude). Note it becomes the Pythagorean theorem when C = 90°.

questions.q: a = 7, b = 8, C = 60°. Find c.
Sides 5, 7, 8. Find the angle opposite 7.

days.guide: Give mixed surveying/navigation word problems; the student sketches, identifies given parts (SAS, SSS, ASA, AAS, SSA) and chooses the law.

questions.q: Two hikers leave camp; one walks 3 km, the other 5 km, with 70° between their paths. How far apart are they?

days.guide: Give the Unit 6 test from the assessment key. Allow no notes (formula sheet only if stated); about 30–50 minutes. Grade it together right away: the student reworks every missed item and explains the error aloud, and you note any skill to revisit next week.

questions.q: What does the Law of Cosines reduce to when the angle is 90°?
questions.a: The Pythagorean theorem, since cos 90° = 0.

weeks.prep: Compass, string, several circular objects (cans, plates), ruler, calculator.
misconceptions: Confusing arc measure (degrees) with arc length (distance). Arc measure equals the central angle; arc length depends on the radius.
Naming a major arc with two letters. Major arcs and semicircles need three letters (e.g., arc ACB).
weeks.assessment_key: Quiz with answers: 1) Identify chord, secant, tangent, radius on a diagram (visual check). 2) Central angle 70° → minor arc 70°, major arc 290°. 3) Arcs AB = 80°, BC = 45° adjacent → arc ABC = 125°. 4) Radius 10, chord 6 units from center → chord length 16. 5) Two chords in the same circle are congruent; one's arc is 100° → the other's arc is 100°. 6) Why are all circles similar? → any circle can be translated to share a center with another and dilated by k = r₂/r₁.

days.guide: Take two circles with different centers and radii. Show the translation that moves center to center, then the dilation with k = r₂/r₁. The student writes the argument.

questions.q: Circle A has center (1, 2), radius 3; circle B has center (−4, 0), radius 6. Describe a similarity mapping A to B.
questions.a: Translate by ⟨−5, −2⟩, then dilate about (−4, 0) by scale factor 2.
