days.guide: Label diagrams with chord, diameter, radius, secant, tangent, point of tangency, central angle, minor/major arc, semicircle. Quiz with flash diagrams.

questions.q: What is the difference between a chord and a secant?
questions.a: A chord is a segment with both endpoints on the circle; a secant is a line that intersects the circle at two points.

days.guide: Teach: minor arc = central angle; major arc = 360° − minor; arc addition. The student solves problems including algebraic central angles.

questions.q: Central angles of a circle are 2x, 3x, and 4x (filling the whole circle). Find each.

days.guide: Prove congruent chords have congruent central angles (SSS with radii) and that a radius perpendicular to a chord bisects it (HL). Solve chord-distance problems.

questions.q: A circle has radius 10, and a chord is 6 units from the center. How long is the chord?
questions.a: Half-chord = √(100 − 36) = 8, so chord = 16.

questions.q: A chord of length 24 is 5 units from the center. Find the radius.

days.guide: Give the quiz in the assessment key. Allow no notes (formula sheet only if stated); about 30–50 minutes. Grade it together right away: the student reworks every missed item and explains the error aloud, and you note any skill to revisit next week.

questions.q: A diameter is perpendicular to a chord. What does it do to the chord and its arc?
questions.a: It bisects the chord and its arc.

weeks.prep: GeoGebra, compass, straightedge.
misconceptions: Using the full arc as the inscribed angle measure. Inscribed angle = half the intercepted arc; central angle = the arc.
Forgetting that a tangent meets the radius at 90°, which creates right triangles for the Pythagorean theorem.
weeks.assessment_key: Quiz with answers: 1) Inscribed angle intercepts a 100° arc → 50°. 2) Inscribed angle 34° → arc 68°. 3) An inscribed angle intercepts a semicircle → 90°. 4) Quadrilateral inscribed in a circle, ∠A = 75°, ∠B = 110° → ∠C = 105°, ∠D = 70°. 5) External point P is 13 from center, radius 5 → tangent length 12. 6) Two tangents from P have lengths 2x + 3 and 5x − 9 → x = 4, length 11. Construction check: incircle (bisect two angles, perpendicular from incenter to a side for radius) and circumcircle (perpendicular bisectors of two sides, radius to a vertex), scored 3/2/1 as in Week 2.

days.guide: In GeoGebra, place an inscribed angle and a central angle on the same arc; drag and record. Then prove the case where one side of the inscribed angle is a diameter (isosceles triangle + exterior angle theorem).

questions.q: An inscribed angle intercepts an arc of 140°. What is its measure?
Why is an angle inscribed in a semicircle a right angle?
questions.a: It intercepts a 180° arc, and half of 180° is 90°.

days.guide: Show opposite angles of an inscribed quadrilateral intercept arcs that together make 360°, so the angles sum to 180°.

questions.q: Quadrilateral ABCD is inscribed; m∠A = (2x)°, m∠C = (x + 30)°. Find x.

days.guide: Prove the radius-tangent relationship (shortest distance argument) and the two-tangent theorem (HL on two right triangles). Practice problems.

questions.q: Point P is 13 units from the center of a circle of radius 5. Find the length of a tangent from P.
Two tangent segments from P are 3x + 1 and 7. Find x.

days.guide: Construct the incircle (angle bisectors) and circumcircle (perpendicular bisectors). For a tangent from an external point P: bisect OP to get M, draw a circle centered M through O; where it meets the circle are the tangent points.

questions.q: Why does the tangent construction (circle on diameter OP) work?
questions.a: The tangent point T lies on a circle with diameter OP, so ∠OTP is inscribed in a semicircle and equals 90°, making PT ⊥ OT.

days.guide: Give the quiz and construction check in the assessment key. Allow no notes (formula sheet only if stated); about 30–50 minutes. Grade it together right away: the student reworks every missed item and explains the error aloud, and you note any skill to revisit next week.

questions.q: A central angle and an inscribed angle intercept the same 80° arc. Give each measure.
questions.a: Central 80°; inscribed 40°.

weeks.prep: Paper plates, string, ruler, scissors, calculator. Leave answers in terms of π and as decimals.
misconceptions: Using diameter instead of radius in A = πr². Circle the radius in every problem first.
Mixing degree and radian mode on calculators when converting. Use the factor π/180 explicitly.
weeks.assessment_key: Quiz with answers: 1) Arc length, r = 6, 60° → 2π ≈ 6.28. 2) Arc length r = 10, 3π/4 radians → 7.5π ≈ 23.56. 3) Convert 45° → π/4; 150° → 5π/6; 2 radians → ≈ 114.6°. 4) Sector area r = 10, 72° → 20π ≈ 62.83. 5) 14-inch pizza cut into 8 slices → area per slice 49π/8 ≈ 19.24 in². 6) Sprinkler radius 15 ft rotating through 120° → 75π ≈ 235.6 ft². 7) Segment area: r = 6, 90° → 9π − 18 ≈ 10.27.

days.guide: Have the student cut a plate into 16 sectors and arrange them alternately into a near-parallelogram: base ≈ half the circumference (πr), height ≈ r, so area ≈ πr². Measure circumference with string to check C/d ≈ π.

questions.q: Explain why the rearranged sectors approach a rectangle with area πr².
questions.a: The base is half the circumference (πr) and the height is the radius r, so area = πr·r = πr².

days.guide: Arc length = (θ/360)·2πr. The student solves forward and backward problems.

questions.q: Find the arc length of a 60° arc in a circle of radius 6.
An arc of length 5π has a central angle of 90°. Find the radius.

days.guide: Wrap a string the length of the radius around the plate's edge and mark the angle: that is 1 radian (about 57.3°). Teach conversions with π radians = 180°.

questions.q: Convert 150° to radians.
Convert 3π/2 radians to degrees.

days.guide: Sector area = (θ/360)·πr². Segment area = sector − triangle. Solve pizza and sprinkler problems.

questions.q: A sprinkler sprays 15 ft and turns through 120°. What area does it water?
Find the segment area for a 90° sector of radius 6.
questions.a: Sector 9π minus triangle 18 → 9π − 18 ≈ 10.27.

days.guide: Give the quiz in the assessment key. Allow no notes (formula sheet only if stated); about 30–50 minutes. Grade it together right away: the student reworks every missed item and explains the error aloud, and you note any skill to revisit next week.

questions.q: In radians, what is the arc length formula?
questions.a: s = rθ, with θ in radians.

weeks.prep: Desmos, graph paper. Prepare the Unit 7 test (assessment key).
misconceptions: Sign errors with the center: (x + 3)² means h = −3. Rewrite as (x − (−3))².
Forgetting to add the same constants to both sides when completing the square.
weeks.assessment_key: Unit 7 test with answers: 1) Inscribed angle on a 110° arc → 55°. 2) Tangent from a point 10 from center of radius 6 → 8. 3) Arc length r = 9, 40° → 2π ≈ 6.28. 4) Sector area r = 4, 135° → 6π ≈ 18.85. 5) Equation of circle center (2, −3), radius 5 → (x − 2)² + (y + 3)² = 25. 6) x² + y² − 6x + 4y − 12 = 0 → (x − 3)² + (y + 2)² = 25; center (3, −2), r = 5. 7) Is (6, 2) on that circle? → 9 + 16 = 25, yes. 8) Parabola focus (0, 2), directrix y = −2 → x² = 8y. 9) Convert 225° to radians → 5π/4.

days.guide: Take a point (x, y) on a circle with center (h, k) and radius r; the distance formula squared gives the equation. Practice writing equations and reading center/radius.

questions.q: Write the equation of the circle with center (2, −3) and radius 5.
Give the center and radius of (x + 1)² + (y − 4)² = 49.
questions.a: Center (−1, 4), radius 7.

days.guide: Model completing the square for both x and y terms, adding (b/2)² to both sides. The student converts several equations and checks in Desmos.

questions.q: Find the center and radius of x² + y² − 6x + 4y − 12 = 0.
Find the center and radius of x² + y² + 8x − 9 = 0.
questions.a: (x + 4)² + y² = 25: center (−4, 0), radius 5.

days.guide: Substitute the point into the equation, or compute its distance from the center. The student proves or disproves points on circles, including one with radius √ form.

questions.q: Does (1, √3) lie on the circle centered at the origin with radius 2?
questions.a: 1 + 3 = 4 = 2², so yes.

days.guide: Define a parabola as all points equidistant from a focus and a directrix. Set distance to focus equal to distance to directrix and simplify; graph in Desmos.

questions.q: Find the equation of the parabola with focus (0, 2) and directrix y = −2.
questions.a: x² + (y − 2)² = (y + 2)² → x² = 8y, or y = x²/8.

questions.q: Where is the vertex of that parabola?
questions.a: At (0, 0), halfway between focus and directrix.

days.guide: Give the Unit 7 test from the assessment key. Allow no notes (formula sheet only if stated); about 30–50 minutes. Grade it together right away: the student reworks every missed item and explains the error aloud, and you note any skill to revisit next week.

questions.q: What does r² represent in the circle equation?
questions.a: The square of the radius — the squared distance from every point on the circle to the center.

weeks.prep: Graph paper, tape measure, calculator. For Day 4, choose a room and look up the price per square foot of a flooring option (e.g., laminate around $2–$5/ft²).
misconceptions: Using the slant side instead of the height in parallelogram/triangle area. Height is perpendicular to the base.
Forgetting to subtract cut-outs (or double-counting overlaps) in composite figures.
weeks.assessment_key: Quiz with answers: 1) Trapezoid bases 8 and 12, height 5 → 50. 2) Parallelogram base 9, height 4 → 36. 3) Regular hexagon side 6 → apothem 3√3, area 54√3 ≈ 93.5. 4) Square with a semicircle on one side (side 10) → 100 + 12.5π ≈ 139.3. 5) Rectangle 12 × 8 with a circle of radius 2 removed → 96 − 4π ≈ 83.4. Floor plan rubric: 4 = accurate scaled drawing with measurements, correct area including any irregular parts, waste allowance (~10%), cost with units; 3 = minor calculation error; 2 = missing waste or units, or drawing not to scale; 1 = incomplete.

days.guide: Review derivations: parallelogram = rectangle rearranged; triangle = half a parallelogram; trapezoid = half a parallelogram made of two copies. The student derives each with sketches.

questions.q: Find the area of a trapezoid with bases 8 and 12 and height 5.
A triangle has base 14 and area 63. Find the height.

days.guide: Show area = ½·apothem·perimeter by splitting into n isosceles triangles; find the apothem with trig (a = s / (2 tan(180°/n))).

questions.q: Find the area of a regular hexagon with side 6.
questions.a: Apothem 3√3; perimeter 36; area = ½·3√3·36 = 54√3 ≈ 93.5.

questions.q: Find the area of a regular pentagon with side 10.

days.guide: Split composite shapes into known pieces, adding or subtracting. The student finds areas of 6 figures with circle parts.

questions.q: A 12 × 8 rectangle has a circular hole of radius 2. Find the remaining area.

days.guide: The student measures a room, sketches it to scale, computes area, adds 10% for waste, and prices flooring.

questions.q: A 12 ft × 15 ft room uses flooring at $3.50/ft² with 10% waste. What is the cost?

days.guide: Give the quiz and score the floor plan with the assessment key. Allow no notes (formula sheet only if stated); about 30–50 minutes. Grade it together right away: the student reworks every missed item and explains the error aloud, and you note any skill to revisit next week.

questions.q: What is an apothem?
questions.a: The perpendicular segment from the center of a regular polygon to the midpoint of a side.

weeks.prep: Clay or play dough, dental floss, paper cutouts (rectangle, right triangle, semicircle), tape, pencil, calculator.
misconceptions: Believing a cube's cross sections can only be squares. Slicing at angles gives rectangles, triangles, pentagons and hexagons.
Forgetting the two bases when computing surface area of a prism or cylinder.
weeks.assessment_key: Quiz with answers: 1) Possible cross sections of a cube → square, rectangle, triangle, pentagon, hexagon (and trapezoid/parallelogram). 2) Cylinder cross sections → circle (parallel to base), rectangle (perpendicular through axis), ellipse (slanted). 3) Rotating a rectangle about one side → cylinder; right triangle about a leg → cone; semicircle about its diameter → sphere. 4) SA of a 2 × 3 × 4 prism → 52. 5) SA of a cylinder r = 3, h = 10 → 78π ≈ 245.0. 6) SA of a square pyramid with base 6 and slant height 5 → 36 + 60 = 96. Lab sketches: full credit for labeled sketches of at least 3 cross sections per solid.

days.guide: Sort solids (prism, pyramid, cylinder, cone, sphere) and count faces, edges, vertices. The student sketches a net for a cube, triangular prism, cylinder and square pyramid.

questions.q: How many faces, edges and vertices does a triangular prism have?
questions.a: 5 faces, 9 edges, 6 vertices (F + V − E = 2).

questions.q: What shapes make the net of a cylinder?
questions.a: Two circles and a rectangle.

days.guide: Mold clay cube, cylinder and cone; slice with floss at different angles and sketch each cross section.

questions.q: What cross sections can you get from a cone?
questions.a: Circle (parallel to base), triangle (through the apex vertically), ellipse, and parabola/hyperbola-shaped curves for other angles.

days.guide: Tape paper shapes to a pencil and spin; the student predicts then names each solid of revolution.

questions.q: What solid forms when a right triangle rotates about one leg?
questions.a: A cone.

days.guide: Compute surface area from nets: sum the areas of all faces. Practice prisms, cylinders (2πr² + 2πrh) and pyramids (base + ½·perimeter·slant height).

questions.q: Find the surface area of a cylinder with r = 3 and h = 10.
Find the surface area of a 2 × 3 × 4 rectangular prism.

days.guide: Give the quiz in the assessment key and collect lab sketches. Allow no notes (formula sheet only if stated); about 30–50 minutes. Grade it together right away: the student reworks every missed item and explains the error aloud, and you note any skill to revisit next week.

questions.q: Can a cube have a hexagonal cross section?
questions.a: Yes — a slice through the midpoints of six edges gives a regular hexagon.

weeks.prep: A stack of coins, a paper cone and cylinder with the same base and height (make from cardstock), rice, calculator.
misconceptions: Forgetting the 1/3 for pyramids and cones. Show the rice demo: three cones fill one cylinder.
Using slant height instead of height in cone/pyramid volume.
weeks.assessment_key: Quiz with answers: 1) Cylinder r = 4, h = 10 → 160π ≈ 502.7. 2) Cone r = 4, h = 10 → 160π/3 ≈ 167.6. 3) Square pyramid base 6, height 10 → 120. 4) Sphere r = 3 → 36π ≈ 113.1. 5) Rectangular prism 5 × 4 × 3 → 60. 6) Oblique cylinder r = 2, height 7 → 28π ≈ 88.0 (same as right, by Cavalieri). 7) Ice cream cone r = 3, h = 10 topped with a hemisphere r = 3 → 30π + 18π = 48π ≈ 150.8.

days.guide: Stack coins straight, then push the stack slanted. The student explains why the volume stays the same: every cross section has the same area at each height (Cavalieri's principle).

questions.q: Why does a slanted stack of coins have the same volume as a straight stack?
questions.a: Each layer has the same area at each height, so by Cavalieri's principle the volumes are equal.

days.guide: Volume = base area × height for prisms and cylinders (right or oblique, using perpendicular height).

questions.q: Find the volume of a cylinder with r = 4 and h = 10.
A triangular prism has a base triangle with legs 3 and 4 and length 10. Volume?

days.guide: Fill the paper cone with rice and pour into the cylinder; it takes three cones. Generalize V = ⅓Bh.

questions.q: Find the volume of a cone with radius 3 and height 8.
Find the volume of a square pyramid with base edge 6 and height 10.

days.guide: Introduce V = (4/3)πr³ and composite solids (cone + hemisphere, cylinder + hemispheres).

questions.q: Find the volume of a sphere with radius 3.
A basketball has diameter 9.4 in. Find its volume.

days.guide: Give the quiz in the assessment key. Allow no notes (formula sheet only if stated); about 30–50 minutes. Grade it together right away: the student reworks every missed item and explains the error aloud, and you note any skill to revisit next week.

questions.q: If a sphere's radius doubles, what happens to its volume?
questions.a: It multiplies by 2³ = 8.

weeks.prep: Kitchen scale (grams), measuring cup, household objects (a rock, a metal spoon, a wood block), calculator. Look up a few CA county populations and areas (census.gov or Wikipedia). Prepare the Unit 8 test.
misconceptions: Inverting the density ratio. Density = mass/volume (or people/area): 'per' means divide by the unit after 'per'.
Mixing units (mL vs cm³ — they are equal; L vs cm³ — 1 L = 1000 cm³).
weeks.assessment_key: Unit 8 test with answers: 1) 5,000 people in 20 km² → 250 people/km². 2) Object with mass 270 g and volume 100 cm³ → 2.7 g/cm³. 3) Volume of a cylinder r = 5, h = 12 → 300π ≈ 942.5. 4) Sphere r = 6 → 288π ≈ 904.8. 5) Composite area: 10 × 6 rectangle with a semicircle of diameter 6 on one end → 60 + 4.5π ≈ 74.1. 6) Cross section of a cylinder sliced parallel to the base → circle. 7) A 355 mL can with r = 3.84 cm → h ≈ 7.67 cm. Design project rubric: 4 = volume equation set to 355 cm³, SA expressed in r, minimum found (table, graph or h = 2r) at r ≈ 3.84 cm, h ≈ 7.67 cm, SA ≈ 278 cm², labeled drawing and comparison to a real can; 3 = correct minimum with minor gaps; 2 = only trial values without conclusion; 1 = incomplete.

days.guide: Explain density as 'amount per unit.' Compute population density of a few CA counties and a BTU-per-cubic-foot heating problem (e.g., a room needs about 5 BTU per ft³ — use the given value from the problem).

questions.q: Los Angeles County has about 9.7 million people in about 4,060 square miles. Population density?
questions.a: ≈ 2,390 people per square mile.

questions.q: A room 12 × 15 × 8 ft needs 5 BTU per cubic foot. How many BTU?

days.guide: Weigh each object, find volume by water displacement in the measuring cup (1 mL = 1 cm³), and compute density. Compare to known values (water 1 g/cm³, aluminum 2.7).

questions.q: A rock has mass 150 g and raises the water level 60 mL. What is its density?
Will an object with density 0.8 g/cm³ float in water?
questions.a: Yes — it is less dense than water (1 g/cm³).

days.guide: Set up V = πr²h = 355 cm³, write h = 355/(πr²), and SA = 2πr² + 2πrh = 2πr² + 710/r. The student builds a table or uses Desmos to find the minimum.

questions.q: For a 355 mL can, what radius minimizes surface area?
questions.a: About 3.84 cm (height ≈ 7.67 cm, where h = 2r), SA ≈ 278 cm².

questions.q: Why don't real soda cans use this shape?
questions.a: Real cans (r ≈ 3.3 cm, h ≈ 12.2 cm) are taller for grip, stacking, thicker top/bottom metal, and fitting machines and cupholders.

days.guide: The student writes up the design with a labeled drawing, the table/graph, and the final dimensions and comparison.

questions.q: What should a design write-up include?
questions.a: The problem, equations, method (table/graph), final dimensions with units, a drawing, and a comparison to a real can.

days.guide: Give the Unit 8 test from the assessment key. Allow no notes (formula sheet only if stated); about 30–50 minutes. Grade it together right away: the student reworks every missed item and explains the error aloud, and you note any skill to revisit next week.

questions.q: Why is a cylinder with h = 2r the most efficient?
questions.a: For a fixed volume, that shape gives the smallest surface area (it is closest to a sphere-like proportion for a cylinder).

weeks.prep: Two dice, coins, a standard 52-card deck. Remind yourself: a deck has 4 suits × 13 ranks; 12 face cards.
misconceptions: Counting a sum like 7 as one outcome instead of 6 ordered pairs. Use the 6 × 6 table.
Adding probabilities of overlapping events without subtracting the overlap.
weeks.assessment_key: Quiz with answers: 1) Sample space for flipping 3 coins → 8 outcomes (HHH, HHT, HTH, HTT, THH, THT, TTH, TTT). 2) P(sum of 7 with two dice) → 6/36 = 1/6. 3) P(sum of 8) → 5/36. 4) P(heart or king) → 16/52 = 4/13. 5) P(not a face card) → 40/52 = 10/13. 6) In a Venn diagram, A ∩ B means → outcomes in both A and B; A ∪ B → in A or B or both; Aᶜ → not in A.

days.guide: Make a tree for 3 coin flips and a 6 × 6 table for two dice. The student counts outcomes for several events.

questions.q: How many outcomes for rolling two dice? How many give a sum of 7?
P(at least one head in 2 coin flips)?

days.guide: Draw Venn diagrams for events from one die roll (A = even, B = greater than 3). Name union, intersection and complement.

questions.q: Roll a die: A = even {2, 4, 6}, B = greater than 3 {4, 5, 6}. Find A ∩ B and A ∪ B.

days.guide: Derive the addition rule from the Venn diagram (overlap counted twice). The student solves card and die problems.

questions.q: P(heart or king) from a standard deck?
P(even or greater than 3) on one die?

days.guide: Roll two dice 100 times and tally sums. Compare experimental frequencies to the theoretical (e.g., P(7) = 1/6 ≈ 16.7%).

questions.q: Why might the experimental results differ from theoretical probability?
questions.a: Random variation; with more trials the experimental frequencies tend to get closer (Law of Large Numbers).

days.guide: Give the quiz in the assessment key. Allow no notes (formula sheet only if stated); about 30–50 minutes. Grade it together right away: the student reworks every missed item and explains the error aloud, and you note any skill to revisit next week.

questions.q: Are 'rolling an even number' and 'rolling a 5' mutually exclusive?
questions.a: Yes — they cannot both happen, so P(even or 5) = 3/6 + 1/6 = 2/3.

weeks.prep: Deck of cards, coins. Prepare a simple medical-testing example (numbers in the guide).
misconceptions: Confusing P(A|B) and P(B|A). Say it in words: 'probability of A given that B happened' and identify which group you restrict to.
Treating draws without replacement as independent.
weeks.assessment_key: Quiz with answers: 1) P(heads and rolling a 6) → 1/12. 2) Are 'draw a heart' and 'draw a king' independent? → P(heart and king) = 1/52 = (1/4)(1/13), yes. 3) P(king | face card) → 4/12 = 1/3. 4) P(two aces without replacement) → 4/52 · 3/51 = 1/221. 5) P(two aces with replacement) → 1/169. 6) A test is 99% accurate for a disease that 1% have; among 10,000 people, 99 true positives and 99 false positives → P(disease | positive) = 50%.

days.guide: Define independence: P(A and B) = P(A)·P(B). Test with coin/die and with card events.

questions.q: P(heads on a coin and a 6 on a die)?
Are 'draw a red card' and 'draw a face card' independent?
questions.a: P(red and face) = 6/52 = 3/26; P(red)·P(face) = 1/2·12/52 = 6/52. Equal, so yes.

days.guide: Model P(A|B) = P(A and B)/P(B) as restricting the sample space to B. Use the card deck.

questions.q: P(king | face card)?
questions.a: There are 12 face cards and 4 are kings: 4/12 = 1/3.

questions.q: P(heart | red card)?

days.guide: Work through: disease rate 1%, test catches 99% of sick people and wrongly flags 1% of healthy people. Of 10,000 people: 100 sick (99 test positive), 9,900 healthy (99 test positive). P(sick | positive) = 99/198 = 50%. Discuss weather forecasts similarly.

questions.q: In the example, why is P(sick | positive) only 50% even though the test is 99% accurate?
questions.a: The disease is rare, so false positives from the large healthy group equal the true positives.

days.guide: Draw cards without replacement and compute multi-step probabilities, adjusting counts after each draw.

questions.q: P(drawing two hearts in a row without replacement)?
P(drawing a king then a queen without replacement)?

days.guide: Give the quiz in the assessment key. Allow no notes (formula sheet only if stated); about 30–50 minutes. Grade it together right away: the student reworks every missed item and explains the error aloud, and you note any skill to revisit next week.

questions.q: If P(A|B) = P(A), what can you conclude?
questions.a: A and B are independent.

weeks.prep: Spreadsheet software; plan two yes/no survey questions with the student (e.g., 'Do you have a pet?' and 'Do you live in a house?'). Arrange to survey 20 people (family, friends, co-op).
misconceptions: Dividing by the grand total when a conditional probability needs the row or column total.
Concluding cause and effect from an association in a two-way table.
weeks.assessment_key: Quiz uses this table (100 students): Sports & Music 12, Sports & No music 28, No sports & Music 18, No sports & No music 42. Answers: 1) P(music) → 30/100 = 0.30. 2) P(sports and music) → 0.12. 3) P(music | sports) → 12/40 = 0.30. 4) P(sports | music) → 12/30 = 0.40. 5) Are sports and music independent? → yes, P(music | sports) = P(music) = 0.30. 6) Marginal relative frequency of sports → 0.40. Report rubric: 4 = clean table with totals, joint/marginal/conditional values, a correct independence test, a conclusion with limitations (small sample, not random); 3 = minor errors; 2 = table only with little analysis; 1 = incomplete.

days.guide: Build the sample table from the assessment key with row and column totals. The student computes joint (cell/grand total) and marginal (total/grand total) relative frequencies.

questions.q: Using the sports/music table, what is the joint relative frequency of 'no sports and no music'?
What is the marginal relative frequency of music?

days.guide: The student surveys 20 people and organizes the results in a two-way table in a spreadsheet with totals.

questions.q: Why should both questions be yes/no or categorical?
questions.a: Two-way tables organize categorical data; each person falls into exactly one cell.

days.guide: Compute conditional probabilities by row and column, then compare P(A|B) to P(A) to test independence.

questions.q: From the sample table, P(sports | music)?
Is P(sports | music) equal to P(sports)? What does that mean?
questions.a: Yes, both 0.40, so playing sports and liking music are independent in this data.

days.guide: The student writes a one-page report: question, table, key probabilities, independence conclusion, and limitations.

questions.q: Name a limitation of a 20-person survey of friends and family.
questions.a: Small, non-random sample; results may not represent a larger population.

days.guide: Give the quiz in the assessment key and score the report. Allow no notes (formula sheet only if stated); about 30–50 minutes. Grade it together right away: the student reworks every missed item and explains the error aloud, and you note any skill to revisit next week.

questions.q: What does a conditional relative frequency compare?
questions.a: The count in a cell to the total of its row (or column), i.e., the frequency within one group.

weeks.prep: Calculator with nPr/nCr (or use the formulas). Prepare the Unit 9 test from the assessment key.
misconceptions: Using permutations when order doesn't matter (committees, lottery picks).
Forgetting to update counts in multi-stage problems without replacement.
weeks.assessment_key: Unit 9 test with answers: 1) P(two red marbles without replacement from 5 red, 3 blue) → 5/8 · 4/7 = 5/14. 2) 4-digit PIN with repetition → 10,000; without repetition → 5,040. 3) Gold/silver/bronze among 8 runners → 8P3 = 336. 4) Choose 3 toppings from 10 → 10C3 = 120. 5) Lottery choose 6 of 49 → 1/13,983,816. 6) P(A or B), P(A) = 0.5, P(B) = 0.4, P(A and B) = 0.2 → 0.7. 7) Game: roll a die; win $5 on a 6, lose $1 otherwise → expected value 0, fair. 8) P(king | face card) → 1/3.

days.guide: Teach P(A and B) = P(A)·P(B|A) with tree diagrams for multi-stage problems.

questions.q: A bag has 5 red and 3 blue marbles. P(two reds without replacement)?
P(first red then blue without replacement)?

days.guide: Introduce the counting principle and nPr = n!/(n − r)! for arrangements where order matters.

questions.q: How many ways can 8 runners finish 1st, 2nd and 3rd?
How many 4-digit PINs with no repeated digits?

days.guide: Show nCr = n!/(r!(n − r)!) divides out the orderings. Compute lottery odds.

questions.q: How many ways to choose 2 people from 5 for a committee?
Probability of winning a 6-of-49 lottery with one ticket?

days.guide: Compute expected value to decide fairness. Discuss product-testing decisions (e.g., sampling items to estimate defect rates).

questions.q: A game costs $1; roll a die and win $5 (plus your dollar back) on a 6. Is it fair?
questions.a: Expected value = (1/6)(5) + (5/6)(−1) = 0, so it is fair.

questions.q: Two players pick who goes first by flipping two coins: A wins if they match, B if they differ. Fair?
questions.a: Yes: P(match) = 2/4 = P(differ).

days.guide: Give the Unit 9 test from the assessment key. Allow no notes (formula sheet only if stated); about 30–50 minutes. Grade it together right away: the student reworks every missed item and explains the error aloud, and you note any skill to revisit next week.

questions.q: When do you use combinations instead of permutations?
questions.a: When order does not matter (selections, groups).

weeks.prep: Assemble a cumulative review packet (one page per strand) and a practice final mirroring the final exam structure. Calculator, compass, protractor.
misconceptions: Relying on memory for formulas without knowing when they apply. Have the student build a one-page formula sheet with a sample problem for each.
Skipping diagrams on word problems. Require a labeled sketch.
weeks.assessment_key: Practice final (sample items with answers): 1) Reflect (2, −7) over the y-axis → (−2, −7). 2) Rhombus diagonals 6 and 8 → side 5. 3) △ABC ~ △DEF, k = 3, perimeter of △ABC 12 → △DEF perimeter 36. 4) Right triangle angle 30°, hypotenuse 18 → opposite 9. 5) Inscribed angle 40° → arc 80°. 6) Circle x² + y² − 10y = 0 → center (0, 5), r = 5. 7) Cone r = 6, h = 4 → 48π ≈ 150.8. 8) P(sum 9 with 2 dice) → 4/36 = 1/9. 9) 6C2 → 15. 10) Proof: base angles of an isosceles triangle are congruent. Grade: 90/80/70 cutoffs; use results to plan Week 36 review.

days.guide: Mixed review of transformations, congruence and proof. The student works problems and one proof; check after each set.

questions.q: Rotate (4, 1) 90° counterclockwise about the origin.

days.guide: Mixed review of similarity and trigonometry: give 8–10 problems (similar-triangle proportions, special right triangles, SOH-CAH-TOA, Law of Sines/Cosines). The student works one set of five, you check, then they do the next set; any miss sends them back to their notes for that problem type.

questions.q: A 30-60-90 triangle has hypotenuse 12. Find both legs.
In right △ABC, angle A = 28°, adjacent side 15. Find the opposite side.

days.guide: Mixed review of circles and coordinate geometry: arcs and inscribed angles, tangents, arc length and sectors, circle equations by completing the square, and slope/distance proofs. The student works in sets of five with a check after each set and adds any formula they forgot to their one-page formula sheet.

questions.q: Find the center and radius of x² + y² + 4x − 2y − 4 = 0.
questions.a: (x + 2)² + (y − 1)² = 9: center (−2, 1), radius 3.

days.guide: Mixed review of area, volume and probability: composite areas, surface area and volume of solids, the addition and multiplication rules, conditional probability and counting. The student works in sets of five; for each miss, they write the correct formula and redo a similar problem.

questions.q: Find the volume of a sphere with diameter 10.
P(drawing a red card or an ace)?

days.guide: Give the full practice final in the assessment key under timed conditions; grade it together. Allow no notes (formula sheet only if stated); about 30–50 minutes. Grade it together right away: the student reworks every missed item and explains the error aloud, and you note any skill to revisit next week.

questions.q: Which three topics had the most errors?
questions.a: Answers vary; the student lists them to guide Week 36 targeted review.

weeks.prep: Prepare the two-part final exam (assessment key). Have the student's error log from the practice final.
misconceptions: Cramming new methods the day before the exam. Focus on the error log topics.
Not checking answers for reasonableness (e.g., a leg longer than the hypotenuse).
weeks.assessment_key: Final exam (sample items with answers). Part 1: 1) Distance (−3, 4) to (3, −4) → 10. 2) Reflect (1, 5) over y = −x → (−5, −1). 3) Interior angle sum of a 9-gon → 1260°. 4) Proof: SAS congruence with a shared side. 5) Dilate (6, −3) by ⅓ → (2, −1). 6) Side splitter: 6/9 = 8/x → x = 12. Part 2: 7) sin⁻¹(0.5) → 30°. 8) Law of Cosines a = 5, b = 6, C = 50° → c ≈ 4.74. 9) Tangent from point 17 from center, radius 8 → 15. 10) Arc length r = 12, 150° → 10π ≈ 31.4. 11) Cylinder r = 3, h = 7 → 63π ≈ 197.9. 12) P(two kings without replacement) → 1/221. 13) 7P2 → 42. Grade cutoffs 90/80/70. Reflection rubric (Day 5): 3 = explains a specific proof's logic accurately and names a career with a concrete geometry use; 2 = general; 1 = minimal.

days.guide: The student reworks the problem types missed on the practice final, explaining each aloud.

questions.q: What is the most common mistake you made on the practice final, and how will you prevent it?
questions.a: Answers vary; a good answer names a specific error (e.g., degree/radian mode) and a check (e.g., test sin 30 = 0.5).

days.guide: Give Part 1 of the final (transformations through similarity) — about 60 minutes.

questions.q: (After) Dilate (6, −3) by ⅓ about the origin.

days.guide: Give Part 2 (trig, circles, volume, probability) — about 60 minutes.

questions.q: (After) Find the length of a tangent from a point 17 units from the center of a circle with radius 8.

days.guide: Return the exam; the student corrects every error and writes the reason for each.

questions.q: Why write a reason for each correction rather than just the right answer?
questions.a: Explaining the error builds understanding and helps avoid repeating it.

days.guide: The student writes a one-page reflection on a favorite proof and a career that uses geometry (architect, surveyor, game designer, nurse calculating dosages in volumes, etc.).

questions.q: Give one specific way a surveyor uses geometry.
questions.a: Using the Law of Sines/Cosines or trig to find distances and property boundaries that can't be measured directly.
